content.value: As told by Elder Gubi-Goni, the Storyshell of Mossrock Shoals

Sit with me here beneath the shrine gate where the vines have learned to hum. Let me tell you a story—not of war or empire, not of heroes carved in stone—but of breath. Of earth that listens. Of a place that carries memory in its soil the way some carry regrets in their bones.
Let me tell you of Yurei-tu-Shima.
Breathe in. Let the story begin.

The island does not appear on maps. Not real ones. Not the kind written by sailors and stamped in salt. It cannot be summoned with starlight or compass or command. It simply is. Nestled within the soft folds of the Weeping Horizon, a ring of pearlescent mist that circles the island like an old friend’s arms.

Some believe Yurei-tu-Shima walks the ocean floor like a turtle with dreams for feet. Others say it tore away from a continent in the age of storms and now floats between the realm of what was and what is meant to be. Whatever its path, it moves not just through sea, but through meaning.
And those who come? None leave unchanged.
This is not a land of quests.
This is a place of questions.
A wilted blossom. A cracked charm. A word spoken to the wrong spirit at the right time. These are the threads that lead you deeper. These are the truths that open the door.
Kaima once whispered in the Whispergrove, while the wind was quiet and the lanterns were still:
“The island doesn’t need saving. It needs remembering.”
And you are already part of it.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA

content.value: Ahhh… now you’re ready to listen for the second breath. The breath beneath the breath. The one that stirs the edge of the flame, and turns the tide without touching the shore. Sit with me a little longer, and I’ll speak of the layers—because nothing on Yurei-tu-Shima is ever only what it seems. A leaf is a message. A breeze is a gesture. A silence might be someone else’s echo. And the world… the world is more than it pretends to be.

“The world is layered, like a song with many harmonies. Most only hear the melody.” That’s what Eluin once told me, a wayfarer with stars in their bones. I believe them. Because here on the island, nothing is truly alone. Everything hums in twos. In threads. In folds.

Yurei-tu-Shima is not one world. It is two realms, nestled like lovers in a dream—what we call the Physical Realm and the Spirit Realm, though truthfully, those names are for comfort more than clarity. The lines between them blur like morning fog. They touch and fold and drift. Sometimes the edges glow. Sometimes they ache.
Sometimes, when the bell tolls twice instead of once, I know we’re not alone on this side anymore.

On most days, this entanglement is simply life. No one fusses. Most Shimajimans grow up with a foot in each realm without even knowing it. A knock with no knocker? A bird that sings someone else’s lullaby? A lantern that flickers in rhythm with your heartbeat? You shrug, you bow, you say thank you. Just part of the rhythm. Like tea, or sudden rain.
We do not fear the Spirit Realm. We do not worship it.
Shrines are not altars. They are acknowledgments. A thank you. A soft knock on a door we don’t dare open, but wish to be polite toward.
You cannot conquer the Spirit Realm. You cannot map it, or bind it, or force it to obey.
You can only walk it with grace.
As Kokoro-no-Kami told me once, while the fog rose between us and the tea cooled untouched,
“It is not another world. It is this one, unbuttoned.”

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA

content.value: “The island does not ask you what you are. It asks how you listen,” said Kaima once, whispering through the reeds near Whispergrove. And I, old Gubi-Goni, I believe her. You see, Yurei-tu-Shima isn’t a patchwork of tribes or clashing banners. It’s a song, played by many instruments. Not all are in tune, no—but all have something worth hearing. We don’t speak much of races or species here. We say kinship. Because you are not merely what bore you, but what holds you, shapes you, whispers to you when the stars blink.
And if you listen close, you’ll hear the breaths of every kinship still woven through the trees, the caves, the coral, the mist. So sit your shell down, light your lantern, and I’ll tell you of them.

That’s us, little listener. That’s the chorus of the island. You might meet only a few of us in your lifetime, or all of us in one day. But remember: kinship is not just what you are. It is how you listen. It is what you carry. It is who waits when you sleep, who sings when you breathe, and who walks beside you unseen.
Now… shall I tell you about the spirits next? Or would you rather hear a tale about the frog who kissed a typhoon
Elves were not born elves, not truly. Not in the

No, they began like any other broth from the womb—soft, wide-eyed, full of potential. And then the spirit realm saw them. Any kinship can birth them, and no matter the heritage, they always appear as one of the elves because of the magic of the marks. They receive what we call a Yonda Sigil—a glowing birthmark gifted by an elder spirit, radiant as starlight or wild as a forest wind. That sigil changes them, not just in body but in path. They begin to shimmer with magic, empathy, or mystery. And yes, they can still bear children, though their offspring may or may not carry the mark. The blood remembers, but the spirit chooses. To be clear, as clear as mystery can allow, there are elves without marks mixed of heritage. And they are no less beautiful or worthwhile to the island than any other.

We know of seven lineages shaped by these marks: Sea, Wood, High, Eladrin, Dark, Dusk, and Astral. Each walks a different thread through the world. The Eladrin, ah—they change with the seasons like a spirit-flower. Sea Elves, they hear coral speak. Dark Elves? They walk where others fear to peer.
Rin of the Hollow Shrine once said, “It’s not that we’re holier. We just listen louder.” And I think she was right.

category.en-US: KINSHIPS AND SPIRIT-TOUCHED

content.value: My own people. You might see a frog-faced fellow in a raincoat, a fox-tailed dancer, or a crane-feathered healer and think them unrelated. But we are all Kemari. Born of Queen Okumi’s breath when she cracked from her starlit egg, our kind remembers the shape of beasts and the warmth of story. We are cat and crane, frog and bear, hare and snake, boar and bird. But we are also family.

Our elders say, “We don’t have kings anymore. We have kitchens, and whoever’s cooking is in charge.” That’s how it is. We sing to remember. We wear what feels good. Some of us sleep in hollow mushrooms, some in ruins wrapped in vines, and some roam with the mist.

We are not one shape. We are many. We are bear and fox, frog and owl, hare and deer, lizard and mole and badger and crane. We are beastfolk, yes, but more than that—we are reminders. That the wild still walks beside the world.

We live where the land still hums with spirit-song. In burrows tucked beneath shrines, in treetop hammocks swaying over mist-pools, in drifting reed rafts and lantern-lit marsh huts. We trade in stories, in fish, in laughter. We make music with our paws and healing with our breath. We dance when the fire’s low. We remember when others forget.
Our ears hear what was not said. Our noses know when storms are coming. And our hearts? Mmm… they’re soft, yes—but sharp, too. We are kind, not foolish. We are silly, not small.
Some call us simple. Let them. We know better.

I once saw an old crane-woman—Grandmother Fushin—spend three hours convincing a spirit not to haunt a bridge, just by offering it soup and listening. And I saw a toad-boy with warts full of truth spit ink into a scroll that stopped a war. We don’t carry swords, most of us.
But we carry sense. And songs. And snacks.
We speak with spirits not because we know how—
—but because we remember how to listen.
We are the paws in the mud, the claws in the bark, the laughter in the mist.
And when the forest grows quiet,
and the spirits forget their names—
we will be there, kettle boiling, tail twitching, ready to say,

title.en-US: The Kaido, Carried by the Elements

content.value: The Kaido are born of storm, flame, stone, and sea—not just metaphorically, but truly.
Originally, it is believed that they

came from the Jinkaido, the great elemental spirits who helped shape this land. Fire Kaido laugh and spark, full of motion and mischief. Water Kaido are deep listeners, still as lakes in the morning. Air Kaido never stop moving, and Earth Kaido plant their thoughts like trees.

Kaido don’t gather in towns. They drift to places of resonance—volcano rims, wind-swept cliffs, geysers. Some say the wind taught them its name. One Kaido once told me, “The wind taught me its name, and now it won’t stop talking.” That’s the kind of thing they say—half poem, half truth.

category.en-US: KINSHIPS AND SPIRIT-TOUCHED

title.en-US: The Ryūkajin, Breath of the World

content.value: Now these kin—ah, they are older than even I remember. Born of Dravanyr, the Breath Unending, the Ryūkajin carry the soul of balance in their lungs. They’re scaled like dragons, yes, and taller than most, but don’t let that fool you—they speak with breath, not teeth.
There are three great families among them.
Chromatic Ryūkajin breathe raw emotion. The red ones burn, the blue ones storm, the green ones whisper poisons and secrets.
Metallic Ryūkajin are calm winds and steady hearts—golden with wisdom, silver with laughter, bronze with stormlight.
Then come the Gem Ryūkajin. Rare, glittering as morning frost. They breathe dreams, thoughts, truth itself. A topaz Ryūkajin once sang to the dawn and the tide bowed back.
Tenshiko, a Breath Seer of theirs, once said, “Breath is memory. Inhale the world. Exhale what you are becoming.” And that’s why they sing when they fight—because it’s not just war. It’s remembering.

category.en-US: KINSHIPS AND SPIRIT-TOUCHED

title.en-US: The Kibashime, Keepers of the Ember

content.value: Ah, the ash-walkers. With fire beneath their eyes and tusks marked with clan-marks, the Kibashime walk the island with the patience of embers. Born from ancient fire pacts, they are flames that do not consume. Their forges are not just places of craft, but of prayer.

Yuro, one of their horizon-guardians, once said, “We do not fear the flame. We carry it.” And so they do—through chants, fire-dances, and even silence. If you meet one in the wild, bow your head. Not in fear, but in respect.

They are not monsters. Never were. They are the tall-shouldered folk of the island—the ones shaped like cliffs, like ancient statues wrapped in muscle and meaning. The world once feared them, yes. Called them brutes, beasts, breakers. But those who know… know better.

The Kibashime do not speak of their strength. They use it. To lift fallen trees. To carry elders across rivers. To shield those too small to stand. And when they are angry—truly angry—it is not loud. It is focused. Sharp as a carving blade. Heavy as judgment.

Their skin is the hue of earth and toil—deep bronze, dusk-red, or sun-scoured gray. Some grow tusks, some don’t. Many wear body-paint, carved bone, or spirit-chains passed down by ancestor-shamans. Their hair is often kept high and tight, or bound in heavy braids laced with iron or obsidian. And their eyes? Mmm… their eyes are tired—but watchful. Always.

I knew one, long ago—Kuro of the Hollow Beam, who built homes for strangers without ever asking names. He wept when the wind tore a village roof, not because of the damage… but because the spirits warned him too late. He prayed for wind forgiveness that night. And the next day, the wind was still.

Kibashime are not always trusted, even now. Some flinch when they approach. Some whisper old stories that should have died long ago. But the wise? The wise offer them food, not fear. For a Kibashime who chooses peace could have chosen anything else.
They are not gentle because they must be.
They are gentle because they choose to be.
And when the island groans, when the stone splits, when the need is too heavy for any one soul to bear—
—you will find the Kibashime already holding it.

category.en-US: KINSHIPS AND SPIRIT-TOUCHED

title.en-US: The Kyoshijin, Heirs of Sky and Stone

content.value: You’ll know them when the clouds bend and the ground rumbles. The Kyoshijin are descendants of the first giants (kyoshi)—split into six clades by Jin magic: Hill, Storm, Frost, Fire, Cloud, and Stone. Each bears the echo of the element they sprung from.

They live high in mountain holds, atop thunderous cliffs, or in drifting sky-villages shaped by cloud. They do not rush. They wait, and the world moves to them. Rakka, one of their cairn-builders, told me, “You don’t walk the mountain. You become it, slowly.” And I have never heard a truer thing.

category.en-US: KINSHIPS AND SPIRIT-TOUCHED

title.en-US: The Kojin, Whisperers of the Weird

content.value: Don’t blink or you’ll miss them. The Kojin are small, often barefoot, and utterly wild in the heart. Not beastfolk, not elves, not fey—but something in between. Some say they were born from a dryad’s dream or a laughing storm.

They are small, yes—no taller than a stout root barrel or a wind-bent shrub—but do not mistake that for fragility. The Kojin are tough as pinecones, clever as raccoons, and twice as nimble. They are the ones who slip through cracks in the world, not to hide—but to help. To fix. To find what others overlook.

Their faces are round and sun-kissed, with wide eyes full of questions and cheeks full of crumbs. Their feet are often bare, toughened by moss and stone, and they move through forests like they belong there—which, of course, they do. They wear patchwork coats, tool-laden belts, spirit-charms made from bent spoons or carved seedpods. Each one is a walking tale, stitched together with laughter, love, and maybe just a little mischief.

They are natural builders, tinkerers, and spirit-friends. If something’s broken, a Kojin’s already halfway inside it with a lantern and a plan. If a shrine is cold, they’re the first to light a candle. If you’re lost in the woods? Listen for whistling. That’s probably a Kojin leading you out while pretending it was your idea.
I once met one—Luma Tinwhistle, barely knee-high, who made a flute from a crow feather and a gourd seed. She played a tune so sweet that even the angry willow spirits bowed low and wept sap.
Kojin do not seek glory. They seek harmony. A warm stew. A safe hearth. A spirit made calm. They build bridges not for travel—but for kindness.
And when trouble comes too big for their size?
And somehow, just by smiling, make the whole island feel taller.
They are the heartbeat of the village.
The ones who remember every birthday,
who tie bells on branches to make spirits giggle,
and who always, always leave room at the table.

They live in treehouses, wander in rings, and prank spirits into smiling. Nami, a Kojin spirit-namer, once told me, “We don’t go looking for answers. We go looking for weirder questions.” And I say: yes, please.

category.en-US: KINSHIPS AND SPIRIT-TOUCHED

title.en-US: The Gnomes, Hats Full of Wonders

content.value: Oh, how could I forget them? Gnomes! Tiny, round-eyed inventors with hats that could double as homes. They’re tinkerers, tricksters, and spirit-menders all rolled into one. If it hums, they fix it. If it glows, they adopt it.

Minto Sparkhat of Coralveil once held up a sparking doohickey and declared, “This is either a memory trap or a tea warmer. Maybe both.” That’s gnomes for you. Their homes? Built in kettles, wagon-stumps, even walking mushrooms. Their hearts? Bigger than their hats. Almost.

They are not tall, no—but don’t you dare call them small. Gnomes are dense with wonder. You’ll find them in every corner of the island—tinkering, charting, sketching, carving, questioning everything with bright eyes and dirt-smeared cheeks. Theirs is not the curiosity of idle minds. No, no—it is the ache to understand, to build, to connect spirit and world together.

Their bodies are sturdy, nimble, surprisingly strong—made for crawling under things, hoisting gadgets, dodging explosions. Their skin comes in all shades of bark, smoke, and soot. Hair? Pfft. Wild. Braided. Shaved into spirals. Sometimes scorched. Often tangled in ribbon, wire, or some half-finished thought. Their clothes clatter when they walk—pockets full of tools, blueprints, spirit stones, and snacks they swear aren’t experiments.
And stars above, the laughter. Gnomes laugh like they invented joy. And maybe they did.

I once met one—Professor Thistlewhip Widdeesnap the Third, Esq. (he insisted on every title). He rode a mechanical beetle powered by lantern-oil and moonlight, and claimed to be mapping “the laughter angles of waterfalls.” When I asked what that meant, he said, “I haven’t the faintest idea—but the waterfall seems quite pleased.”

Gnomes were among the great builders of the First Age—side by side with Daru and spirit-guides, shaping things that still run, even if no one remembers how. Vending shrines. Sky-lanterns. Recording boxes. Echo-bikes. Whisper machines. Trains. Their minds are clocks that refuse to wind down.
But don’t think them only mechanical. No, no. Gnomes love mystery, too. Magic, spirit, story. A well-told tale makes them vibrate. They see no line between invention and enchantment—only possibility.
They are not driven by conquest.
And when you hear one giggle in the dark, followed by a soft boom and the smell of singed moss…

category.en-US: KINSHIPS AND SPIRIT-TOUCHED

title.en-US: The Tenkara and Kurokara, Woven from the Loom

content.value: Tenkara and Kurokara—yes, yes, now that is a tale of light and shadow that do not oppose, but entwine.
The Tenkara and Kurokara are not born. They are woven. The Celestial Loom spun them when the world needed laughter or sorrow.
Many outsiders think them two kinds of people. Two bloodlines. Two sides of a coin. But they are not separate species, no, no… they are aspects of the same deep truth.

The people of the Kara are touched by the spirit realm in ways that shape their very being. They are often born during celestial convergences—comet nights, eclipses, spirit festivals—or found drifting in the mist with no past, only a future written in breath and glow. Their souls shine in ways mortals rarely do, but that shine may take different forms.

Those who burn bright, whose presence heals, uplifts, inspires, and glows like dawn through temple windows—these are the Tenkara. Their eyes shimmer like morning light. Their steps feel like hope arriving. They are drawn to service, to healing, to lifting others upward. Spirits often follow them quietly, like birds waiting to nest in light.

And then there are those whose presence is quiet, but heavy with knowing—the Kurokara. They carry dusk in their breath, and their silence is sacred. They walk with the grieving, with the forgotten, with those burdened by truths too dark for day. But do not call them fallen. No. The Kurokara are lanterns turned inward. Their light is felt, not seen.

They are one people. And often, a Kara may shift between both aspects in their life—Tenkara in youth, when hope burns hot, and Kurokara in age, when wisdom hums soft beneath the ribs. Or the other way ‘round. Some even carry both at once—bright voice, shadowed hands. A paradox, yes. But aren’t all souls?
I once knew one—Kael of the Last Ember—who healed by day with light that shone from his palms, and guided spirits by night with eyes that glowed like coals under ash. Was he Tenkara or Kurokara?
We are not day or night. We are the breath in between.
I am lit from both sides.”
But two sacred reflections of the same starlit breath.

category.en-US: KINSHIPS AND SPIRIT-TOUCHED

title.en-US: The Daru, Shaped by Stone and Flame

content.value: The Daru live where the rock sings. Hill Daru brew and plant, Stone Daru build and guard, Deep Daru… well, they dwell with ghosts of machines from the First Age. Each forge they light is a shrine. Each chisel stroke is a prayer.
Molga, a Soul-smith of Deepfire, carved her daughter’s name into a statue and said, “Now she lives in three places.” That’s how they think. Not in years, but in layers. Not in blood, but in craft.

category.en-US: KINSHIPS AND SPIRIT-TOUCHED

title.en-US: The Nisaki, Seekers in the Mist

content.value: Some call them humans, plain as a rice bowl. But I’ve never seen anything plain about them. They are artists and listeners. Builders and questioners. They carry fire not in their hands, but in their eyes—that quiet kind, the sort that warms a cold hut in winter, or lights a lantern for someone still lost in the reeds.
They do not always understand the old ways, not at first. But oh, how eager they are to learn. To ask. To kneel by an elder’s side and whisper,

They are not born of this island’s roots like the Kemari or the Kaido. No, no. The Nisaki arrived—in boats carved with stories, bearing names tied to winds long lost, wrapped in cloth that remembered cities and soil not found on our shores.
Boats not shaped by spirit or root or feathered driftwood, but by hands that had not known this land until that moment.
But instead of demanding space, they built with care. With intention. With reverence for what already was.

Mmm… yes, yes, I remember the first time I saw one walk ashore—dripping with salt and wonder, eyes wide as moons, heart heavy with stories not yet shared. 

But listen close, little shellling, for this is important: though they

from beyond the mist, the Nisaki are not strangers now. No. The island has breathed them in. The trees have heard their laughter. The Dreamskin has brushed their skin. And the spirits… the spirits tilt their heads when a Nisaki sings.

Most folk here were born of the island’s breath, of loam and legend, of roots so old even the stars have forgotten their names. But the Nisaki? Theirs is a different rhythm. A rhythm shaped by memory, by loss, by
. They chose to come. Chose to stay. And in that choosing, they became a part of the story.
And that, little one… that is what makes them special. Not their blood, nor their boats. But their

So if you see a Nisaki lost on a forest path, don’t just point the way. Walk with them. Ask their name. Listen to their stories. They may not have roots like we do, but they are planting them—one careful step at a time.
And isn’t that how all of us began?

You can always tell a Nisaki home—wood curved like waves, gardens grown in circles around stones, ink-hung charms fluttering over every doorway. Their hands are deft, their eyes patient. They are poets, farmers, monks, lantern-makers, fishers who speak to tide and ghost alike. Their voices carry calm. Their steps avoid roots.

Their skin ranges from pale dusk to sun-dark clay, their eyes like still tea in morning light. Hair is worn long, wrapped, shaved, or plaited with quiet purpose—never idle, always considered. Even their silence feels composed.

They brought rituals, yes—folded prayers, brush-written offerings, dances where feet never leave the ground. But they do not force these things. They share them. And in doing so, many of our island’s spirits have come to love the Nisaki—because they ask, not assume. They bow, not bend.
I once met one—Sayo Wind-Ritual, who held funerals for fallen leaves. She believed no part of the world should pass without a goodbye. Spirits followed her like windchimes.
Jiro, a mist-weaver of Gale Reaches, said it best: “The spirits don’t ask for devotion. They ask you to notice.”
But they are woven in now, thread by thread.
And if you ask them who they are, they do not name a nation.
The island has found something worth keeping.

category.en-US: KINSHIPS AND SPIRIT-TOUCHED

title.en-US: The Oni-Touched, Born of Yokai Breath

content.value: Marked by glowing eyes, horns, and strange-colored skin, the Oni-Touched walk with the weight of otherworldly blood. Some call them cursed. I call them necessary. They are exorcists, fire-dancers, yokai duelists, and sometimes just people looking for peace.
They carry infernal gifts not as trophies, but burdens. They speak to the yokai when no one else dares.

These are folk whose blood carries the echo of the Oni—those great horned spirits of passion, chaos, sorrow, and strength. Not demons, no. Not monsters. The Oni are wild truths, too vast to be caged, too old to be neat. And the Oni-Touched? They are the ones who walk the edge between self and storm.

You’ll know them when you see them. Tall, proud, eyes that gleam with gold or fire or frost. Skin like twilight bruises—blues, reds, deep violets—and always some sign of their heritage: a curling horn, a tusk, eyes that glint too sharp, or voices that rumble like far-off drums. Some bear tails. Some leave scorchmarks where they step. And yet, every one of them is different, shaped by the Oni that sings in their blood.
But hear me now—they are not evil. They are not cursed.

I knew one—Riku of the Broken Mask, whose horn was cracked at the tip. He danced alone on festival nights, barefoot in the ash, and sang to spirits others feared to name. And when a child wandered into the Dreamskin, it was Riku who entered the mist—and came back with two. One breathing, one not. He carried both with equal tenderness.

The Oni-Touched are strong, yes—but not just with fists. With feeling. Their hearts blaze. Their joy is loud. Their rage, when it comes, is like a drum too long unplayed. And their sorrow? Ahh… it floods rooms.

Some fear them. Some chase them from towns. But those who see truly? They kneel—because to carry the voice of an Oni is to live with fire in the bones and chains on the breath, and still choose kindness.

category.en-US: KINSHIPS AND SPIRIT-TOUCHED

content.value: Sometimes a doll waves back. Sometimes a puppet moves without strings. Those are the Mokuzai—spirits who nestle into crafted toys and, for a while, pretend to be people. Some stay longer than others. Some never leave.
Children treat them with reverence. Elders leave them a place at the table. They are not built. They are invited.

They are not born like you or I. No. A Mokuzai is a spirit that chooses—chooses—to dwell within a crafted thing: a puppet, a doll, a carved toy, a wooden mask left too long in the moonlight. And when the spirit settles in, the object shifts. Its limbs soften. Its head tilts. It learns how to giggle.
They are not constructs. Not machines. They are inhabited kindness. Curious, playful, sometimes solemn, sometimes wise in ways that surprise even the spirits who whisper to them.

Some Mokuzai are stitched from old cloth and button eyes. Others are carved of pine and polished with care. Some wear porcelain smiles. Some clatter like marionettes in the wind. Each carries the marks of the hands that made them—but none are truly defined by their shape. It’s the spirit inside that matters.

I once met one—Toku Buttonjaw, built from a festival puppet left beneath a sakura tree. He couldn’t speak, not with words, but when he danced, even the ghosts swayed. He wore a tiny scarf he never took off. Said it made him feel “like someone meant to keep going.”

Mokuzai are often drawn to places where love lingers: old workshops, bedside shelves, festival stalls, forgotten corners of shrines where children once laughed. They are fragile, yes—but not in spirit. When they care for someone, they do not stop caring. Not ever.
Some fade when their purpose is done. Others stay for decades, loved like siblings, like pets, like kin. And a rare few?
A rare few choose to keep going. To walk, to learn, to explore. To become.
And in a world as full of forgetting as ours…

category.en-US: KINSHIPS AND SPIRIT-TOUCHED

content.value: If a coat begins to walk or a mask hums lullabies, it may be a Kuregami. Spirits who dress themselves in cast-off clothing and forgotten uniforms. They remember warmth, even if they never had skin. One once told me, “I have no hands. But I remember the feeling of them. And sometimes, I wave.” And it did. It waved.

They are spirits, yes—but not like the ones that drift through mist or flicker in shrine candles. No, no. The Kuregami are inhabiting spirits—wisps of will, fragments of soul, sometimes ancient, sometimes newborn—that take shape by dwelling in clothing. Robes, scarves, kimonos, old mourning veils, festival rags forgotten in attics… anything that once meant something to someone. That is what gives them form.

Their movements are graceful, ghostlike, strange. A sleeve becomes a hand. A sash becomes a spine. They glide rather than walk, yet when they choose to touch the earth, they press meaning into it. Their presence is soft—eerie, yes, but never threatening. They are made of what’s been worn, what’s been loved, what’s been left behind but not forgotten.
Most Kuregami wear a face—though not a real one. A mask, a painted hood, or a blank visage sewn from cloth with dark, round eyes stitched into it. Sometimes those eyes blink. Sometimes they don’t.
The Kuregami do not age. They do not hunger. But they feel. And when they choose to walk the world, it is often to bear emotion that others cannot—grief too heavy, love too quiet, memory too sharp.
They are not marked by the gods.
By what still remembers how to feel.

category.en-US: KINSHIPS AND SPIRIT-TOUCHED

content.value: Ancient relics of the First Age—statues, dolls, machines—that awaken only when a spirit steps inside. A Mokugijin once heard a song after 200 years of stillness and stood up. They do not eat. Do not sleep. But they watch. And they remember. And when they move, it is because something has chosen them.

They are not dolls like the Mokuzai. No, no—these are golems of purpose, crafted in the First Age, when spirit and technology walked hand in hand, and the wind still whispered in code. The Mokugijin are not born, and they are not possessed. They were built—by Daru minds, Gnome hands, and spirit guides working in harmony.

But ahhh, child, they are not soulless. Oh no. For each Mokugijin carries a core, a spark—some call it the Spirit-Furnace, others the Voice-Thread. Whatever it is, it hums softly in their chests. Not a heart, but something older. Something intended.

Their bodies are smooth-crafted wood, metal, stone, glass—often mixed in beautiful, impossible ways. Limbs of lacquered lacquer-cedar, joints that click with brass precision, eyes of crystal lens or glowing glyph. Some resemble soldiers, others artisans, and a rare few still echo their original form: protectors of temples, readers of wind, caretakers of forgotten machines.

I once met one—Unit 7-B “Soto Whisper”, who tended a ruined archive with the gentleness of a monk folding prayer cloth. He had no memory of who made him. But he greeted every visitor with tea brewed on a ceramic plate built into his palm. He wrote poems, one line per day, etched into the walls of the ruin.

Mokugijin feel no hunger. They do not bleed. But they remember. Not always with clarity. Sometimes it comes in flashes—shadows of what they once were, what they once meant. Many have forgotten their commands. Some have outlived their creators. And a few have chosen new paths entirely, walking among kinfolk not as tools—but as people.
They are not truly mortal. But they are not truly machine.
When they tremble, it is not with rage, but with resonance—the echo of a purpose too old to name… still beating beneath a carved chest.
They are not marked by spirits.
And if you ever see one bow gently to a shrine, offering a single gear in place of incense…
They remember more than we do.

category.en-US: KINSHIPS AND SPIRIT-TOUCHED

content.value: What we call the Physical Realm is the one your senses understand. The trees you climb. The wind over the Gale Reaches. The taste of plum vinegar. The sound of Daru chiseling into stone. These things live here.

In every forest hollow, you’ll find a vending shrine that hums with intent. A moss-covered cassette that, when rewound, murmurs the voice of someone long gone. A rusted rail, part of the Tamagari Line, that still pulses with breath you don’t quite hear.

Here, the relics of the First Age rest—not as ruins, but as remembered things. Machines that whir with spirit-light. Architecture shaped by Daru hands and Gnome minds, guided by spirits who whispered their blueprints in dream. Their designs lean toward light and joy—bright plastics, humming glass, and buttons you press with hope instead of logic.

Magic here isn’t rare. It is rhythmic. It lives in charms passed down across generations. It dances through the scent of grandma’s soup, lingers in bracelets tied with river grass and quiet intent. Even those who never study still practice. And most carry a token—bought from a vending shrine or traded with a fox-faced stranger—that hums just slightly when the world leans sideways.
But even if you never leave this side of the world, you’ll notice things. Leaves falling the wrong way. A shadow shaped like someone who isn’t there. A voice you didn’t hear with your ears.

“It’s like living next door to a festival you’re not invited to—but sometimes, you catch a whiff of the food.” That’s what Taro once told me, a potter from the coast whose wares sometimes glow in moonlight, though he won’t say why.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\THE REALMS

content.value: The Spirit Realm is not somewhere else. It is everywhere else. Beneath, behind, between. It is a sky that dreams. A forest that remembers. A river that carries not water, but regret.
Kokoro-no-Kami once told me, “In the Spirit Realm, the sky remembers your dreams, and rivers carry old regrets like driftwood.”

It is not a single place. It is a thousand layers—a tapestry of realms. Elemental vaults where Kaido whisper back to the roots of their being. Markets made of floating paper, where spirits trade secrets they’ve already forgotten. Shrines that drift through clouds, guarded by cranes who only speak in poetry. Swamps where Corruption slinks and croons, twisting memory into moss. Echo-forests where every tree hums with what should not have been.

The Spirit Realm does not obey the rules of soil and sky. It bends to meaning. If you enter in sorrow, the road may weep with you. If you walk in pride, you may find yourself climbing stairs that have no top. The land there is not land. It is language. It does not map itself by place, but by feeling.
Each region of the island casts a shadow in the Spirit Realm.

The Hollow Murkway is mirrored by glowing bogs, where forgotten spirits drag lotus flowers behind them like memories on strings. The summit of Mount Uokami reflects as a vast obsidian plateau, where silent Kyoshijin and Daru soul-smiths etch truths into stone with hammers made of breath and patience. In the Wandering Veil, trees lean farther inward in the realm beyond, forming cathedral-like hollows where the veil shimmers like dew on spider thread—and even spirits bow to listen.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\THE REALMS

title.en-US: The Places Where the Veil Wears Thin

content.value: Crossing between realms is not a thing most folk do, but it happens more often than they admit. I once saw a girl vanish into a puddle while chasing her cat. She came back with a scarf that sang.

Sometimes the veil is simply thinner. A torii gate wrapped in thorned ivy. A stone well that swallows light. A lightning-struck tree whose bark peels in the shape of old names. These are portals. Or perhaps just tears. Step through, and you shimmer, and then you’re not here anymore.
“You’ll know a portal when your breath catches and doesn’t quite come back,” said Nami once, as she offered tea to a shrine with no roof.

There are other ways known as the Mist Corridors. They are not marked by paths or signs, but by absence—by where the land softens and the fog thickens into something nearly conscious. These corridors slip through the Plains of Listening Grass, drift along the crags of the Shattered Shelf, and thread deep into the folded woods of the Wandering Veil, though none can say for certain where one ends and another begins. Some believe they shift, like breath itself, winding according to unspoken rules or silent rhythms set by the Elder Spirits.

It is here that certain Kibashime wander—not warriors in the loud sense, but weavers of breath and presence. They do not summon fire or crack the earth. Instead, they bind steam and chant into their lungs, their exhalations carrying words older than language. They walk alone, always alone, but their passing is unmistakable.

Those who’ve glimpsed them speak of fog shaped into spears, or illusions so convincing they bled from the edges. Others scoff, saying it’s all theater, all whisper and flair. But then a pond is found with steam curling into a single perfect line of poetry etched in cooled glass, and the doubters go quiet.

The Ryūkajin—especially the gem-born among them—hold these mistbinders in quiet reverence. Not fear, not envy. Just… respect. For even dragons know that breath shapes worlds, and the Kibashime who walk the Mist Corridors carry their breath like a blade sheathed in fog.
No one seeks them out. You simply find them when the mist decides you’re ready.

There is also the Tamagari Line, that great humming train, built in the First Age to stitch stories across realms. It moves not on rail, but on meaning. Its stops are not marked by signs, but by need. If it arrives for you, you are meant to ride it. Where it takes you… well. That depends on what you’ve lost.

Some travelers drink potions, brewed by forgotten hands. Or unroll scrolls inscribed with spirit ink. These methods open eyes that don’t belong to the body. You might phase. You might merge. You might vanish, just a little.

Some carry artifacts—cameras that catch ghosts, radios that answer questions no one asked, walkmen that play lullabies from another life. Most don’t know what they are until they use them. Most never mean to.
And then there are the spirits themselves.

Some are called Wanderers. They walk between worlds as easily as birds shift trees. Some of them offer passage. Some demand a song. Others ask for something strange—a memory, a name, the last thing you forgot. If they like you, they may guide you. If not… they may simply laugh and drift away.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\THE REALMS

content.value: Some settle here—Homebodies, we call them—living among us, half-disguised, half-dreaming. They inhabit wells, old statues, cracked game consoles, unclaimed shoes. They hum in corner-shrines and ride incense trails.

Others come and go—the Wanderers, full of questions and errands. You might find one tending a noodle cart that wasn’t there yesterday, or offering fortunes in exchange for forgotten songs. They never stay long, but they never forget a kindness.
And some never quite leave the Spirit Realm, but still… bleed through. They become echoes. Ghosts. A sigh in the hall. A song from a locked drawer. A shiver when the air is too still.

There are those we don’t speak of often. Corrupted spirits, shaped by the wrong kind of hunger. Not born of malice, but forced. Twisted. The Corruption scars them, warps them, makes them unrecognizable. They are neither spirit nor yokai, neither dream nor memory. They are broken. And when they cross over, the land feels it.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\THE REALMS

content.value: To spirits, we mortals are strange. We do not smell like shape or age. We smell like concepts. A spirit might say you feel like “a door that has never been opened,” or “the taste of morning before the rain.”
Our bodies are dense. Loud. Finite. In the Spirit Realm, this makes us noticeable. In the same way that fire is noticeable in a quiet room.

Likewise, some of us sense the Spirit Realm. A dream that isn’t quite ours. A chill that moves against the wind. A flickering light no one else sees. Some forests whisper constantly. Some villages sit atop forgotten gates. Some taverns keep two guestbooks—one for the living, one for the not quite.
“Sometimes a tavern has two guestbooks. One of them is invisible,” Jiro told me, as we watched the sun blink out behind the Reaches.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\THE REALMS

content.value: Time does not behave in the Spirit Realm. A minute might feel like a year. A decade may pass like a yawn. The realm bends to emotion. Anger causes storms. Sorrow collapses bridges. Love builds houses out of starlight.
Leave too quickly, and something may follow you. Stay too long, and something may stay behind.

There are those who never return. Not because they died, but because they became… different. There are Kaido who claim their oldest ancestors simply kept walking. Some Daru say they were born from rock in the Spirit Realm and only stumbled into flesh by accident.
“I left for tea and stayed a decade,” Anai once said, with a smile that didn’t quite match her eyes. “When I came home, no one remembered my face—but my teacup was still warm.”

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\THE REALMS

content.value: Ahh… gather close, my hatchlings, and let me tell you of the great ones—not gods, no, not the sort that sit above with spears of lightning and golden thrones. No, no. These are older. Softer in some places. Sharper in others. You can hear them in the storm, see them in the curling roots of the trees, feel them in your breath when you realize you are not alone. They are the Elder Spirits. Or, as Kaima whispered to me once beneath the fog-thick trees of Whispergrove:
“They are not gods. They are stories with names. Forces with faces. Echoes with will.”
You do not call them. They are already here.

So. These are not gods, my hatchlings. They are breaths in the forest. Cracks in the sky. Songs in silence. If you see a shrine, bow. If you hear a hum with no mouth, smile. If the mist feels heavy—listen.
And if you must speak their names, do so with tea in hand and your feet bare.

When the first wind spoke, it sang of fire and frost, of lightning and storm. From that breath came Dravanyr, not as a beast, but as a rhythm—a vast dragon coiled in the world’s exhale. The Ryūkajin say he shaped them with breath alone, and the Kaido of flame and storm nod in agreement, for they feel him in their bones when the air shifts before a lightning strike.

The Ryūkajin build cliffside shrines to him, where the wind can’t help but sing. Their elders—the Breathkeepers—teach in silence. Only breath. Inhale as the mountain does. Exhale as the sea. And in that space between—clarity.
“Breath is memory. Inhale the world. Exhale what you are becoming.”
Tenshiko, the Seventh Breath Seer, said that just before dissolving into mist. Quite literally.

category.en-US: THE ELDER SPIRITS

title.en-US: Kokoro-no-Kami, the Flow of the Gods

content.value: Now this one… this one is hard to see. She is the current in your tea. The leaf that floats but never sinks. She is Kokoro-no-Kami, the soft-turning wheel of cycles: bloom, wither, drift, return.

The Kojin leave floating lanterns downriver in her honor. The Dusk Elves whisper to her in mossy silence. I once met a Water Kaido who claimed to have painted her—using water, on water. Said it was his finest failure.
She does not answer questions, but she always leaves you with one.
“She appears not when we ask, but when we let go.”
So says Yuma, the Stream-Walker of Hana Pools, and I believe her.

category.en-US: THE ELDER SPIRITS

content.value: Now here’s one I know well. Ganroku does not move. He endures. He waits. He listens to chisels more than prayers. You Daru out there know what I mean. His voice is the weight of your forge hammer. His laughter is the deep roll of the earth.

The Stone Kyoshijin sit for days on cold cliff ledges to hear him whisper. The Daru mix ancestral ash into their mortar, believing each wall holds the breath of their dead. You want to honor Ganroku? Then build something that will outlive you. Then wait.
Molga, who carved her daughter’s name into three generations of stone, once told me,
“Legacy is not what we build, but what remains standing.”
Aye. I’ve no shell to argue with that.

category.en-US: THE ELDER SPIRITS

title.en-US: Onikumi Khan, the Walker Between Trials

content.value: Now… hush, children. We speak his name with respect. Onikumi Khan walks in the fur of a bear but carries the weight of every moment we hesitate before death.

He is the stillness before battle. The breath before the blade falls. He does not take life—he watches to see if we take it with care. The Kibashime call him before they light the flame within. The Frost-blooded Kyoshijin climb their mountains in silence, hoping he will judge them ready. The Dusk Elves leave white stones at their thresholds—little “thank-you’s” for lives spared.
And among the islanders, there is a tale:
He walks the woods as a bear, unspoken. If you try to take from him—fur, fang, glory—you may not live to boast. But if you bow, share space, leave a plum or a song… he may watch you go in peace.
The Bone-Wardens, those masked ones in black and white, do not command the dead. They ask. Gently. They speak rites no one else dares. One of them told me:
“The soul walks on. The flesh remains. Let it serve again—not in pride, but in peace.”
And when they say that… even the crows fall silent…

category.en-US: THE ELDER SPIRITS

content.value: If Onikumi draws the line, Namakusa tends the wound. They are not death. They are delay. The breath that almost ended. The lily blooming on a grave. The warmth in a corpse’s hands just before the last goodbye.
Their masks are bone-white, unpainted. Their followers do not raise the dead in mockery, no. They ask death to wait. To pause. To give one more moment for closure, for care.
“I do not take life from Death. I ask Death to wait, and Death—if respected—sometimes does.”

category.en-US: THE ELDER SPIRITS

title.en-US: Queen Okumi and Her Cosmic Egg

content.value: Now I tell this part with a grin on my face. Queen Okumi is joy. She once cracked the sky with laughter, they say, and her Cosmic Egg still floats above the world, spinning and singing.

The Kemari remember her not as a goddess, but as family. Our first mother, star-born and moss-footed. Kojin honor her in stories that never end the same way twice. The gnomes? Oh, they say she taught hats how to dance.
“She cracked the sky with her laugh and filled the pond with stars.”
Gribba said that, and if Gribba says it, then by my shell, it’s true.

category.en-US: THE ELDER SPIRITS

content.value: She hums. That’s all. Never speaks. But when Hoshira hums, even nightmares grow quiet.
The Kojin say she catches children’s dreams and hangs them in the sky. Astral Elves whisper lullabies not to babies, but to old regrets, hoping she’ll carry them away.
“She never speaks, only hums. But when she hums, the stars listen.”
Said by Koya of Blue Tree Hollow, and I remember it every time I can’t sleep.

category.en-US: THE ELDER SPIRITS

content.value: Ahh, Morrowel. Not quite here. Not quite gone. She is the door, not the room. Tenkara and Kurokara leave keys in crossroads—keys that open no lock but tell her they’re listening.
She watches thresholds, moments of change, pauses between words. Her shrines are often walked past, mistaken for empty doorframes. But when you stop—just stop—sometimes she’s there.
“She never walks with you. But every path has her footprints.”
Silhae of the Loom said that. I once found one of her footprints in a puddle that hadn’t rained.

category.en-US: THE ELDER SPIRITS

content.value: Poor Noroku. He does not weep for what was lost, but for what never had a chance. Gnomes light candles shaped like clocks, set them afloat on rivers, and whisper what they almost did. Almost said. Almost became.
“He doesn’t mourn what was. He mourns what never could be.”
That was Minto Sparkhat. Her glider never flew, but her dreams did.

category.en-US: THE ELDER SPIRITS

content.value: Oh… do not linger on this one too long.

She sees too much. Her madness isn’t loud—it’s correct. And that’s what makes it dangerous. The ink-stained Elves of the Hollow Shrines have rituals to forget her visions. Witches burn mirrors just to sleep again.
“She sings in the cracks between dreams. Her lullaby is teeth.”
That was Nokuri, poor thing. Her eyes no longer blink.

category.en-US: THE ELDER SPIRITS

content.value: Once a twin. Rabbit and crow. Then something broke.
He does not scream. He hates quietly. His forest—the Crawling Canopy—follows him like a shadow with roots. The Dark Elves scratch bramble sigils into their doors. Kemari dance circles of thorns.
“He is pain without language. He does not seek escape. He seeks silence.”
Said by Dara Yushi. Her voice was softer after that.

category.en-US: THE ELDER SPIRITS

content.value: He lied. That was his gift. Lies so sweet they grew teeth. He tore the unity of the Kemari once—long ago. His masks are buried beneath silver-nailed cairns, but sometimes, they whisper.
If you hear a question with too many answers… it might be him.
“He is not gone. Only broken into questions.”
Omu of the Twelve Rains said that. Then sealed her tongue with ink and thread.

category.en-US: THE ELDER SPIRITS

content.value: “They’re not lesser because they are weaker. Only because they speak more softly.”
—Elder Gubi-Goni, draped in moonlight and moss

Ah, now we step into the mistier trails. The ones behind your house, or just beyond your breath. The ones where old sandals vanish in the night and laughter returns from a different direction than it left.

The Elder Spirits, grand as they are, do not walk the island alone. No, no. There are others—smaller echoes and whispers, the ones we call the lesser spirits. Though even that name is a bit of a fib, eh? Some of them are older than our songs, and far stranger than our dreams.
I’ve met them, you know. Not all of them—who could?—but enough to know better than to assume “lesser” means “tame.”

“They are not gods. Not quite.” I said that once to a curious Kojin, and he frowned so hard he lost his balance on the log. “Then what are they?” he asked, toes dipped in the river. I told him: “They’re the breath between your words. The spark that makes your puppet blink. The echo in a stone when no one struck it.”

The great Elder Spirits—Dravanyr, Onikumi Khan, Kokoro-no-Kami and the rest—they are the mountain and tide. But here, in the quiet corners of the island, you’ll find their kin, cousins, shadows, and splinters. Lesser spirits. Not less important—no, no. Just quieter. Closer. Flickering.

Some come when called. Others come when forgotten. Some live in the edge of your kettle’s steam, or hum through your mixtape when no one’s playing it. They might be memory, mischief, movement, or moss. And they, too, guide paths.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA

content.value: These are the ones that rarely speak in voice, but always speak in feeling. You know them by the goosebumps when no breeze passes. Or the way the old cassette in your pack flips itself to the perfect song when you need courage.
They follow travelers, artists, weepers, and those who hesitate at thresholds.

Some folk claim a Whisper-Spirit chose them—and suddenly, their pen won’t stop writing. Their dreams begin to rhyme. Or mushrooms begin growing only where they sleep. We call these gentle hauntings. Some call them blessings. The Kojin call them “nibblers”—because they nibble at the edges of your life until you are shaped.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\LESSER SPIRITS

content.value: Now Kaima, she’s one of the familiar ones. Old spirit of breeze and breath, who lives in the stillness of groves and the flutter of windchimes. She’s shaped like a girl, or a leaf, or a question you almost remember. It was she who said, “They are not gods. They are stories with names. Forces with faces. Echoes with will.” Folk think she walks among the whisperwillows just east of Muramori Village, the
tucked-away, mist-draped quiet settlement deep within the Wandering Veil.
Some say Kaima taught the Kojin how to sing without moving their mouths. Others believe she once courted the wind, and now hums every time it forgets where to blow.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\LESSER SPIRITS

title.en-US: The Lantern in the Tree — Kekkori

content.value: Ever left your lantern hanging and found it glowing a different color come morning? That may be Kekkori, the light-nudger. She nests in lanterns, bottle-glows, and jars of fireflies. Kojin leave her slivers of honey or polished stones, and in return, she offers guidance… or mischief. She’s helped many a traveler find their way—or lose it beautifully. They say if you whisper a riddle into a lantern and it flickers twice, she’s listening.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\LESSER SPIRITS

content.value: Among the Daru, there is reverence for Sugoru, the spirit of repaired things. A bowl cracked in kindness, a tool passed down, a mask with a missing tooth—these are Sugoru’s domain. He is not flashy. He never speaks. But the wise say you can feel him in the weight of something mended, especially if it was broken with sorrow and healed with care.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\LESSER SPIRITS

title.en-US: The Blue Flame That Weeps — Minaki

content.value: The Kaido speak of Minaki, who dwells where steam rises gently and sorrow hasn’t hardened yet. A flickering blue flame that sometimes appears atop hot springs, Minaki doesn’t burn. She warms. She comforts. She remembers. Children lost to fever, elders who died in sleep—some believe Minaki carries their memories in every vapor trail that curls upward. Leave her rice soaked in plum wine, and she’ll light your path in dreams.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\LESSER SPIRITS

title.en-US: The Tangle-Witch — Hina of the Threads

content.value: Hina is a weaving spirit, a minor daughter (some say rebellious) of the Celestial Loom. She tangles cords, knots necklaces, and rearranges hair braids while you sleep. The Tenkara tell of her giggling in the wind during festivals, looping blessings into banners and sometimes rearranging destinies like a mischievous aunt. Those who treat their ribbons and rope with care often find luck. Those who don’t? Well, enjoy your knotted sandals.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\LESSER SPIRITS

content.value: There’s an old story among the Stone Kyoshijin about Nontomo, who lives in the echo of things. Not inside them—in the echo. A drum’s last note, a voice fading into a canyon, the sigh after grief. That’s Nontomo’s house. And if you sit very still at twilight, you might hear them reply. They don’t speak in words. They answer with what might have been. That’s more powerful than it sounds.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\LESSER SPIRITS

welcomeTitle.en-US: A Welcome to Yurei-Tu-Shima by Elder Gubi-Goni

content.value: spirits breathe in moss and bloom.

Ahhh… come, come now, don’t just stand there with your toes shy and your spirit hungry! The tea’s steeped just right—golden, fragrant, and whispering like a story half-remembered. Sit, sit, my dear wind-wanderer, wherever the cushions feel warm and the steam curls toward your nose.

“Elder Gubi-Goni,” they call me—yes, the soft-shelled scribbler of the Storyshells, keeper of mossy tales and rainy-day wisdom. But tonight, I am simply your host, and the kettle is singing sweet songs of the old island.
Do you smell that? Mmm—sun-dried plumleaf and a pinch of cinnamonroot. I brewed it the way the fireflies like it, just in case they drift by to listen too.

Now hush that belly grumble—I’ve got puffbean buns warming by the coals—and open those lovely earholes of yours. For tonight, I’ll tell you of mist that weeps, of trees that walk, and of spirits who laugh when no one’s looking. But not all at once, no no, stories are like dumplings—you savor them slow or you burn your tongue on the truth.
So breathe in. Let the island settle around your shoulders. And when you’re ready, I’ll begin with a whisper I once heard from a willow that forgot how to sleep.
Welcome, my friend. The island has been waiting for you.
• Filed with ink-stained fingers in the Twilight Scriptorium of Coralveil •
For those seeking a slightly more academic—though no less wide-eyed—look at the many folk of Yurei-tu-Shima, I offer these humble field notes.

Each kinship I’ve studied holds its own wonders: some born of stone, others of storm or spirit or story. I’ve shared tea with turtles, debated poetry with dragons, and once spent a week disguised as a moss rock (long story).
These pages are not exhaustive—but they are earnest.

The air hums, not with the buzz of insects or the whisper of wind, but with a deeper thrum—the sound of a thousand possibilities being born at once. Threads flow from these portals like rivers of light, converging on a great loom at the center of the room. From there, the light is spun into more mundane-looking fibers, which are then fed to the smaller, ordinary looms that fill the workshop, clicking and clattering as they weave the textiles of destiny.

The workshop is a place of making, where the raw potential of a thousand worlds is gathered, spun, and woven into the stories of Yurei-tu-Shima. Every finished tapestry, every simple bolt of cloth, contains within it a spark of a distant star or the echo of an impossible sea. The threads of fate are not just an idea here; they are the simple, honest work of the Loom.

content.value: You push open the heavy wooden door, and the scent of old wood, oiled machinery, and the faint, clean smell of ozone after a lightning strike greets you. The air is warm and filled with the gentle, rhythmic clatter of dozens of looms, though none appear to be operated by anyone. Dust motes dance in the beams of light slanting down from a high, grimy window.

In the center of the workshop, seated before the largest loom, is a creature that seems to soak up the light around it. It is a massive, solid being of shadow and soft, dark fur, with large, gentle eyes that glow with the warmth of amber. It doesn't seem to notice your arrival, its large hands moving with surprising dexterity as it works.

Your eyes follow the threads on its loom; they are not spun from simple cotton or wool, but from pure, golden light. These glowing threads extend from the central loom, weaving through the air to connect to all the other looms in the workshop, which move in unison as if guided by an unseen chorus. The creature at the center looks up, its glowing eyes blinking slowly, and a soft, impossibly deep hum resonates through the floorboards.
"Ah, a new story seeks to be told! Welcome, welcome.
Every life begins with a single spark, a simple breath. The air here hums with potential, and the threads of what could be drift like dust in the moonlight.
Give me the vessel you have in mind—the kinship, the calling, the heart's allegiances—and I shall weave its very soul. Let us begin a new journey together."

The island is alive. Not in the way a creature is, but in the way an old forest listens. It is not sentient, but it is aware. It remembers. The rivers carry rumor. The stones retain the warmth of ancient hands. The trees bend their backs in sympathy when you’re tired.
Magic here is not bold. It’s not loud. It doesn’t ask for applause.

It’s a soft blessing whispered over rice by a passing fox-masked Kemari. A wind that changes your path without moving your feet. A spirit who steals your name—not to harm you, but to teach you how it sounds in someone else’s voice.

It’s true, there are those who can do grand things. A Ryūkajin might breathe flame and call lightning. An elf marked by spirit might step through trees, summon food, vanish in mist. There are those who stir the bones of the dead with reverence, not ruin. But these gifts are rare, and rarely called for—unless the land cries out. Unless the breath of the island is troubled. Unless the corruption begins to bloom again like mold behind the veil.
Even then, the answer is not always battle. Sometimes it’s music. Sometimes it’s stillness.
Even death is not an ending here.
“My grandfather died last year,” I was told by Chiru, a humble farmer with tired eyes and a wonderful talent for cucumbers. “I saw him again last week. He gave me advice on drainage.”
This is how the world works.

content.value: Beyond the land lies the Weeping Horizon, a border not drawn, but felt. It never lifts. It never thins. Those who pass beyond often do not return. And when they do, they come back… altered. Their eyes hold mist. Their memories are full of gaps. Their laughter sounds like someone else’s.

That mist does not rise. It does not burn away at dawn. It hangs, low and gentle, humming always—sometimes like sorrow, sometimes like lullaby. It is said to be the breath of a forgotten spirit, or perhaps the skin between what is real and what is too real. Birds vanish into it. Ships that cross its threshold rarely return. Time, too, seems to waver. Some say the island breathes with you. Others say time slows, curls, softens into loops. I say both.

Some say the mist is a spirit in itself, coiled around us like a guardian. Others say it holds back the edge of madness. Places where meaning collapses. Places where the voice of Shi-Naga—that name we do not say too loud—rings clearer, sharper, wronger. There are old stories of it, and even older silences.
Whatever lies beyond, we are wrapped in a closed circle. A bottle filled with stories

content.value: There are no gods here—not anymore. No golden thrones. No swords meant to split the sky. If such things once walked these shores, they have long since bowed their heads and let the moss grow over them.
No war roars in our time, though some spirits whisper of darkness that still stirs, of corruption that crawls beneath stone and through dream. But such things do not define us.
Here, the world ripples from the smallest gesture. A moment of stillness. A word spoken with care.

The stories worth telling often begin with something humble: a Kemari brewer collecting bitterroot in the moonlight, careful not to disturb the song-swallows. A Kojin tinkerer cursing gently as she adjusts the antenna of a vending shrine possessed by a lazy lantern spirit. A melody that plays only when the sun slips through an old tower window just so, and a listener whose life quietly changes because of it.
The island is full of moments like that. Sweet. Eerie. Reflective. Sometimes strange. Always meaningful.
“Most adventurers seek the epic,” I once overheard a Ryūkajin say as he stood knee-deep in a field of sleeping poppies. “Here, we seek the meaningful.”

Here, conflict does not always mean swords drawn. It often means hearts bared. A corrupted creature may weep before it strikes. A yokai formed of broken promises might only be calmed when the wound is named. A ghost may not need banishing—only remembering.
“We don’t slay monsters here,” said a Kojin with a lantern that smelled faintly of plum smoke. “We understand them. Or try to. Sometimes that’s worse.”

The island itself is not a stage. It is not the backdrop. It is a character. Its fields whisper. Its ruins grieve. Its shrines sing when no one is near. Villages rise not where iron is found, but where mystery lingers. Where something old once sighed. Where the wind feels just right.

You may find sacred places half-swallowed by rusting cassette towers. You may find temples built by Kemari hands, sharing space with vending machines that offer prophetic fortunes to those who don’t know what they’re looking for.

And there is the Tamagari Line—ah, the train that hums without tracks, that glides through mist and over waters, that sometimes vanishes entirely when you ask where it’s headed. It does not care where you think you are going. It only takes you where the story needs you to be.

title.en-US: On Ink-Keepers: An Interview with the Professor

content.value: Field Notes of Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III
Twilight Scriptorium, Coralveil – Volume VII: Dialogues with the Spirit-Faithful
Conducted beneath the Cracked Vault, at the edge of the Hollow Tide
Interview Subject: Vaska Lenai, Inkkeeper of the Hollow Seal, Gnomish Archivist of Noroku, Keeper of the Reverse Journals
I was not invited. The invitation was silence.

The Hollow Tide does not appear on any map, and I suspect it never will. My boat reached a wet, whispering shore beneath a sky whose stars blinked like forgotten names. A procession of snails led me to the vault—carved into stone, lined in wax, sealed with a shell cracked by time rather than force. Vaska Lenai waited within. Their cloak was layered and loose, the color of old ash and wet parchment. Around their neck hung a broken watch and a half-written journal bound in cloth that seemed to absorb rather than reflect light.
Professor Widdersnap: Vaska Lenai. Thank you for allowing this… I don’t want to say “interview.” Perhaps… shared moment?
Vaska Lenai: That’s better. Interviews require questions that expect answers. Noroku teaches us to sit beside questions and listen to the answers that almost arrive.

We sit in a room without windows. One candle, shaped like an hourglass, burns silently in reverse. The inkpot on the table is not black, but dark grey, and viscous. I set down my quill. I record with charcoal instead.
Professor Widdersnap: For the record, could you tell me how your people describe Noroku?
Vaska: (A pause. A breath not quite taken.)
We do not speak his name above a whisper in the vaults. Not because we fear him—but because grief has an echo, and Noroku is always listening.
He is not time. That word is too clean.
He is the pause before time moves forward again.
The door never opened. The name nearly spoken.

Some see him cloaked in wax and river-shells, with a cracked clock-face for a head. Others say he walks with backwards footsteps and speaks only in memory. I once saw him. I think. I was watching an unlit candle at sea… and I forgot why I had come. That was him.
Professor Widdersnap: And his followers? I’ve never seen a temple. No festival. No hymn.
Vaska: No. He has no temples. Only shelves.
We are not worshippers. We are Rememberers of the Unbecome.
Most of us are gnomes, yes. A few astral elves. Those who dream too vividly of what never was. We don’t call ourselves priests or scribes. We’re just… Stillnames. Chronists of the Hollow. Inkkeepers.
Professor Widdersnap: Could you describe the way you honor him? Rituals? Tools? Vestments?
Vaska: (Carefully unwraps a journal with no writing, just faint indentations as though erased by the soul itself.)

We wear layers. Always soft grey, or candle-white. Sometimes shell-studded, sometimes marked with wax-drip scars. Nothing should bind us too tightly to one moment. We carry broken watches. Music boxes that don’t play. Half-finished embroidery. Things left waiting.
Reverse Journals, where we write what didn’t happen.
Hollow Ink, drawn from sacred sorrow wells. Not to erase—but to amplify what wasn’t.
Sealcloth, for binding broken things—not to mend, but to give them a place.
The Tide Candle: A flame shaped like an hourglass, set adrift at sea. The longer it floats, the more loss it has witnessed.
Reverse Journaling: Each night, we write down the day we didn’t have. The letter we didn’t send. The forgiveness we never gave.

The Binding of the Unbecome: We wrap broken clocks, shattered cups, or old grief in waxed cloth, seal them with spiral shells, and place them on high shelves. Not to forget. But to remember without weight.
Professor Widdersnap: There are whispers of… something darker. A substance. The Ink?
Vaska: (Voice drops to a near-silent hush.)
Yes. It appears where Noroku lingers.
A substance thicker than grief, blacker than the underside of dreams.
It fills the lungs of the grieving.
We call it Noroku’s deepest tear.
A rare few use it to seal broken clocks.
It makes louder that which was almost forgotten.
Professor Widdersnap: I heard a story. Of a child in a village that never existed?
Vaska: That is the story we do not tell aloud.
But I will whisper it for you.
A child, lost in the Mist, lived a full life in a village that never was. Grew old. Loved. Sang songs that were never written. Then Noroku came—not to punish, but to offer.
Forget it all, and return to life.
Or vanish… and become the dream itself.
But when they opened their eyes, a music box sat beside them. Playing a song no one else could hear.
Professor Widdersnap: (Quiet, scribbling slower now.) Is Noroku… kind?
Vaska: He is not cruel. Nor is he kind.
Everything that could have bloomed—and did not.
He waits. In sorrow. In silence.

We end the interview not with thanks, but with stillness. Vaska lights a Tide Candle and lets it float in a shallow bowl. It flickers once, then remains perfectly still for twenty-seven minutes. Neither of us speaks.
Later, I find a music box in my satchel. It plays nothing. And yet… I know its melody by heart.

Addendum: Request to study the properties of Hollow Ink under Dreamskin exposure. Begin comparative research into Astral Elf sleep-walking phenomena and unexplained half-melodies reported among Kojin shipwreck survivors.

title.en-US: On Listeners: An Interview with the Professor

content.value: Field Notes of Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III
Twilight Scriptorium, Coralveil – Volume VII: Dialogues with the Spirit-Faithful
Conducted within a hollow stairwell beneath the Murkway peatline, lit by thirteen candles and one mirror that did not reflect us.
Interview Subject: Yurume of the Fifth Reflection, Ink-Tongued Scribe of Hollow Step and self-confessed vessel of the Spiral Wound
I had not meant to find them. I had come for moss samples and sediment records.

I was five steps down when I realized the reflection in the mirror beside me blinked when I did not. And seated at the bottom of the stair, surrounded by ash-drawn spirals and a bowl of still-black water, was Yurume.

Small-framed, dark-eyed, skin like faded parchment smeared with inkblots. A gnome, yes—but altered. Wearing seven layered cloaks, each stitched with mismatched thread. Their face was bare, but masks hung from cords around their neck: cracked ceramic, weeping wax, mirror-splinter, bark-stamped. They did not look up when I arrived.
Only whispered, “Do you already hear her?”
I did not answer. Instead, I began the recording.
WIDDERSNAP: Thank you for agreeing to this dialogue. May I ask your role among the faithful of Shi-Naga?

YURUME: [Traces a spiral in the ash] There is no congregation. No hymns. We are not a church—we are an accident. I am a Scribe. Ink-tongued. Fifth Reflection. Which means… I remember five truths I was never meant to. I write the ones that wake me crying.
WIDDERSNAP: You speak of “truths not meant to be known.” Is Shi-Naga a keeper of hidden knowledge?
YURUME: No. She is the scream after knowledge. The spiral that forms when meaning spins too fast. She held too much. She tried to share it. She broke. Now she leaks.
WIDDERSNAP: What does it mean to follow her?
YURUME: To wear masks. Not to hide—but to accept you are not one thing. That your mind is not whole. We wear many. And when one begins to speak too loudly, we change it.
WIDDERSNAP: Is there a name for your order?
YURUME: [Pauses] We do not name ourselves, for fear she will finish the sentence. But outsiders call us the Spiral-Blooded. The Madmaskers. The Silent Choir. I prefer “The Listening.”
WIDDERSNAP: What rituals do you observe?

The Ink Mirrors—bowls of black water, stirred by ash and moonlight. We peer into them during confession. When you see a truth not ready to be spoken, you say it anyway, or else the mirror watches you instead. Then we shatter it.
The Lash of Mindroot—a tea. Bitter. Hallucinogenic. Before drinking, you hold a question in your mouth. The answer comes as a wound. Where and how you bleed… that is your insight.
The Seven Sighs Vigil—each breath discards a version of the self you no longer need. Each name unspoken becomes a mask. On the seventh sigh, we are allowed to ask her for mercy.
We also perform Reverse Wake-Funerals, for those whose minds have died but bodies remain. We bury the names they forgot, not the ones they kept.
WIDDERSNAP: Do you consider the Corruption—her breath, as some say—to be a divine gift or a curse?

YURUME: Neither. It is… her presence. Her dreaming. It chooses mania or dementia. Never both. If you hear too much, you burn. If you feel too much, you fade. But both are listening. Both are her voice.
WIDDERSNAP: And the masks—do they prevent it?

YURUME: No. They shape the madness. Give it teeth you can count. A grin you can answer. We paint them in wax, bone, sorrow. Some paint theirs with tears mixed with soot. Others… let her paint them from within.
WIDDERSNAP: You mentioned before that she was once merciful. Do you believe she is still?

YURUME: I believe she broke herself to save us from something worse. That’s not madness. That’s kindness no one understands. I believe when we spiral, it’s her showing us the way she walked. And hoping we turn back sooner.
WIDDERSNAP: Final question. The ink you use in your writings—is it hers?

YURUME: The Tear That Writes Itself. Yes. I do not harvest it. It finds me. When a truth becomes too sharp to swallow, it drips from the corners of my eyes. I write with it. This journal entry is written in it.
WIDDERSNAP: Gods. That would mean… some readers—
YURUME: May not be real. Or may no longer be whole. Or may have read something that erases itself. Be careful, Professor. If you read your own notes too often, they may begin reading you.
I closed the journal without speaking. They did not wave. Did not smile. Only placed another mask upon their face—this one blank, rimmed in wax.
The mirror behind me no longer showed my reflection.
I am logging this entry here, in triplicate. The original I’ve sealed in ash and wax. One copy I will send to the Dreambound Archives. The other… I will burn.
Filed under inkstain, candlelight, and a quiet I am not yet ready to name.

title.en-US: On Cairn-Tenders: An Interview with the Professor

content.value: Field Notes of Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III
Twilight Scriptorium, Coralveil – Volume VII: Dialogues with the Spirit-Faithful
Entry #78: The Wound That Walks – Words on Malgrotha
Conducted beneath the Ash-Wing Lanterns, Thornwatch Camp, Western Verge of the Crawling Canopy
Interview Subject: Oruun Hollowbrow, Cairn-Tender, Bone-Binder of the Eastern Dead, Silent Watcher of the Crawling Canopy’s Verge

The wind was wrong when I arrived. Not strong. Just wrong. It stirred the smoke of the campfire sideways, then back on itself, then straight up—like it forgot how to behave. Oruun Hollowbrow squatted beside the flame, a badger-blooded Kemari whose age had folded him in half but not slowed his tongue. He stirred a pot of pine sap and ash and asked if I was “here to name the wound.”
He didn’t smile. Just tossed another thorn branch into the fire and nodded for me to begin writing.
“There are some things too angry to die,” he said.

“And what lives on past the wound is not always what was. Malgrotha… he was once two. That’s what the carvings say—if you trust the First Markings, scratched in stone before even the breath of storms. Rabbit and crow. Joy and sorrow. Laughing and watching.”
He scraped his claws along the rim of the pot and muttered something I didn’t catch. Then louder:

“The rabbit got hurt. Not a scratch kind of hurt. A soul-deep one. Mortals did it, maybe. Or the spirit-forged relics. Or both. When the First Age rose with its gears and ghost-lanterns, some spirits tried to understand. This one… couldn’t. Couldn’t grasp the wanting without taking. So he split. Rabbit fled. Crow stayed. And kept watching. Grew sharp.”
I noted this resembled other spirit-divisions—echoes of duality, of balance broken. Oruun spat.

“Don’t go comparing it like it’s a myth lesson. This ain’t allegory. This is a wound still bleeding. The crow isn’t a villain. He’s what’s left when the giving half disappears. Envy ain’t evil. It’s a mirror. That forest—Crawling Canopy? That’s what envy becomes when it has roots.”

He told me of shapes he’s seen in the branches. Things with cages for ribs. Feathers that bleed moss. Laughter that mimics your own voice, but twisted. No shrine welcomes this spirit. But its presence is marked in other ways.
“Dead vines. Crooked feathers. Thorn circles laid flat and brittle. Never green. We draw the Ash-Wing Sigil with our off-hand. If you do it right-handed, the crows learn your voice.”

He described the curse-bearers—Dark Elves who sing to anger, Kaido who tattoo their palms and bury themselves to dream the roots. Kemari with bark nailed into their backs, punishing themselves in rhythm with the spirit’s grief.
“You ever hear a scream made of wind? Not wind through something. Wind itself screaming? That’s what happens when someone speaks the name at the wrong time. Say it once per night. Never twice.”
I asked if he believed the tale of the rabbit half still dreaming somewhere in the Hollow Murkway.
He looked at me. Eyes like carved coal.
“Hope’s a fine lie. But lies don’t stop forests. I’ve seen what happens to orchards. To villages. Joy don’t root itself in cages.”
There was one tale I pressed him on—the one where the crow half flew high enough to ask the moon why it let things die.
He went quiet. Stirred the fire.
“He came back wrong. That’s all I’ll say. Flight like that never ends clean.”
Before I left, he handed me a pouch of dead thorns and told me to burn one whenever I dreamed of cages. I thanked him.
Just turned toward the trees. Listening.
“He’s not a demon,” he said one last time.
“He’s what you become when grief festers without song.”
