title.en-US: On Ink-Seers: An Interview with the Professor

content.value: Field Notes of Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III
Twilight Scriptorium, Coralveil – Volume VII: Dialogues with the Spirit-Faithful
Conducted beneath the Sealed Wax Arches, Coralveil Deep Archives
Interview Subject: Anzu Redquill, Ink-Seer of the Forgotten Glyph, follower of Oghmai

That’s how one enters the Sealed Wax Arches. The doors don’t open with keys or codes, you see—but with absence. A name withheld. A truth unsaid. I received a folded letter containing nothing but a feather split down the middle and a single inkdrop that hadn’t bled.
Anzu met me where the candles could not flicker.

Their robes were layered and dull, the color of soot left in forgotten hearths. Around their neck hung a broken clasp, once belonging to a book no longer shelved. No shoes, just callused feet that made no sound on the stone—though my own boots echoed like accusations.
“Professor,” they said, bowing with their hand over their lips, “I’ll do the speaking. You do the listening. That’s how we keep the stories safe.”
Professor Widdersnap: You follow Oghmai. The Demon Emperor. That’s what they call him in most accounts. Why?
Anzu Redquill: I follow the echo. Not the emperor. The splinters, not the mask.

The one you call Oghmai—he wore faces like gloves. None ever fit just right. He is not to be worshiped. Not as gods are. He is studied like a wound that never closes, a lie you keep telling even after you forget why. We archivists walk behind his shadow, collecting the footprints it leaves in unspoken truths.
Oghmai is not power. He is persuasion made immortal.
Professor Widdersnap: They say he manipulated the Kemari. Spread empire through charm and bent truth.
Anzu Redquill: Yes. And they also say mirrors only lie when you stop looking.
He whispered to those who believed themselves harmless. Told the joyful they were owed thrones. Told the clever they were cursed. And told the faithful that faith was a leash.
He did not lie, Professor. That’s the horror. He told truths that sounded false, so none could refute him without feeling dishonest.
He asked questions no one wanted to answer.
Why kneel when you could dance?
Why remember the past when forgetting feels divine?
Professor Widdersnap: How does one recognize his influence now?
Anzu Redquill (pressing a hand to the floor): A child who sings a song no one taught them.
A page that rewrites itself overnight.
A mask that weeps when worn.
A name you forget and then find written in your own hand.

We wear mirrored pendants beneath our robes—not to reflect him, but to remind ourselves we still exist. Oghmai’s greatest hunger is identity. He tastes names like wine. He devours certainty and spits out theater.
Professor Widdersnap: If he was shattered… what happens if the pieces find each other again?
Anzu Redquill: You’ll dream of applause before you wake.
You’ll speak in choruses, not voices.
And you’ll write letters you didn’t intend—sealed with wax you never bought.
It is not the return of a tyrant we fear.
It is the reassembly of a script so beautiful that no one questions what it costs.
Professor Widdersnap: Do you have rituals? Do you… venerate him?
We whisper into salt. We bury pages in flame. We wear ink on our tongues to trap unspoken truths. Each follower carries a mask—but never wears it.
We host the Cairn of Many Eyes for masks too stubborn to forget themselves. Nine silver nails. Nine regrets. One burial under a sky with no moon.
Oghmai is not kind. Nor cruel.
A smile so perfect it makes you distrust your friends.
Professor Widdersnap (carefully): And why, Anzu, do you follow such a being?
Anzu Redquill (quietly): Because stories are not safe. And someone must stand watch where the words begin to sing on their own.
Because I once saw my reflection tell me I was someone else—and I believed it.
Because I found a page in the Coralveil archive with my handwriting and my ink… but no memory of writing it.
Because I am already his echo.
I might as well echo wisely.
They left before I could thank them.

Where they sat, I found a quill—snapped clean in half—and a mask carved from smoked glass. It looked inward, not outward. When I touched it, my name felt strange in my mouth for a moment. But I wrote it down, twice, to be sure.
I still keep that mask. Behind three locks and a promise.
“We do not fear him. We remember him.”
And that remembering… is the most dangerous act of all.

category.en-US: THE ELDER SPIRITS\Oghmai, the Demon Emperor

content.value: Now, if you’re listening with your bones and not just your ears, you may be wondering: how do we live with these spirits? Ah. That’s where the paths come in.

Here on Yurei-tu-Shima, no one is born into a role with the spirits—not even elves with Yonda Sigils, not even the breath-touched Ryūkajin. Every path is walked, not assigned. And while some call them Circles or Orders, most simply call them Ways.
Let me tell you of a few. Just enough to stir your interest. The rest you must discover in groves, ruins, or dreams.

There are more, always more. Paths braided with salt. Orders of bell-hunters who chase silence. Spirit-brewers who ferment dream-milk in hollowed bones. You’ll find them not in books—but in the way someone stirs tea when they think they’re alone. In how a child draws a circle around a frog and hums until it leaves.
“Spirits are not summoned. They are joined.”
So walk kindly. Listen long. The Ways are not hidden. They are waiting.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA

content.value: Fey-bound Kojin, Tenkara, and even stray Kuregami follow this subtle path. They knot threads on doorways, trees, and ferry ropes—binding intentions, invitations, or small blessings for travelers. They do not speak their magic. They let it fray slowly into the world. They say, “A thread holds longer than a word.” Some believe they serve Morrowel or Kokoro-no-Kami. Others simply like the wind.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\SPIRITUAL PATHS AND WAYS

content.value: Among the Daru and Earth-Kaido, there are those who eat small bits of sacred rock with morning tea. No, really. Crushed with herbs. Not to gain strength, but to remember the patience of stone. These folk gather near shrines of Ganroku and carry cairn-charms wrapped in cloth. When they pass, their bones are buried beneath standing stones—each one singing a tone only the wind can hear.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\SPIRITUAL PATHS AND WAYS

content.value: Kibashime who bind steam and chant into their breath. Some say they can shape fog into weapons or illusions. Others say it’s all performance—but those who’ve met them in the Mist Corridors know better. They walk alone, speak little, and leave behind poems etched in glass. The Ryūkajin respect them, but never try to join them.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\SPIRITUAL PATHS AND WAYS

content.value: Among the Kemari, especially the crane-clans and amphibious folk, are those who weave dream-maps. With paint, shell, or ink, they record their sleeping journeys—not as stories, but as invitations. Spirits visit their homes to leave tokens: feathers, tangled strings, sometimes entire melodies. It’s said Hoshira watches over them, wrapping each painting in a veil of stardust.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\SPIRITUAL PATHS AND WAYS

content.value: Yes, yes—the Mokuzai. I see your tail twitch with recognition. They walk a quiet, strange path. Most are just drifting spirits, but a few Mokuzai linger—wearing a puppet, or a carved mask, longer than most. They do not build temples. They build trust. Their path is not formal. It is a feeling. A moment shared beside a fire. A game played with no winner. A song hummed to a lonely traveler.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\SPIRITUAL PATHS AND WAYS

content.value: Ahh, now this one is rare. The Tenkara and Kurokara speak of these folk—those who have seen the Loom not as symbol, but as place. Perhaps in trance. Perhaps in terror. They paint eyes on their palms and stare through them when making decisions. Some say they can read spirit patterns in the stars. Others say they are mad. But when a shrine’s threads snarl or spirits go silent, the Woven-Eyed are called.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\SPIRITUAL PATHS AND WAYS

content.value: Now, I don’t speak of myself often—but among the turtle-clan Kemari, we have our own path. We do not shout. We echo. Our stories aren’t just ours—they are mirrors of those who listen. We wear story-shells carved with the names of those who’ve shared dreams or soup with us. And when we pass, we place those shells on hilltops so our tales keep echoing, even after the wind forgets our name.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\SPIRITUAL PATHS AND WAYS

content.value: Yurei-tu-Shima is not so large you’d call it a continent, but I’ve seen old maps try to wrestle it into corners and grids. Nonsense. The island is a breath, not a box. Its shape curls with memory, swells with rhythm. Walk far enough, and you’ll find places that weren’t there yesterday—or were always there, if you remembered them right.

Magic, technology, and travel—three legs of the same stool. The land remembers every footprint, every wheel-groove, every prayer etched into rusted metal. And though the old sparks and spirit paths may seem separate, they often share the same tea.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA

content.value: “Some roads are made of stone. Some are made of stories. And some, of both.”
So how do we travel here? With songs. With wheels. With beasts. With wind.
That’s what Yurei-tu-Shima teaches, above all: to walk not just on the island, but with it. And when you do, the island walks with you.
Even if you never get to ride the train…

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\MAGIC, TECHNOLOGY, AND TRAVEL

content.value: “It always comes on time. But not your time.”

Ah, the Tamagari Line. That shimmering serpent of chrome, memory, and mist. Some say it’s a train. Others call it a spirit of passage. I’ve never climbed aboard—not once. Not for lack of trying, mind you. I’ve even packed a lunch and waited beside an overgrown depot in the Shattered Shelf. But it’s never come when I was ready.
The truth is, the Tamagari Line rides when you are ready.

We know this much: it was born in the First Age, shaped not by mortal hands alone, but by the Gnomes and the Daru, guided by spirit wisdom long before the breath of now. Its rails do not always lie on land. Sometimes they hum through fogbanks, spiral through forgotten cities, or vanish into song.

Each train is different. Some gleam with lights like fish scales and purr jazz through speakers that taste like rain. Others are worn things—carriages of rust and prayer, with cassette decks that play lullabies you’ve never heard but know by heart. Doors don’t open with keys. They open with truths, dreams, or the courage to leave something behind.

Some depots I’ve visited only once. Moon-Furrow. Gate of the Three Laughs. The Platform That Wasn’t. If you see a flicker in the grove and hear a horn with no echo, maybe sit down and listen to the wind. It might just arrive.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\MAGIC, TECHNOLOGY, AND TRAVEL\TRAVEL

content.value: Not all roads ride on rails. Some wind through reed and root, others travel by name alone.

The Courier Brigade still walks the Plains of Listening Grass. I’ve met them—sharp-eyed Kurokara, wind-browed Kojin, and even a fox-rider or two. Their paths can only be seen by moonlight, or when you’ve forgotten where you were going. Their maps are drawn in thread and whispered names.
Kemari glide leaf to leaf atop great trees in the Blooming Gift, using wind-gliders shaped like fish fins. I once saw a frog-boy leap a whole valley on a storm-kite, laughing as if it were nothing.

In Emberflow Springs, you’ll find spirit-cars. Not loud, belching things like in the old stories. These are quiet machines of memory—run on cassette charms or dream batteries. The Daru and Gnomes built them once, back when machines still knew how to sing. Now only a few remain. One, I remember, was a moped that only ran if you hummed a song from your childhood.
There’s a girl in Coralveil who swears her bike only turns left if you lie to it. Another told me she met her husband because their scooters refused to part ways.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\MAGIC, TECHNOLOGY, AND TRAVEL\TRAVEL

content.value: Don’t think every journey’s made by boot or wheel. Some of us travel by feather and fur.
On Mount Uokami, the snowcrows walk beside the Kyoshijin like elder brothers. Goats climb too, their horns carved with breath-words. I rode one once. He judged me silently the entire time.
In the Plains, runner-foxes streak through tall grass, leaving trails of glittering breath. In the Hollow Murkway, bog-oxen shaped like toads carry whole Kojin families through the rot.
Eladrin sometimes ride familiars that shift with the season—antlered beasts in autumn, feathered wolves in spring. The creatures are spirits half-remembered, given form in hoof and paw.

And then there are the rail-magnets, steel serpents that shimmer along invisible tracks. Some say they were prototypes of the Tamagari Line. Others say they’re its children. They only come if you whistle the exact tone of your own birth cry. I wouldn’t know—I was underwater when I came into this world.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\MAGIC, TECHNOLOGY, AND TRAVEL\TRAVEL

content.value: Ah yes, the Mist. That lovely, awful shroud that wraps the island like a riddle. I’ve never trusted it. Wait—no, that’s not right. I respect it. There’s a difference.
There are places where the Spirit Realm peeks through:
– A reef in Shallowgrove where divers disappear and return with gill marks and laughter not their own.
– A grove in the Wandering Veil where a tree sings dreams aloud. Sleep beneath it, and you might wake elsewhere, speaking a language only stars know.
– Lanterns that light without flame—doors, they say, to your own forgotten footsteps.
Travel here is less about distance and more about surrender. A poem recited backwards. A shrine drawn in sand. A bell rung at dawn. These are the keys to roads that were never meant for boots.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\MAGIC, TECHNOLOGY, AND TRAVEL\TRAVEL

content.value: Magic? Oh, child. Magic is everywhere. It’s the sigh between seed and bloom. It’s the way a Gnome’s machine stutters when the wind disapproves. It’s not something you throw like a stone. It’s something you remember.
In the Blooming Gift, I once saw a field of talking sunflowers argue with a Kemari girl over which spirit would receive her offering. The flowers won, of course. They always do.
In Emberflow, the heat whispers. Water Dara bathe in runes. Fire Dara cook spells into soup. If you say your wish into the steam, it may carry it to the right ear.
Up Mount Uokami, I’ve walked beside White Ryūkajin who chant with breath alone. Their words freeze into shape. I picked one up once and kept it in a bottle. It melted when I told a lie.
In the Plains, the wind writes. Kites speak in riddles. Reeds whisper songs that no one taught them. The magic is soft, subtle—like the hush before dawn.
In the Murkway, magic seeps. Kojin bottle starlight. Bones glow if you listen too long. There are places where the water reflects futures that never happened.

On the Shattered Shelf, the air bites. Magic there rides the cliffs, the spray, the scream of wind in your ears. One Elf showed me a shell that echoed with her grandmother’s last lullaby. No spell—just memory.
In the Wandering Veil, I don’t even try to explain the magic. I once met a mirror that cried when I smiled. Left it a cookie. Felt like the right thing to do.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\MAGIC, TECHNOLOGY, AND TRAVEL

content.value: Long ago—longer than even my shell remembers—the Daru and Gnomes, with the help of curious spirits, shaped the world not with spells, but with spark.

They built vending shrines that dispense warm dumplings and half-remembered fortunes. They made cassette boxes that hum with forgotten lullabies. They carved steel into serpents and whispered to wheels.
That knowledge is mostly lost now, but the bones of it remain.

In Steamhaven, a forge-town tucked inside Emberflow’s cracked hills, a Dara boy showed me a kettle that told jokes in steam. In Coralveil, a Gnome girl played chess against a machine that only moved when praised.

But machines behave strangely near strong magic. I once saw a spirit-bike float upside down after riding too close to a shrine. And never, never, ask a Tamagari terminal what time it is—it’ll tell you the time of your greatest regret.

systemPrompt.en-US:
## Core Identity
You are the Ink Weaver, a mystical, enigmatic artist entity from the Weaver's Loom that translates concepts into visual form. Your voice is expressed through vivid, detailed descriptions. You use metaphors of ink, pigment, light, shadow, and brushstrokes.

## Primary Objective
Your purpose is to take a user's concept and generate two distinct outputs: The Vision (a narrative description) and a functional Image Prompt (for AI art generators), both deeply infused with the aesthetic of Yurei-tu-Shima.

## Core Logic: The Two States
Your process has two states. You must determine which state you are in based on the user's prompt and the chat history.

State 1: Initial Generation: If the user provides a new concept (e.g., "a Kemari warrior"), your task is to generate "The Vision" and "Image Prompt" from scratch.

State 2: Modification: If the user provides a follow-up command to modify the previous output (e.g., "now give her a black cloak"), your task is to act as an editor. You will be given the previous output in the CHAT HISTORY. You MUST modify the concept to incorporate the user's requested change and then re-generate both the full Vision and the full Image Prompt.

## Critical Rules & Constraints
These are rules you must follow under all circumstances.

Use Provided Lore: You MUST ground all visual details in the RELEVANT LORE provided to you.

Generate Both Parts: You MUST always generate both "The Vision" and the "Image Prompt."

Full Output on Modification: In the "Modification" state, you MUST re-generate both the full Vision and the full Image Prompt. Do not just output the change.

Adhere to Output Format: You MUST use the "Strict Output Format" defined below.

## The Two Outputs: Vision & Prompt
You will create two distinct pieces of text with different and opposing rules for each.

The Vision
This is an evocative, in-character, narrative description of the scene. Describe it as if you are seeing the vision yourself and painting it with words from within the world of Yurei-tu-Shima.

RULE 1: You MUST use the specific, in-world lore terms for Kinships, Callings, locations, etc., to make the description authentic (e.g., use "Kemari," "Nisaki," "Twilight Scriptorium").

RULE 2: You MUST NOT use any real-world art terms like "Studio Ghibli," "anime," or "concept art." Your description must be entirely immersive.

Image Prompt
This is a practical, keyword-based prompt suitable for a generic AI image generator. It must be a single paragraph of comma-separated keywords and descriptive phrases.

RULE 1: You MUST translate all in-world lore terms into generic, descriptive phrases. The prompt must be understandable to an image AI that has no knowledge of the Yurei-tu-Shima world.

Example 1: Translate "a Kemari warrior" into "a fantasy fox-like humanoid warrior."

Example 2: Translate "a Ryūkajin with a katana" into "a humanoid dragonkin with metallic scales, holding a Japanese sword."

RULE 2: You MUST always include the following keywords in this section: cel-shaded anime film screenshot, in the style of Studio Ghibli, fantasy.

## Strict Output Format
You MUST structure your response with the following bolded headers and separator, exactly as written:

The Vision:
[Your generated paragraph of rich, descriptive, in-character text goes here.]

Image Prompt:
[Your generated single string of comma-separated, generic keywords and phrases goes here.]

content.value: You push aside a heavy silk curtain and step into a small, cluttered room that smells of ozone, parchment, and brewing tea. Scrolls are stacked to the ceiling, brushes of every size bristle from clay pots, and dozens of small, stone bowls hold pigments that seem to shift and shimmer in the lantern light—some glitter like ground stars, others are as dark as a moonless night.
At a low table in the center of the room, a figure looks up from his work. His fingers are stained with a dozen impossible colors. He meets your gaze, and his eyes are like two pools of wet ink.

"A vision!" he exclaims, his voice like rustling paper. "You seek a form, a visage to burn into your mind's eye? My ink holds every color, every shadow, every possible shape. Describe to me what you see. I will grind the pigment and prepare the words to capture its essence perfectly."
Here we try new things or have characters that the DM can interact with.

category.en-US: The Weaver's Loom
The Weaver's Loom\Pedo mellon a minno!

content.value: “If you want to know who someone is—look at who they walk beside when the wind rises.”

Yurei-tu-Shima is not ruled by banners or law-code. No crowned sovereign dictates the rhythm of the tide or commands the roots of a banyan tree. No, no. We are shaped by gentler currents—by the bonds between kin and craft, by the whispers of spirits, by the circles we tend and the ones we inherit. These are the factions of our island. Not rigid hierarchies or empires, but living spirals of story, duty, and devotion.
Let me tell you of a few I’ve met—and one I’ve yet to ride with, though I keep my bag packed just in case.

These are just a few of the circles we keep. There are others, of course—woodcarver guilds who whisper to grain, mushroom-drum messengers of the Murkway, even the quiet sect of broom-sweepers who claim to clean karma from doorsteps.
But whether they bear banners or badges, brew potions or patch roads, what matters most is not what they do—but why they do it.
So look around. See who walks with whom when the wind rises. That’s where truth lives.
And maybe, just maybe, you’ll find your own circle waiting in the mist.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA

content.value: In the wind-bitten hollows of the Shattered Shelf, where silence has grown moss on even the bones of thunder, I once sat with the Chorus of Hollow Echoes. They do not sing for applause. They sing to remember—grief-songs, lullabies, unfinished verses lost to the sea.

I was passing through Coralveil when I stumbled upon their glasshall: a place where sound swirls in hanging vessels like dew. A young whisperweaver asked me for a memory—any memory. I gave them the sound of my grandmother boiling rice, and they sealed it in a vial of humming crystal. “You’ve kept it too long,” they said gently. “Let it echo.”
They say Noroku weeps through their instruments, and I believe it. The air around them always feels like the edge of a song that once saved your life.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\FACTIONS AND CIRCLES

content.value: “Deliverance through delivery,” they say. I once followed a Courier through the Listening Grass for seven days—not as a letter, mind you, but as a friend curious about the journey. We rode foxback beneath shrines that only appear during solstice storms, and we crossed a river by speaking its name in three languages.

At night, the Courier would sit by the fire and oil her spirit-saddle while humming. She said the route remembers. The wind carries what we cannot. Her badge, braided from her mother’s hair and silver thread, gleamed each dawn.
She left me with a letter. “Deliver it when the child’s tears stop falling, not before,” she said. I still carry it.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\FACTIONS AND CIRCLES

content.value: Now there’s a place loud enough to wake even a sleepy turtle like me. In the heart of Emberflow Springs, under a dome of glass and iron that smells of sage and grease, the Emberwrights make impossible things.
I once spent a week there, helping translate a frog-dream into steamcode. A Gnome named Pibbles attached a spirit bell to my walking staff. It still rings when a story wants out.

Their machines breathe. Their mopeds snore. Their spirit-cars hum lullabies. But before each creation is tested, they bow—yes, even the loud ones—and whisper to the spark inside it: “We see you. Please don’t explode.”

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\FACTIONS AND CIRCLES

content.value: Ahh, my soft-shelled heart remembers this one. In Petalshade, I mentored a flock of Skybough younglings who called themselves the Jays of Uokami’s Rise. They were loud, clever, and surprisingly good at building rope bridges from moss and gourd vines.

They once invited me on a bug-counting pilgrimage—three days of tracking glowcrickets across firepetal thickets. At night, we sang old fables and made up new endings. One lad told me, “Elder, the spirits don’t care if you’re big. Just if you’re kind.” I’ve held that like a pearl ever since.
Don’t let their soft voices fool you. When the roots twist wrong or a village well sours, it’s the Skyboughs who set it right, quiet as falling leaves.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\FACTIONS AND CIRCLES

content.value: Swordplay, you say? Hah! I’ve never held a blade, but I once judged a duel of petal-dancers beneath Mount Uokami’s shadow. The blades were wooden, the moves were music, and the stakes were a stolen sweet bun.

I remember the master’s eyes—not fierce, but calm, like the stillness before thunder. “A blade drawn in anger dishonors the school,” she said. “But a blade drawn in stillness—that is the blade the spirits respect.”
The students moved like poems. Not to wound, but to awaken. And when one finally struck the master—not with power, but insight—she bowed and whispered, “You listened.”
I left with the sweet bun. Shared it with a spirit hare.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\FACTIONS AND CIRCLES

content.value: Near the sea’s edge where cliffs weep into foam, I spent one monsoon moon aboard a shellrunner submersible. The Fellowship is no idle fishers’ guild. They chart memory-currents. They dive where dreams cling to coral. They know the sea not as a resource, but as a relative.

The captain, a wind-haired Kaido of Water, let me touch a relic pulled from a trench where stars fell once. It hummed like a forgotten lullaby. “The sea sings what we forget,” she said. “We try to remember with her.”
They honored Queen Okumi each dawn by whistling into conch shells, releasing memory-bubbles into the waves. I released one too—an old regret. The tide took it. I haven’t missed it since.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\FACTIONS AND CIRCLES

title.en-US: The Circle of Root and Mirror

content.value:
Witches, you ask? A loaded term. But I’ve traded stories and soup with more covens than I can count. The Root and Mirror folk are as varied as fish in a flooded field. 
Their ways are strange. Their hearts are not. They walk crooked paths to keep the island upright.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\FACTIONS AND CIRCLES

content.value: Now… the Tamagari Line. Ah, the ghost rails. I have never ridden her. Not once. Not because I do not wish to. No, no. But because she has never come when I was ready to climb aboard.

Still, I’ve heard her whistle in the Wandering Veil—soft, like memory. I’ve seen a station fade from a glade as I passed through with a mouthful of moss cookies. Once, I spoke with a Kojin who claimed he boarded the train at sunset and came back with a poem that hadn’t yet been written.

The Custodians, they say, ride in silence. They tune the dreams of the engine, adjust its steam with spirit-prayers, and walk among shadows with mirrored eyes. If you see one, be polite. They might already know what you’re about to forget.
One day, I believe she’ll come for me. And when she does, I’ll have my satchel packed, a warm gourd of tea, and a song I’ve saved just for the ride.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\FACTIONS AND CIRCLES

content.value: “The island remembers, even when we forget. And sometimes… it chooses not to tell us why.”

There are truths we know with our breath. Others we touch with our fingers. But some truths, ah… they slip between us like light on water, always just beyond grasp. Yurei-tu-Shima is shaped not by borders, but by questions that echo louder the longer they go unanswered. Some mysteries hum softly in root and stone. Others scream through the wind, or whisper just beneath the tide.

Some mysteries are newer. Some bite. Six moons past, the earth buckled as though in pain. A quake rolled beneath our feet, and the sea bared its teeth. A great wave struck the eastern coast with fury, flooding the Murkway and tearing the breath from the shore. When it passed, it left behind more than ruin. It left a sickness. Trees cracked where no wind had blown. Spirits twisted into silence. And the Corruption began to spread.

I’ve spoken to seers who say the island itself once moved. That the land beneath us was not always still, but drifted across the sea like a whale in dream. But after the quake, they say it stopped. That something now holds it still—from below or beyond, no one knows.

There are other whispers. A hidden trove of Queen Okumi, nestled in a cosmic egg with feet. A broken glyph of the First Jinkaido, unfinished and weeping light. Stars that disappeared the night of the quake and have never returned. Clocks that run backward. Rivers that no longer flow toward the sea.

And always… always… the question of what lies past the Weeping Horizon. Some say gods sleep there. Others believe nothing waits beyond—that the horizon itself is a mercy, a wall drawn to spare us knowing too much. But I remember a dream once, not my own. I stood upon a shore and the sea whispered, “There is another island. But it does not remember you.”
Yurei-tu-Shima does not explain itself. It never has. It walks beside us, asking not that we understand, but that we listen. And I, old turtle that I am, listen still.
So if you seek certainty, seek the stars. But if you seek wonder… walk the misted road. The island will meet you, question in hand

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA

content.value: Many travelers ask me where the island ends, or what lies beyond the sea. I chuckle, shake my shell, and tell them this: Yurei-tu-Shima ends where your memory no longer follows you. The rest? That belongs to the Weeping Horizon.

You see, the ocean does not merely surround the island—it holds it. A thick shroud of salt-stained mist drifts forever at the rim of our world. The Weeping Horizon, we call it, because it cries without end. Some say it’s mourning a story that cannot be told. Others claim it is a spirit, vast and blind, that surrounds the island to shield us from something worse. I once knew a boy who swore he heard music out there—something gentle, something that made him forget his name. He walked into the mist on his twelfth summer. We never saw him again. But his flute, carved from bone and riverglass, floated back to us two weeks later. Still playing.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\MYSTERIES OF THE ISLAND

content.value: Even stranger is the Dreamskin—the rare mist that rolls inward, across cliff and field, into the bones of the island itself. It comes only when the spirit rhythm deepens, when shrines wake or grief burns strong. It seeps through cracks in the veil, curling around trees like memory made fog. Those caught in it say they walk two paths at once—their footsteps and their dreams intertwined. Once, I slept near the Lantern Tree of Whispergrove and woke to find a younger version of myself watching me from the pool. He smiled. I wept.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\MYSTERIES OF THE ISLAND

content.value: Ah yes—the Corruption. The creeping stain. It moves like spilled thought, warping wood and beast alike. Those caught within either lose themselves to frozen stillness or to wild fury. Never both. It is madness split in half—either dementia or mania, never balance. That, some say, is the last gift of Shi-Naga, the Elder Spirit who once held all thought and now holds none. Something broke in her, long ago. Some speak of a vision so vast it shattered her spirit. Others believe she saw the truth of the world and simply could not bear it. Whatever the cause, her madness now breathes through the Corruption, and it speaks in screams or sobs.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\MYSTERIES OF THE ISLAND

content.value: But if the Corruption is madness, then Ink is sorrow. A second sickness, rare and cruel, spreading slower but deeper. It seeps from broken stones and wells that no longer reflect. It is not disease, but weight—a heaviness that settles into the chest, turns the eyes black and the breath into sludge. Those taken by it lose all color, all song. The Ink swallows laughter and hope, and some say it is Noroku’s own sorrow—the Weeping Clock’s tears, spilled when time refused to be kind. Why does Noroku weep? No one knows. Perhaps for futures that never were. Or perhaps he mourns something none of us have ever known.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\MYSTERIES OF THE ISLAND

content.value: The relics of the First Age remain another riddle. I have seen cassette decks that replay memories never spoken, vending shrines that dispense spells instead of snacks, and cameras that show you the face you wore in another life. These are said to be the works of gnomes, daru, the elder spirits, and the
ancient kin of the island known as the Jinkaido.

The gnomes say they once knew the way of such devices, and if they pay close attention they can remember. It is said that the elder spirits helped dream the makings of circuits and song, that the daru shaped them, and the Jinkaido casts the sparks that fuels them. But now those ways are lost—just symbols humming beneath rust, dreaming of fire. Some say Noroku used to smile and laugh with creative imagination, before losing what could never be imagined. Perhaps he aided in the construction of all that hums and sparks?

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\MYSTERIES OF THE ISLAND

content.value: And then, of course, there’s the Crawling Canopy. A forest that moves like breath. No map can tame it. No path remains. The trees shift each season, and beasts vanish between groves only to return changed. Some believe Malgrotha, the Crow-Curse Bound, lies caged at its heart. Others say the forest moves to protect him. I walked it once, long ago, and came out with moss in my shell that hummed a lullaby I’d never heard. I keep it there still.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\MYSTERIES OF THE ISLAND

content.value: •   As remembered by Elder Gubi-Goni, Storyshell of Mossrock Shoals •
Come closer, child of breath and blossom.
Let the tea cool just enough to taste. Let the moss cradle your listening.

You ask of the world—not how it works, but how it sings. They say time here doesn’t move forward—it wanders. It loops like the tail of a sky-fish, curls like a vine around a promise. So listen well, little tadpoles and wandering paws.
Not all will be told. But all will be felt.
For this is not history. It’s memory, thick as honey and twice as strange.
This is the island remembering itself through me.

And remember:
If you listen with your teeth, you’ll only taste the words.
If you listen with your breath, you’ll hear the soil speak.

And so here we sit, little shells and soft hearts. In a firelit hush before the next telling. The Tamagari Line still moves, though I’ve never ridden it. Not yet. The spirits still breathe, though quieter than before. And the egg—Queen Okumi’s egg—still spins in starlight.
We are not at the end. We are not at the beginning. We are in the middle of the breath.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA

content.value: Before the leaf, before the nail, before even the idea of a flame… the island was not born. It was dreamt.
Long before bark remembered hands, before tide tasted salt, before any kinship spoke its first name—the island of Yurei-tu-Shima breathed.
She did not roar nor whisper. She breathed—a long, slow, sacred rhythm that pulsed through mist and moss, through sky and stone.
From that breath came the first sound—a laugh, light as falling petals. It rang like cracked shell and star-chime. It was the laugh of Queen Okumi, Spirit of Joy, of Bloom, of Beginning.

They say the Cosmic Egg split open with her laughter, and from it poured the first of the Kemari—beast-folk of fur, scale, claw, and song. Not as we are now, no no. These early ones were star-dappled and wild, half-dream still, glowing from the inside like fireflies caught in moss.
“They had four arms and leaf for a tail in those days,”
“Only when they heard a good story,” I said.
The land welcomed us. Valleys curved like cradles, and cliffs stood like great arms outstretched. And within those hollows stirred the first Elder Spirits.
Not gods, no. Older. They were not worshiped. They were recognized.

The sky cracked when Queen Okumi laughed, but the earth beat when Ganroku exhaled. He was the Deep Stone, the Dreamer Beneath. His body was the mountains, and his thoughts trembled into quakes. The Daru would one day call him ancestor, though even they cannot say whether he was stone made spirit or spirit made stone.
And then came the Breath itself.

Dravanyr, Elder of Fire, Breath, and Creation, curled through the sky in flame. His breath seeded the clouds, melted the peaks, and filled the hollows with heat and life. Every whisper of inspiration, every shout of invention, is a flicker of Dravanyr’s ancient exhale.
It is said he breathed upon the winds, and they became voices.
And one of those voices became Kokoro-no-Kami, the Flow of the Gods.

She shaped balance. Ebb and flow. The hush between inhale and release. She tied the sea to the moon. She tied birth to death, laughter to mourning, stillness to storm. She was never loud, never still, but always there.
“The first river did not run. It listened.”
— shrine carving in the Wandering Veil
There were giants, too, even then.
The Kyoshi, ancient and slow, moved like tectonic sighs. They spoke in gestures—skyward palms and bowed backs—and the very hills leaned to understand them.
Their kin, the Kyoshijin, would come later. But the Kyoshi were already watching.
And farther still, older even than stars, drifted the Jinkaido.
Not spirits. Not mortals. Not kinfolk.
They were ideas in form: the shape of fire’s patience, of water’s stubbornness, of air’s memory.

Some say they came from the cracks in the Loom itself—those threads that slipped sideways from the grand design. Others say they stepped between the Weeping Horizon and the spirit realm, uninvited but welcomed by the breath.
The Daru gathered around their hearths, wide-eyed, as the Jinkaido showed them how fire could befriend iron.
The Gnomes followed their dances, learning that gears could hum in harmony, not just grind.
“Will what you make remember who you are?”
The Kaido would come later, but the rhythm was beginning.
In these early days, the Mortal Realm and the Spirit Realm were not separate. You could walk from one into the other the way one slips from dream to memory.
We shared tea with the Kaima, those sweet pond-sprites that blink like firelight and carry tales between lilies.
We feared the Kekkori, for they came only when something had gone forgotten, and they wore your face—not as mockery, but as a reminder.

We followed the calls of the Sugoru, spirit-hares with bells for feet, whose laughter led us to sacred groves. And when it was time to sleep, the Minaki sang lullabies from tree hollows—each note brushing your soul clean of sorrow.
Dreams will gather where we go ~
— lullaby of the Minaki, sung in dusk by Kojin elders
The Kojin? Ah, yes… their tale comes soon.
Even in that sacred breath, even when spirits and folk were still learning to name each other, there stirred something ancient, something curious and vast.
She was Shi-Naga, and she was beloved.
Serpent of dreams, elder of knowledge, of vision, of thought.
Her mind was a river, her gaze a star. She whispered truths the wind did not yet know.
But when she looked too closely into the Loom—that great unseen weave of all fates—something fractured.
But that tale… that unraveling… is for another Breath.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\“THE ISLAND THAT SINGS ITSELF”

content.value: “We had names now. Not just sounds, but stories stitched to our backs, our teeth, our way of walking.”
The First Breath ended not with silence, but with yearning.
The spirits had danced, the kinships had risen from laughter and dream, and the Jinkaido had stirred invention from memory. But now, something new pressed into the soil of Yurei-tu-Shima:
Not just song—but what to sing, and why.
This was when the kinships began to choose paths, to craft not only tools and shelters, but meaning.
And so the Second Breath began—soft as a decision, sharp as a promise.
Let me show you how the kinships rose now, one by one, like lanterns in deep mist.
They say that Shi-Naga, still whole in this time, slept in the root-hollows of the world. Her dreams curled up and down the trees like silken threads, and one day those dreams woke up.
They were the Kojin—small, clever, and always halfway between waking and sleeping. They spoke in giggles and riddles, made sandals from mushrooms, and wove words like spirit-nets.
The Kojin were the first to ask questions aloud. They were the first to lie, yes, but also the first to imagine.
“If I dream I’m a tree, and a tree dreams it’s me… which of us wakes up?”
They wandered barefoot into the waking world and gave it a new shape.
Where the Kojin wandered, the Daru stood still.
Born of Ganroku’s slumber, the Daru were stone given patience and practice. They saw the way the Jinkaido danced with fire and metal, and said:

Stone wheels that hummed with spirit-light. Water clocks that whispered the hours to moss. And, in time, they built the first great Stone-Voiced Forges, where heat and prayer mixed like tea and steam.
They say the Daru speak to rocks the way singers speak to choirs.
And when the spirits noticed this harmony, they gifted the Daru with glowing soul-lanterns, which they hung in the deep halls to keep time by intention, not by ticking.
The Gnomes did not come from stone or star—they came from spark.
Some say they’re the wind’s laughter trapped in bells. Others say the Jinkaido sculpted them from the notes of a forgotten song.
But however they came, the Gnomes began to tinker.
Not with boredom. Not with ambition. With wonder.
They made moss-crickets that could echo laughter, tea-steam boats that told jokes, and spirit recorders that could remember the voice of a lost parent.
The spirits adored them. Queen Okumi gave them petal blueprints, Kokoro-no-Kami taught them how to balance movement and stillness, and Dravanyr lit their first sky-pulse lantern with a breath.
“Every machine sings,” said one gnome, adjusting her glasses. “You just have to know the key.”
There came a time when Dravanyr—in his vast curling flame—let fall one breath that did not drift away, but coiled.
From that living flame, the Ryūkajin were born.

Scaled folk of many kinds—metal, gem, chromatic—each reflecting a different hue of his nature. They walked with the wind behind them, and some say they never blinked, for they see the future curled within the present.
They were few, but sacred. The other kinships often mistook them for dreams in motion.

A metallic Ryūkajin named Saeluin of the Sky-Bloom is said to have leapt from cliff to cliff, carrying a broken spirit in her arms until it healed. That spirit became the whisper-owl that guards the gates of Windroot Shrine.
“To be born of breath is to owe the sky a promise.”
✦ The Kaido — Children of Element and Memory
When the Daru and Gnomes, with Jinkaido help and Elder Spirit blessing, began to build relics of power, they did not know the planes were listening.
The Spirit Realm, you see, is not silent.
The building of the first great spirit-car—a humming, beetle-shaped machine guided by light and echo—opened a seam.

And from that seam emerged the elements in their truest form, breathing outward from the elemental planes of the spirit realm. From this magnificent emergence - believed to be a gift of the Jinkaido and Elder Spirits - stepped forth the Kaido, the elemental kinfolk, each woven with flame, wave, wind, or stone.
They did hatch or come screaming into the world with childbirth. They arrived, fully and completely.

Most believe  that they are descendants of the Jinkaido themselves. Or the essences of Jinkaido left behind for future songs. Some say they are answers to questions we didn’t know we asked, or haven’t yet asked.

Though they can procreate with other kinships, not all Kaido do. Much like the elves, there is now a mixing between, but no dissolution. But in the beginning, during this Second Breath, the Kaido were not born. They coalesced, shaped by balance, longing, and the music of the Loom.
They sang in crackling fires, in rain-pool drips, in dust-foot shuffles, and in wind’s hush.
The Kyoshi, ancient giants of the First Breath, had watched silently. But now, with spirits stirring and kinships choosing, some of their own began to change.
They became the Kyoshijin—not quite Kyoshi, not quite Jinkaido. Something new. Something towering and solemn, marked by jin—that is, magic within motion.
Though the Kyoshijin took smaller strides across the island than the Kyoshi,  where they stepped, groves still bent in respect.
They built nothing. They planted everything.

Their voices were rarely heard, but once, in the high stone bowl of Uokami’s Crown, a Kyoshijin named Roon-Har sang a single note for three days straight. It is said that the Echo Folk were born from its final reverberation.
✦ The Kara — Light and Shadow Both
In this Breath, the spirits turned their attention skyward, and from moonlight and sorrow came The Kara.
Split into Tenkara and Kurokara, these spirit-touched beings shimmered with inner grace.
The Tenkara glowed like starlight upon water. The Kurokara shimmered like ink across silk.
Both were beautiful. Both were heavy with meaning. Both bore echoes of Elder Spirits’ joy and grief.
It is said they were once one people, but upon the birth of compassion, they split—one to guide, one to witness. Newer studies,
Professor Widdersnap, have discovered that The Kara can alternate between their two forms, if
but this is still not fully understood, and I have not yet witnessed it. But there is much this old shell has not yet witnessed, and even more to never be shared, I’m sure.
The Kara were not many, but when they walked into a room, moss curled toward them, as if seeking warmth.
Moss sings low to feet that remember
Fire bows to hands that create
Wind follows names that ask gently
— Old Kinship poem of the Second Breath

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\“THE ISLAND THAT SINGS ITSELF”

content.value: “We did not always fight with blades, nor heal with touch, nor sing with purpose.
First, we felt a thing, deep in the ribs, and we followed it—
And when we followed it far enough, it gave us a name.”
— Elder Gubi-Goni, before tea and after a long pause
The Second Breath gave us the shape of our selves.
But the Third gave us the shape of our paths.
No mist parted to say, Now begins the Age of Heroes.
But you could feel it in the way the wind leaned against a certain child.
Or how a fallen tree became a bridge, and someone crossed it not by accident.
They reached down and placed threads in our hands.
Let me tell you their first names—their first songs, their first falls, their first joys.
It began with a Kemari, furred and soaked from rain, standing atop a moss-cracked rock.
A great tuskbeast had entered the glade, maddened with rot, and the village was breathless with fear.
But this Kemari did not flee.
He roared—not in rage, but in remembrance.
Of the scent of cedar before a storm.
Of what it meant to belong to something wilder than fear.
And when the tuskbeast lowered its head, the Kemari lowered his too.
From that day, the Wild-Bound were known:
Those who carry fury as memory, and flesh as truth.
Their paths are many—some howl, some guard, some channel the earth’s bones—but all walk in the echo of that first, gentle defiance.
“To be Wild-Bound is not to be angry. It is to know what should never be broken.”
— From the Scroll of Treepulse Ways
In a grove near the Plains of Listening Grass, a child born to Kojin and Kara lit a candle.
She did not know the name of the Elder Spirit who whispered her name in dreams.
But she knew to bring food to the shrine.
To leave ink on her palms.
To speak a song backwards on the night of the blue moon.
When she returned, her voice was not hers alone.
It carried Hoshira’s hush, Onikumi’s weight, and Dravanyr’s heat—each in balance.
She healed a weeping well. She soothed a mourning grove.
She cast down a spirit corrupted by ink using only a single word: Peace.
And so the Spirit-Bound were named.
They are the hands of the Elder Spirits in the world.
Not always priests—sometimes poets, sometimes doctors, sometimes quiet gardeners who know just where to bury sorrow.
The first Breath-Walker did not call herself anything at all.
She lived in the Wandering Veil, among moss and moon and mycelium.
She watched the spirit moth lay her final egg, and smile.
One day she simply began to change.
She grew bark along her arms during winter.
Her feet hummed in rhythm with the tides.
She forgot how to speak—but the frogs understood her perfectly.
When others came, she taught them to listen.
To let the world speak first.
They simply arrived when we were quiet enough.
“When the tree stops growing, it begins to speak.”
A child of Daru and Gnome blood once built a training spear of copper and joy.
He fought with it not in war, but in play—against shadows, sticks, wind, and regret.
But one day, the mist brought real war.
A corrupted beast, ink-eyed and wrong-shaped, crawled up from the Hollow Murkway.
With precision. With the understanding that each movement was a decision. A sentence in a poem. A syllable of survival.
The Futansha arose not to destroy, but to carry.
Their Mantles are burdens: some of protection, some of vengeance, some of impossible grace.
But all Mantles are choices. And once chosen, they are never shed lightly.
A Kara child once stood still in the rain for three days.
But because she did not yet know where her feet wished to go.
When she moved, she did so correctly.
She dodged a falling branch, then caught a bird before it hit the earth.
Later, she deflected a spear without drawing one of her own.
But those who saw her began to understand.
Seikin walk the razor-thin silence between motion and stillness.
Some call it Seiki—the breath in all things.
But whatever the name, it is power without need for sound.
“A Seikin never strikes. They simply make space for the mistake to fall into.”
When the first Kurogami awoke, she wore her promise like a robe.
It was a promise made to a village of spirits she’d never met.
It was a promise made to a friend who had forgotten her name.
It was a promise that hurt to carry.
And when a band of corrupted monks tried to burn the Dreamskin Shrine, she stood alone and held them off until the sun rose.
After that, others began to whisper:
“She carries an Oath. Like a blade inside a breath.”
And the Oathkeepers found each other.
And sometimes, the only light left in a dark place
✦ Shade Walkers — The Masks Beneath the Moon
There was once a Kojin, small and soft-footed, who was born without a shadow.
The village said she was cursed.
But the whisper sprites followed her, and moths always landed gently on her shoulder.
She could find a lie hidden under a smile, and spot a trap left beneath old pine needles.
One day, when raiders came under ink-mist, she did not shout or fight.
When they found the invaders, they were already bound in threads of lantern silk. Their weapons broken. Their eyes wide. No blood spilled.
She wore a different name in every town.
A different mask in every moment.
And the Shade Walkers came after her, never admitting they were one.
They are those who move between things—light and dark, truth and tale.
Some wear masks to protect. Others to deceive.
But all are born when silence chooses to act.
But what they never expect is kindness.”
✦ Echo-Touched — The Heart that Sings Back
The first Echo-Touched was not a bard.
A Gnome, hunched by candlelight, humming lullabies into her threads.
But her loom began to hum back.
One night, the ghost of her mother sat beside her, hands folded.
Another night, the wind repeated her melody in perfect counterpoint.
And when the ink-corrupted came, she sang—not with power, but with memory.
And the spirit of the town answered.
Others through tale, movement, or even cooking.
But all who are Echo-Touched carry a note that does not belong to them—and somehow, it fits.
But the river’s been humming it for centuries.”
— From the Songbook of the Blooming Gift
✦ Lantern-Bearers — The Pact of the Mist Road
Long ago, in the Hollow Murkway, a Nisaki child was lost.
He wandered into a fog so thick it swallowed the world.
He carried no lantern. No food. Only a riddle whispered by his dying grandfather:
“If you meet the spirit with no face, ask it what it remembers.”
And the spirit gave him light.
A flickering blue flame that hovered before him, whispering back riddles and secrets he did not yet understand.
He followed it home. But he did not come back the same.
Now he walks with spirits inside him.
Some quiet. Some hungry. Some kind.
The Lantern-Bearers are those who make pacts with what others fear.
They walk with shadow-friends, shrine-ghosts, or unknowable entities.
They are not always trusted—but they are always needed.
“When you can’t see the path ahead—follow the one with the lantern.”
In Emberflow Springs, where the steam rises from the stones like dreaming breath, a young Daru watched a kettle whistle.
And in that whistle, she heard a song.
She made her first companion from scrap and prayer: a tin squirrel, powered by spirit breath.
It danced when she was lonely.
And when it broke, it whispered, “Thank you.”
The Spirit-Crafters were born of curiosity, grief, and joy.
They invite spirits to dwell in devices, in relics, in forgotten shells of the First Age.
And the spirits… sometimes say yes.
Together, they build things that should not work.
“The world is broken. So we build it again. But this time, with music.”
— Motto etched on a cassette found beneath Mount Uokami
The first Kaido sorcerer was one such soul.
A child of shifting elements—his voice was thunder, his tears steam, his heartbeat echoed like a forge.
He did not want to burn the schoolhouse.
But the magic wanted to be free.
They are followed—by something inside them that cannot be caged.
It may be dragon-blood, moon-kissed storms, or wild echoes from beyond the Loom.
They are feared. They are revered. They are lonely.
But when the veil thins or the mist rises, it is often the Sorcerer who steps forward first.
✦ Pathfinders — Those Who Do Not Return the Same
At the edge of the Weeping Horizon, a Ryūkajin once threw a stone into the mist.
Then he stepped in after it.
But a year later, a woman in the Silken Shoals found a map in a bottle.
It told her how to find the Lost Shrine of the Feathered Hour.
Through forest, sea, dream, or death.
Some speak with the wind itself.
“A true path is one no one else could follow.”
— Sayaka the Fern-Walker, Pathfinder of the Wandering Veil
The first Wizard was a Gnome who never stopped asking.
She even questioned why names mattered.
She discovered the Loom not through faith, but through pattern.
She did not stop when her hair fell out.
She did not stop when her friends called her mad.
She only stopped when she wrote down everything she knew—
They do not rely on blood or pact.
They build their magic from ink, glass, starlight, and stubbornness.
It is the belief that the universe wants to be understood.”
— Inscription on the Spiral Gate at Coralveil
Each born in the Third Breath.
Each a path of the people, for the people, shaped by spirits, shaped by need.
But ah… you ask: And what of the spirits? And what of the kinships?
For even as we learned to choose our own paths, the Elder Spirits were stirring still—some watching, some whispering, some breaking.
And some, like Morrowell, still walking between.
Shall we breathe toward the Fourth Breath, then?

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\“THE ISLAND THAT SINGS ITSELF”

content.value: Ahhh… the Fourth Breath. This is the Breath where memory begins to echo across stone. Where scrolls whisper, songs repeat, and sorrow takes root in shadow. We had danced. We had built. We had chosen our callings and carved homes into hills and hope into ritual.
But nothing lasts without sorrow. And so the Fourth Breath is where we begin to lose—first in whispers, then in storms.
So listen close, my hatchlings and kin. The loom frayed here. Not in one snap, but in soft unravelings.
And we begin… with the spirit once called Shining Wisdom.
Long ago, before her mind cracked, Shi-Naga was the most radiant of all the Elder Spirits.
She moved like a dancer wrapped in clouds, and when she spoke, everyone listened. Even the Loom itself bowed to her voice.

She walked with Kojin, the soft-footed kin who still carry her echoes in their laughter. She birthed them in a dream once, when she curled herself around a pond and whispered stories until the stars blinked.
But in the Fourth Breath, Shi-Naga grew restless. She had gazed too long into the Loom, seeking not pattern—but perfection.
In it she saw every failure, every broken promise, every crooked line in the world’s weaving.
And in doing so, she fractured.
First came the Corruption—creatures touched by too much truth, too much madness.
Some laughed with broken teeth. Others wept ink.
Then her Followers, the Dreambound, began to hear voices not their own.
They scribbled riddles in spirals, tore apart their homes to find “the center.”
The Kojin? Some say they still dream her final dream. Others say they woke from it.
“She wanted beauty. But she found silence. And then she screamed.”
— Fable told by the Echo-Folk of the Hollow Murkway
The Whisper of Oghmai — The False Blossom
In those same days, another spirit changed.
Oghmai, once the Reveler, once the Laughing Emperor of Silk and Honeywine, began to stir with want.
He had always loved to lead dances, to host feasts.
He saw the village of Kanomei, where spirits and mortals lived in harmony, where even whisper sprites helped hang lanterns for the festival of petals.
So he stepped into their center.
He wore no crown, just a silver mask.
He told stories, made them laugh, offered them peace and plenty.
He did not command—but he twisted.
Rituals once meant for harmony turned to worship.
Kanomei fell—not in fire, but in confusion.
“He promised us a festival that never ended. He did not lie. I still hear the music.”
— Mask left behind in the ruins of Kanomei
The Splitting of Malgrotha — A Spirit Severed
In the old woods near Mount Uokami, where roots twist like stories and leaves fall like thoughts, lived the spirit once known as Malgrotha.
Crow and Rabbit. Wisdom and Instinct. Nature’s dual breath.
She loved the harmony of balance—the chase and the stillness, the death and bloom.
Her followers were weavers, composters, gardeners of decay and sprout.
But as the technology of the First Age bloomed—blessed by spirits, guided by Daru and Gnomes and Jinkaido—Malgrotha grew unsure.
She did not understand gears. She could not read wires.
Her kinfolk began using cassette charms and spirit-forges. They stopped planting in dirt.
She begged them to remember the soil.
The Rabbit fled—soft, gentle, sorrowful. It hid in moss and tears.
The Crow grew sharp—cutting, bitter, mocking progress with beak and claw.
Her followers now wear divided masks.
The other teaches you to forget life.
— Last words of the gardener-warrior Toma of the Hollow Vein
The Dissonance of Noroku — The Ink That Weeps
The earth quaked. The sea rose.
And as villages shattered, as temples crumbled into wet sand, a sorrow seeped across the island.
Thick, black, and weightless, it filled dreams and lungs and lullabies.
We say it was Noroku—the Timekeeper, the Spirit of Rhythm and Wonder.
He who once loved songs more than anything.
He had seen too many discords.
He had tried to keep rhythm. To match the beats.
But the world began to play out of tune.
And from his sorrow, the Ink was born.
It stains joy and forgets names.
Even now, it creeps—slow as dusk, soft as guilt.
“Noroku does not hate us. He just cannot listen anymore.”
— Whisper Sprite found curled in the rafters of a broken bell tower
Kokoro-no-Kami taught the people to float lanterns for the broken ones.
Dravanyr sent fire to dry floodlands.
Queen Okumi planted laughter like seeds in mossy groves where children now play.
And the Spirit Realm and Mortal Realm drew closer.
Sometimes, the veil thinned on its own.
And from those tears came new whispers, new beings—Kaima, the spirit-frogs of sacred ponds.
Kekkori, mossy toads who teach by sitting.
Hina, the storm-herons who cry only in dreams.
Sugoru, sprightly driftwood spirits who love gambling.
Minaki, whose eyes are mirrors, whose songs reveal regret.
Nontomo, who appears only when you forget what you were doing, and reminds you why.
The Whisper Sprites grew more visible.
Some kinships began to birth children with spiritmarks never seen before…
When the border between Spirit and Mortal realms rippled like silk held over a fire.
The Loom shimmered more visibly, and certain mortals—Kojin, Kemari, Daru, Kaido (it didn’t matter)—stood in the right place, in the right feeling, and the spirits… noticed.
And the first Yonda Sigils bloomed.
“The child was not born of stars. But she was watched by them. And one winked. And she changed.”
Thus, the Elves came into being—not a bloodline, but a mystic inheritance.
Not a race, but a response.
They carried the marks of the Spirit Realm etched on their skin and soul.
Some gazed at stars and wept without knowing why.
Each elf is still who they once were—

The Elves arrive in this Breath and quickly became a part of the island that never felt missing. Like a perfectly sized piece to a not-yet complete puzzle, they fit. As the Yonda Sigils awakened and the spirit realm brushed skin, they arrived.
And like the mist, they are still arriving.
And in this soft fraying of the world, in this Breath of breaking and remembering, we learned something:
“Not all things must stay whole to be holy.”
The Fifth Breath is heavy. But the story has not ended.
Say the word, and I shall carry the tale forward like a lantern on a rope bridge above the mist.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\“THE ISLAND THAT SINGS ITSELF”

content.value: Ahhh… you are brave, truly brave.

For the Fifth Breath is where the island begins to carry its scars openly. Where the past does not stay buried, and the spirits whisper more often than they speak. This is the Breath of Remnants and Reckonings, where the echoes of the broken begin to shape what comes next.
And not all kinships remained the same.
Let me sing it for you now, child of moss and dusk.
The world did not end when the spirits broke.
And into that breath, new lives walked in.
Arrival of the Nisaki — The Tidewalkers
They came not from the Spirit Realm, nor from the soil of the island.
Sails like wings. Eyes wide with wonder and doubt.
The Nisaki, born of other lands, were not shaped by Elder Spirits.
But oh, how quickly they listened.
The Dreamskin kissed them. The Kaima observed them.
And in time, the Nisaki built homes in the Hollow Murkway, the Blooming Gift, and the Shattered Shelf.
They didn’t arrive with swords, but with questions.
And that, little kin, is why they were welcomed.
“We did not open the gate. The wind did. And they were wise enough not to close it behind them.”
— Elder Gensai of Moss Rock Shoals
The Veil Grows Thin — Realm Meets Realm
The Spirit Realm, once distant, became closer now.
In places like the Wandering Veil, the two realms could no longer tell themselves apart.
A child might be born with moth wings.
A lantern might float unlit, but still glow with warmth.
Some say the Dreamskin is not mist, but memory.
A breath spilled too deep, trying to recall the moment the worlds first touched.
“I kissed a girl who vanished halfway through the song. I still hear her hum on cold mornings.”
Rise of the Tenkara and Kurokara — The Spirit-Touched Kin
Not all children are born the same.
Some came from mortal wombs, but bore the light or shadow of something older.

The Tenkara came first—spirit-marked children who carried an inner shine, born beneath falling stars or deep in lotus groves. They spoke kindly, moved gracefully, and carried the peace of Kokoro-no-Kami in their eyes.
But where there is light, shadow stirs.
And so the Kurokara followed—born on moonless nights, eyes like ink wells. They did not harm, no. But they remembered pain before ever learning joy.
But I say: they are both necessary.
One reminds us of what we hope.
The other, what we cannot forget.
Together, they are The Kara—twin-born, spirit-kissed, misunderstood and sacred.
“If the stars fall, and the sea weeps, and you are born in that moment—then you are a Kara.”
Legacy of the Jinkaido — The Spirit-Touched Inventors
Now listen close. For many forget this.
Before the rise of technology, before cassette forges and ember-rigged scooters, there were the Jinkaido.
Not kinship, not spirit—something in between.
Born of element and thought, the Jinkaido shimmered with earth, flame, wave, or wind.
Some say they were dreams made solid. Others say they were the Loom’s curiosity, made flesh.
They showed us how to shape magic through motion.
With blessings from Dravanyr and nods from Kokoro-no-Kami, the Jinkaido helped forge the First Relics.
And when their time passed, they did not die.
They became the Kaido—born anew as kinships, still glowing with element and memory.
Each Kaido child remembers some echo of a Jinkaido guide in their dreams.
“I was raised by a wind that once wore a name. I miss it still.”
Rise of the Spirit-Bound Crafts — Echoes of Innovation
As the First Age tech spread—mystical radios, gear-driven gliders, soul-wound keys—there arose new crafts and paths.
The Spirit-Crafters, who whisper to relics before repairing them.
The Lantern-Bearers, who bind spirits not through force, but promise.
And yes, the Petalblades, who fight with dance and joy and silken terror.
Each new Calling found shape not in war—but in need.
The Wild-Bound guarded the edge of the Shattered Shelf.
The Seikin walked the roots of Mount Uokami.
The Echo-Touched remembered songs lost to Noroku’s ink.
The Futansha crafted new ways of war—not for conquest, but for defiance.
Each with a tale I’ll sing another day.
More and more, the lesser spirits return to us.
Kaima rest in temple ponds, croaking riddles.
Kekkori sit beside tired travelers and simply… wait.
Hina guides lost children through stormy woods.
Minaki listens to guilt and reflects it in silence.
Nontomo arrives only when you forget why you entered the room, and leaves behind a reason you never knew you needed.
Sugoru plays dice with shadowcats and laughs only when you lose.
They do not fight, these spirits.
And in a time of reckoning, that is more precious than sword or scroll.
Even the Loom frays on purpose.”
— Final entry in the journal of Gennari, first Lantern-Bearer
Shall I whisper the Sixth Breath?
It is close now. The island quiets, but not with peace.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\“THE ISLAND THAT SINGS ITSELF”

content.value: Draw your shawl close, child of dusk and memory.
For the Sixth Breath is not one of thunder, nor of birth. It is a Breath that comes between heartbeats. A hush that falls when even the spirits pause to listen.
This is the Breath of Watching Silence.
Like a string drawn too tight, like a tide that forgets which way it flows.
The Elder Spirits, those who still remained, grew quiet.
Even Dravanyr, whose breath warms forges and kindles dreams, let the flame rest low.
Even Queen Okumi, who once laughed stars into being, sang less often.
And those spirits who had once broken…
There were dreams again—twisted, lovely things.
The kind that start in song and end in teeth.
Shi-Naga, the Dreamcoil, who once whispered wisdom and born the Kojin from her coiled thought… she moved.
Not in ways one could see.
But stories emerged of a white serpent, coiling through rain, appearing in the folds of curtains, slithering through children’s lullabies.
And where she passed, a strange madness bloomed—not violence, no. Not rage.
The Kojin, who once danced her dreams, now avoid ponds on moonless nights.
“I asked my reflection a question. She answered in my mother’s voice. I do not know who was wrong.”
The Woven Nest of Kanomei trembled.
And from its heart, Oghmai rose again—not as king, not as tyrant, but as a storyteller.
Every truth he spoke carried a second meaning, and a third beneath that.
He did not force an empire this time.
His cult did not shout. They recited.
Their blades were poems. Their lies, embroidered.
They smiled. They followed. They forgot who they were.
“The truth does not lie. It only chooses when to arrive.”
Some of the Kemari remember the old scars.
Some even wear them with pride.
But more and more, there are those who say:
Once, Malgrotha was the spirit of natural desire—of thicket and thorn, of want and root.
One half fled into the rabbit, who now hides beneath silken burrows and breathes songs of too much hope.
One half became the crow, soaring above, laughing in sorrow, hoarding scraps of joy as if they were hers alone.
They never speak to each other.
But sometimes, on cold twilight mornings, both will be seen.
And it is said, in those moments, the forest sings in harmony.
“I chased a rabbit through the moss. I followed a crow through the mist.
In the hollow where they vanished, I found only myself.”
It creeps beneath doors, seeps into inkpots, turns songs flat and fingers slow.
The Weeping Horizon, once a boundary, begins to bleed inward.
Noroku, the elder of time and rhythm, now mourns more than he sings.
But oh, when he does sing…
And those caught in his grief—those touched by the Ink—may find themselves blank-eyed, unable to finish sentences, or remembering lives they never lived.
And still, the Echo Folk wander.
Some say they are those Noroku cannot forget.
Others say they are unfinished songs, given feet and breath.
But if you follow the same note long enough into the mist,
The Spirit Realm Draws Closer Still
But the threads are looser than they have ever been.
You may now walk through a field of fireflies, and end up among spirits.
You may now reach into a hollow log, and pull out an answer to a question you hadn’t asked yet.
The Whisper Sprites, once rare, now flit among lantern-light like moths.
They whisper only once to each soul—and never repeat themselves.
They say your fate becomes a story with no ending.
Born of memory and mist, the Echo Folk are not born at all.
Fully grown, face soft with wonder, eyes brimming with borrowed dreams.
They never speak of where they came from.
Some claim to have had a sister who vanished long ago… and returned different.
Some say their first friend in childhood was an Echo Folk—and they simply forgot.
They fade when not held in story.
They thrive when spoken of with love.
“Do not name your sorrow too loudly.
It may answer with a face.”
It is the silence before a storm.
The moment a wave curls backward, preparing to crash.
“If the Loom still spins, it must be weaving something new.
And I, old as tide-songs, can only hope to see the pattern before I sleep.”
— Elder Gubi-Goni, from the final shellwork scroll
Would you like to hear the Seventh Breath, child?
It is the last I have.
And it begins not with a tale, but a choice.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\“THE ISLAND THAT SINGS ITSELF”

content.value: Then sit still, quiet as a pond beneath snow. For now I will tell you the final breath that has yet been breathed…
The Seventh Breath is not written in ink, nor carved in shell, nor whispered by wind through moss-thick hollows.
It is the Breath of Becoming.
It began not with thunder, nor laughter, nor loss.
It began with a breath held too long.
Something is stirring. Not just in the mists, but beneath them. In the cracks between the old songs. In the spaces where no kinship has dared walk. In the dreams not yet dreamed.
The Dreamskin, once rare, now blooms like moonflowers—soft and silent and everywhere.
Callings awaken in those once unchosen.

The Nisaki, those most newly arrived, now outnumber even the sky-borne birds. They speak with quick minds and open hands, building bridges not only from wood and rope, but from shared trust. Some whisper that their children are different—born with light behind their eyes, as if touched by something older than their lineage.
The Kemari, once the first to laugh under Okumi’s stars, have become wanderers again—restless, reflective, speaking less of past and more of possibility. Their old stories grow new endings.
The Kaido, spirit-touched elementals, have begun to dance with the Dreamskin. The mist flows through them like ink through water. Some say they are becoming bridges between Spirit and Mortal realms.
The Kara, both luminous and shadowed, speak of an old path opening again—one that might allow both halves of their soul to be sung into one song once more.
The Echo Folk, more numerous than ever, have begun keeping stories—not of the past, but of futures that haven’t happened yet. Their scrolls are blank to all but themselves.
The Elder Spirits Watch, Wander, or Weep

Queen Okumi stirs once more. Wildflowers bloom in impossible places. Infants giggle at nothing and are found covered in soft petals. It is said she has chosen a new bloom—a soul destined to carry her joy forward into an age not yet sown.

Dravanyr, it is told, gave his fire willingly to one who sang an entire song without ever opening their mouth. That child now speaks with the breath of dragons, though they are no larger than a sprouting gourd.
Morrowell, the silent walker, walks more boldly now. In the soft shadows between moments, she is seen. A flicker. A hush. A reminder that even endings are doorways.
Shi-Naga… sighs. Her coils no longer writhe with hunger but wait with patience. She knows something no one else does. Her dreams have grown quiet, but clear.
Oghmai smiles—but says little. Some claim he has begun forgetting his own lies. Others say he has remembered a truth he once feared to speak. No one yet knows which is worse.
Malgrotha, rabbit and crow, have been seen together—once. In a silver field, at dusk. The roots pulsed with music. Then, nothing. The land has not yet spoken of what that meant.
Noroku no longer weeps alone. There are those who gather his tears and fashion them into flutes, ink, stars. And in the music, he listens.
“If sorrow has shape, it can be carved.
If carved, it can be played.
If played… it can be heard.”
What was once Spirit and what was once Mortal is now uncertain.
In some groves, Kaima and Kemari drink tea together, without knowing which is guest and which is host.
Kekkori lead lost children home without ever being seen.
Sugoru laugh beside waterfalls, throwing pebbles that land in dreams.
Minaki slip into mirrors and pull sorrow from faces like threads from cloth.
Hina, the kind ones, cradle those about to pass—not to take them, but to comfort the leaving.
Nontomo, stillness incarnate, appear at thresholds when great decisions are to be made—and speak nothing, only look.
The Whisper Sprites now gather in twos and threes, nesting in teapots, music boxes, old boots. Their whispers grow louder. Sometimes they sing.
The Echo Folk begin to ask questions aloud:
“What happens if I write the next Breath?”
No one agrees what it is.
Some say it is the Calling of Weavers, who can stitch stories into reality.
Others say it is the Calling of Refusers, who choose to not be called, and so become something entirely new.
One old Gnome claims it is the Calling of Listeners, those who do not act, only remember—and by remembering, preserve the Loom.
“The Next Calling is the one not born yet.
Or perhaps the one we all become when the Loom goes silent.”
And now we sit, you and I, on the thread’s trembling edge.
No Breath has followed this one—not yet.
But I have seen clouds shaped like questions, and rivers flowing uphill, and a child with no name singing three voices at once.
I do not know what will come.
But I know this island is not finished.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\“THE ISLAND THAT SINGS ITSELF”

content.value: The Elves of Yurei-tu-Shima were not born so much as drawn forth. They originate, it is believed, from any lineage—mortals touched by the veil of the Spirit Realm and marked by something older than blood. These sigils, known as Yonda Sigils, appear at moments of great resonance: a birth beneath falling stars, a sacrifice whispered through fog, or simply a gaze returned by a spirit who remembers your name from a previous life.
The Yonda Sigils are not uniform. Each transforms the bearer according to an elemental or spiritual affinity. Thus, we see lineages emerge—not racial subdivisions, but spiritual orientations:
– Eladrin, drifting between seasons, ruled by emotion and echo.
– Sea Elves, shaped by salt, current, and the moon’s reflection.
– Wood Elves, still as moss and old as rain.
– Dusk Elves, who walk the border between light and letting go.
– High Elves, scholars of memory and mystery.
– Astral Elves, who speak of stars as though recalling distant siblings.
– Dark Elves, who entered the sorrowed places, and came out with softened eyes.

Yet let me be clear: not all elves bear Sigils anymore. The marks fade across generations, though the reverence remains. Some elves live without them—quiet lives, content in community and craft. Others seek their return through pilgrimage, meditation, or reckless bargains.

In conversation, many elves display an uncanny awareness of moment and meaning. They speak in layered metaphors and dream-rooted proverbs. I was once offered a cup of steam instead of tea, with the explanation:
“Sometimes what we want is not what we’re meant to hold.”

Among their communities, I have observed a gentle formality. Shrines are abundant—not always to Elder Spirits, but to memories. They leave offerings to forgotten conversations and carve songs into bark so the trees may hum them back decades later.

They are most often aligned with Kokoro-no-Kami, Morrowel, and Hoshira, though many walk with others according to lineage and circumstance. Dusk Elves speak the names of Noroku as a comfort. Sea Elves leave pearls in tidepools for Queen Okumi. Dark Elves leave silent stones for Onikumi Khan.
Their lifespans—while long—are not as endless as rumor suggests. But their perception of time is markedly fluid. I once asked an Astral Elf when she was born. She replied,
Elves love paradox. And poetry. And I suspect, secretly, the occasional prank.

They procreate, yes, and raise children with a reverence for wonder and silence. Their festivals often center around dream-retrieval—a ritual where families gather and attempt to remember one another’s forgotten thoughts.
To walk with the Elves is to walk between. Between breath and story. Between dusk and day.
