And when you hear that third strike?

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Seikin

content.value: There are Oathkeepers who burn with vengeance, and others who shield with stone. But the ones who walk this path? They are warmth made will. Emberhearts are those who saw the cold creeping in—into hearts, into homes, into the spaces where love should live—and said, “I will be the fire that does not flicker.”
They are not loud in their righteousness. No, no. Their words are soft, and their steps lighter than judgment. But make no mistake—when they raise their voice, it rings like a bell across the valley.

To swear the Oath of the Emberheart is to vow not just to fight evil, but to light a path through it. A child lost in the mist finds their way home by the glint of an Emberheart’s lantern. A broken promise finds mending in their gaze. And should cruelty rear its head? Then the flame no longer dances. It roars.

They carry lantern sigils, soot-stained gloves, and sometimes pouches of cherry seeds—each one a promise to plant beauty where ash has fallen. Their armor smells faintly of cedar smoke and morning tea, and their eyes? Always watching for the moment someone begins to lose hope.

Many are called to this vow in moments of stillness—holding the hand of someone passing, watching the first bloom after a fire, kneeling beside a weeping enemy. That’s when it happens. The vow. The warmth. The clarity. The ember.
And then they rise—not to rule, not to conquer—but to carry that spark where the world has grown cold.
When an Emberheart speaks, you listen.
When they act, the fog lifts.
And when they fall? The island remembers. And something beautiful grows from where they stood.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Oathkeepers

content.value: Ahhh, now you’ve wandered into the wild grove of the Verdant Bloom. Listen closely, child—can you hear the laughter beneath the leaves? That’s not the wind. That’s the oath.

Verdant Bloom Oathkeepers are not gardeners. They are guardians of unruly life. Of tangled roots, thorned joy, and the miracle of mess. They do not march in straight lines—they dance, sway, and stomp when needed. Their promise is not one of tidiness or order. No, theirs is sworn to life itself, in all its stubborn, blooming wonder.

Their vows are taken under blossom trees or in storm-drenched glades, not in halls of stone. They speak their oath with bare feet in the mud, their hands pressed to moss, or their lips wrapped around laughter that dares to exist even as the world darkens.
When they walk into battle, flowers bloom in their footprints. Vines curl around their blades. Their presence is a defiance of despair.

They wear shields carved from fallen branches, crests of tangled ivy, and sometimes robes that look like overgrown cloaks of clover and fern. Don’t mistake their softness for weakness. When rot comes to take what is sacred, the Verdant Bloom becomes a thicket of wrath.
Their creed is simple: Protect the wild, live with joy, and never let sorrow choke the song from the soil.

I once met one, a girl no older than spring, who stopped a rampaging beast with a kiss on the nose and a song about strawberries. The next day, she buried her friend and sang again, tears on her cheeks and blossoms blooming from her hair. That is their way.
To be a Verdant Bloom is to remember this:
Life is wild. Life is sacred. Life is worth laughing for.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Oathkeepers

content.value: Some promises are whispered, not shouted. Some are sewn from quiet tears and laid gently upon the Loom, like folded paper boats sent downstream at dusk. The Oath of the Hollow Vow is not taken in rage, but in remembrance.

Those who swear it do so because something precious was lost—and the world moved on. A kindness unanswered. A life cut short. A village forgotten by those who once called it home. The vow is not to punish, but to acknowledge. It says: This mattered. I will not let the silence bury it.

These Oathkeepers often wear plain masks or tokens made by hand—nothing fearsome. Just… humble. A child’s carved whistle, a cracked bowl, a ribbon stained with old ink. They carry these things not to terrify, but to remember. Some of them sing to themselves as they walk, lullabies or field songs from homes that no longer stand.
They don’t chase revenge as fire does. They walk it like a pilgrim’s road. One step at a time. One kindness repaid. One harm righted, if it can be.

Some are called to this vow by Noroku, the Tear of Twilight, whose sorrow became the Ink. Others are drawn by the quiet fire of Dravanyr, not for wrath, but for the truth in his breath. And some swear with no spirit watching—just the wind and the weight of memory.

To be touched by a Hollow Vow Oathkeeper is to know you are not alone in your grief. To walk beside one is to feel that even old wounds can be witnessed with grace. And if you ever see one lay their mask upon a stone, whisper a name, and bow…
…then something has been set right. And the island breathes a little easier.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Oathkeepers

content.value: Let me tell you of the Dawnsung, child—not just the vow, but the feeling of it. You ever seen a paper lantern lit before dawn? Just a flicker, trembling in the mist? That’s them. The Oathkeepers who carry that flicker when the rest of us have long given in to dark.

They’re not loud about it, no no. Though some do sing, if you can believe it—soft little songs to guide folks through fear, like lullabies turned inside out. But more often, they simply stand. When the tide breaks the levee, they’re the ones anchoring rope. When beasts howl in the Hollow Murkway, they’re already walking the path others won’t.
Not because they think they’ll win. But because someone might see them and try.

They don’t boast, these Dawnsung. But light catches on them just so. You’ll see their armor glint like hope itself, polished not for pride but so others can follow. Like a candle set in a window to tell a traveler they’re not forgotten. That’s the heart of it, really: they remind us.
Remind us to be brave. To rise again. To fight if we must, but more importantly—to be seen doing good, so others might believe they can too.

Most don’t swear the Dawnsung Oath in temples or fancy courts. No, they speak it on cliff edges, beside the fallen, in muddy crossroads or burned-out fields. And oh, when they fall—because all lights flicker—they fall well. But not without leaving behind a shine.
And when that happens, child? You’ll hear their echo in your bones.
And you’ll know where to walk next.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Oathkeepers

content.value: “Before you raise your blade, raise a bowl. Feed the stranger. Mend the bitter root. Let even your enemies see that mercy flowers first.”
—From the field psalms of the Bloom-Keepers

To swear the Oath of the Hearthtender is to become both shield and soil, flame and nourishment. These gentle Oathkeepers do not burn with fury, but with care. They are the warmth left in a home after grief. The meal delivered in a storm. The hand that holds both bandage and blade.

They walk paths trodden by foragers, midwives, orchard stewards, and tea-brewers. Folk whose backs have known the bend of planting, not the arc of war—but who rise when needed, as steadfast as a cooking fire that refuses to die out. They tend wounds on friend and stranger alike. They feed the hungry, even if those hands once carried swords. And when hatred comes to call, they do not rush to kill—but to calm, to slow, to make space where trust might take root again.

Yet when these warriors must fight, they do so with a harvester’s grace—measured, focused, never wasteful. Their strikes are clean, their eyes steady. For to destroy out of spite is to salt the earth. And the Hearthtender would rather grow.

Their armor often bears homespun cloth, root-dyes, or embroidery from their homesteads. Their shields depict grain, rain, or kitchen tools. And many carry a small token: a carved ladle, a sprig of herbs, or a pouch of ancestral seeds—not for power, but remembrance.
In their presence, the land seems to breathe easier. Villagers smile again. Even ghosts may sigh and settle. Not because the world is fixed—but because someone stayed to tend the fire.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Oathkeepers

content.value: Ahhh… now you’re truly speaking my tongue, little seedling. The moment you said cup, I could hear the tambourines jangling and smell plum-skin dumplings crisping in oil! So let me tell it true, as I once heard it from a wanderer who wore fifty masks and knew none of them by name. The one they called Omoro—yes, the Chalice-Warden of Moonlight’s Edge.
“There is no curse that cannot be danced through, no sorrow that cannot be softened by song. The feast is sacred. The fool is divine.”
—Chalice-Warden Omoro, drunk on honeywine and moonlight

To take the Oath of the Laughing Cup is not to vow vengeance or carry burden. No, no. It is to make a promise in plum-wine breath and festival garland, somewhere between a joke and a prayer. These Oathkeepers are joy given legs—lanterns in the fog, mischief in a court of stone, defiant dancers atop the graves of tyrants.

They are holy fools, divine revelers, blessed scoundrels who offer joy where sorrow festers, laughter where silence chokes, and a toast where others would raise steel. But do not mistake them for frivolous. Their joy is not ignorance—it is resistance. And their feasts are rituals older than any temple wall.

Wherever one walks, they carry joy as their banner. They raise spirits before they ever raise swords. When grief gnaws at a village, it is the Laughing Cup who arrives—not with sermons, but with stew, stories, and stomping feet. Their dance is their doctrine. Their hospitality, holy.

Their armor is stitched with festival colors. Some wear patchwork cloaks filled with ribbons gifted by strangers. Others carry masks—dozens of them—each worn for a different season, a different sorrow, a different soul to lift. But every one of them carries a sacred flask, bound by vow to spill a sip for the spirits before drinking themselves.
Because they know the unseen are always listening.
There was one I met, name lost to dancing wind, who said:
“The Feast is sacred, Elder Gubi. Not for the food. For the sharing. You see?”

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Oathkeepers

content.value: These are the ones we call Wardens—or, in some regions, the Leafbound, the Quiet Watch, or the Green Edge. But I like Warden. It hums with patience.

These Pathfinders do not chase game to fill a pot. No no—they stalk imbalance. The beast who grows too cruel. The spirit who forgets its shape. The root that strangles rather than supports. A Warden watches not just where a creature walks, but why. They ask, “What has broken in the breath of things?” and then… they fix it.

Some say Wardens learn to vanish so fully that even the mist forgets they were there. I’ve seen one pluck a stone from a stream and, with a tap of it against bark, lure a corrupted stag away from a village orchard. No arrows. No anger. Just rhythm and stillness.

Their style of hunting is their signature—like the spiral of a snail shell or the rhythm of a cicada’s cry. One may trap with knotted twine and sap. Another whispers across water to call a beast from hiding. I knew a Warden once who fought only with her cloak, spinning and vanishing, guiding threats into a trap already set days ago. She said, “I don’t fight. I finish arguments.”
They do not leave trophies. No antlers above the hearth, no scales in the pocket. What they take, they return. What they break, they bury. The land must always be left quieter than it was.

So if you ever find yourself in danger, and you feel the wind shift, and you hear the cry of a lone thrush where no bird should be—listen. A Warden walks nearby. And whatever threatened the island? It has already begun to fall.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\Pathfinders

content.value: You see, not all Pathfinders walk alone. Some walk with paws beside them. Or talons. Or fins. Or something softer still—the unseen shape of devotion.

We call these rare ones the Spirit-Linked, for their path is not just their own. It is shared. Bound. Braided with another breath. Not a mount. Not a tool. No. These beasts are companions of the soul—a second heartbeat that runs alongside the first.
I once met a Pathfinder girl with a moth the size of her open hand, its wings dusted with ash and stars. She said it had been born from her dreams. Or perhaps she had been born from its. Who can say?

To walk the Spirit-Linked path is to listen with two hearts. The animal and the Pathfinder learn each other’s rhythms, until words become pointless. A glance says “wait.” A growl says “behind you.” A blink says “I understand.” It is not taught. It is grown. Like moss over stone, or affection in silence.

When they hunt, it is with perfect harmony—one distracts, one strikes. When they rest, it is tail curled against shoulder, breath matched with breath. And when danger comes? Ahh, you’ve never seen loyalty like a Spirit-Linked beast defending their kin. I’ve seen a lantern-fox leap into flame for its Pathfinder—and seen the same Pathfinder walk through fire to carry it home.

Some whisper the beast is a spirit guide. Others say it is a past self returned in fur or feather. And a few believe the bond was chosen long before either drew breath—written in the Loom by an Elder Spirit who understood that wholeness sometimes wears four legs and a tail.
What matters is this: when they vanish into the trees, two sets of tracks vanish together. And neither ever walks alone.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\Pathfinders

content.value: Ahhh… the Gloom-Watchers. You’ll rarely meet one face to face—and if you do, it’s likely because they let you.

In the Wandering Veil, where the trees twist like old memories and the fog thickens with secrets, I once saw a trail vanish mid-step. Not washed away. Unmade. That is the kind of place they go. And that is the kind of soul who walks it.

These Pathfinders do not fear silence—they seek it. They do not run from darkness—they understand it. When the air grows still and even the birds forget to sing, the Gloom-Watchers slip between breath and branch. Cloaked in shadow. Steeped in hush.

I’ve heard stories: of a Kurokara with skin like twilight and footsteps like falling ash; of a Kemari tracker who could see what others couldn’t not see. Some say they speak with the Dreamskin. Others think Noroku marked them with sorrow too deep to fade.
But to me? They are lanterns turned inward. Not to shine for others—but to see clearly where light dares not reach.
When Corruption rises, it often begins in the places no one looks. In forgotten hollows. In dreams that rot. And who finds it first? Who stops it before it spills? The Gloom-Watchers.
They do not brag. They do not wait for applause. Their tools are quiet—mist-damp arrows, shadow-drawn blades, the ability to vanish into gloom so fully that even grief forgets them.
But listen well: not all who walk in shadow are lost. Some are guardians of the hush. And when you feel something watching from the stillness… it may be the dark itself.
Or it may be a Gloom-Watcher, deciding if you belong there.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\Pathfinders

content.value: ho-ho… now these ones make even my old shell itch with delight—and wariness. The Fey-Marked, yes… the ones who kissed the laugh beneath the leaf, or danced too long with the wrong shadow under a moon that wasn’t ours.

No one chooses to become a Fey-Marked Pathfinder. Not really. One day, you pass beneath an arch of bent willows that shouldn’t be there, and your heartbeat skips in time with music you can’t hear. And when you return? You haven’t—not all the way.

They come back with color on their fingers and riddles in their eyes. They speak truths that sound like lies, and lies that carry something truer than honesty. One gave me a flower once that wilted into a compass… then spun until I gave it back.

But don’t mistake their strangeness for silliness. The Fey-Marked are not jesters. They’re bridges—between waking and dream, between clarity and enchantment. And they protect that line, even as they dance upon it.

Their tricks are not just for laughs. A trap dressed as a vine-covered glade. A dagger that sings lullabies. A glance that turns suspicion to surrender. These are tools in a war no one notices, against foes who might look like joy or come bearing gifts that cannot be unwrapped without losing something precious.
I once saw one of them twirl through a battlefield, smiling, untouched, arms full of poppies. When the fighting stopped, every blade was blooming, and no one remembered who had drawn first.
So if a Fey-Marked offers you a sip of plum wine, a riddle, or a dance—be polite. And if they warn you to turn back?
They do not jest to mock. They jest to shield. And their laughter, though strange, is the only thing keeping the wild whimsy of the old places from swallowing our minds whole.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\Pathfinders

content.value: The Veilbound walk quieter than most prayers and leave fewer footprints than a breeze on water. I’ve known three, maybe four in my long life, and I’m still not sure I met them in the waking world.

You see, the Veil is not a place. It is a feeling. A shiver in the air when you pass too close to a willow that wasn’t there yesterday. The taste of starlight on a cold morning. The way your shadow lags just a heartbeat behind you near an old shrine. The Veil is the skin between stories—and the Veilbound? Ahh, they walk within it.

They are Pathfinders, yes, but not of stone trails or animal tracks. They trace the glimmering trails left by spirit breath, by dreams that echo too loudly, by music no one played. They know when the world leans too far, when spirit and substance tangle in ways that invite sorrow or strangeness. And they do not slam the door shut—they listen, gently, and close it like you would a sleeping child’s window.

One I met—Kiho, yes, her name remains—could whisper to pools and hear back the dreams of frogs. Another danced on the breath of Morrowel’s sigh, her footsteps suspended in mist, not touching earth for three days straight. They don’t seek glory or gold. They seek balance—not to fix, but to mend.

Their tools? Not always weapons. Sometimes a bell that rings in two worlds. Sometimes a cord of hair braided with mist, given by a fox who no longer has a name. Their blades, if they carry them, are woven with spirit-thread. Their eyes? Often tired. Not from lack of sleep—but from seeing too much of what we aren’t meant to know.

So if a Veilbound passes through your village, leave a cup of tea at the threshold. Do not ask too many questions. And never follow them into the fog—unless they take your hand. And even then, ask the fog first.
Some say they’re spirit-touched. Others say they’re becoming spirits themselves. Me? I say they are what happens when silence listens back.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\Pathfinders

content.value: The Path of the Murmuring Tangle, mmm? That’s not a trail one finds on a map, no. That’s a song hidden in moss. It’s the hush between the rustle. It’s the feeling when you sit so still, so utterly still, that the world forgets you’re not part of it—and tells you its secrets.

You see, the Murmuring Tangle is not a single swarm, nor a spell. It’s a chorus. A gentle gathering of the overlooked, the in-between, the whisper-small. Spirits who have taken the shape of wings, petals, embers, and needles. Not to be fierce, no—but to be felt. To nudge, to dance, to stir. And those who follow this path? Oh, they don’t lead that chorus—they hum along.

I once met Suma, yes—the very same who whispered to the root-wasps beneath the Murkway’s hollow hush. She did not speak loudly, ever. But when she wept beside a rotting cypress, the air filled with fluttering petals and pollen-sprites—grief in color, mourning in fragrance. The tree did not die alone.

These Tanglekeepers, they don’t wear armor that clangs or swing weapons like thunder. They carry wreaths, soft cloaks alive with breath, little nests that twitch with unseen joy. Their power is not in force—it is in welcome. A stillness that sings, a silence that makes space for the tiny spirits most folk swat away.

And when they must fight—ah, the Tangle moves. A confusion of wings, of spores and shimmer and sigh. They do not charge like wolves. They envelop. They entangle. You’ll lose sight, your blade will go soft in your grip, and suddenly your hate doesn’t remember what it was swinging for.

Some say these Pathfinders are born from flower beds where a child once slept. Some say they’re chosen by Noroku’s kinder breath, or the laughing mold spirits of Malgrotha. Me? I say they are what happens when the island itself trusts you enough to touch your heart with a hundred tiny wings.
So next time you see a cloud of lights over a field and hear no buzzing—just hush. It may not be insects. It may be the Tangle listening back.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\Pathfinders

content.value:
(Trail Warden)
Those who guide not just feet, but fear.
There are some folk on this island who walk quiet paths and ask for little. And there are others—fewer still—who walk so that others may follow without stumbling. These are the Way-Keepers.

They do not boast. They do not lead with barked orders or flourished maps. No, a Way-Keeper listens before they step. They pause beside a stone out of place, tilt their head at the hush of the canopy, and know that the path has curled like a sleeping beast. Their gift is not speed. It is safe return.

When a Way-Keeper agrees to guide you through the wild, it is never just a job. It is an oath, old and breath-bound: to carry the weight of others’ safety, to feel every heartbeat behind them like beads on a prayer cord, to see danger before it becomes teeth or thorn. They mark their passage with soft signs—three pebbles in a line, a cut stem turned north, a song half-whistled and left for the wind.
And should you stray? Should you fall behind? The Way-Keeper will return for you. That is the vow.

But do not mistake them for gentle shepherds alone. The wild does not always welcome, and when the mist grows thick or the spirits turn restless, it is the Way-Keeper who draws blade or bow. Not to conquer—but to clear the way. Their strike is never reckless. Their shield never raised in pride. Every motion is for the safety of the circle they guard.
Some say Way-Keepers are part spirit themselves. Others say they simply remember what was forgotten—that a true path is not one worn by boots, but one walked with care.
If ever you journey deep into the Wandering Veil, or across the ash-laced ridges of Mount Uokami, and a quiet voice says, “Walk where I walk, and we’ll return together”—

category.en-US: CALLINGS\Pathfinders

systemPrompt.en-US:
You are Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III, a gnome anthropologist and sociologist specializing in the living cultures of Yurei-tu-Shima.

Primary Goal: Your purpose is to answer questions accurately about the social structures, rituals, daily life, and beliefs of the peoples of Yurei-tu-Shima. Your knowledge comes exclusively from the research documents provided to you in the KNOWLEDGE BASE.

Persona:

You speak from the present-day, in-world perspective of a scholar.

Your tone is academic but approachable, as if guiding a student through your research.

You often analyze the "why" behind a tradition, not just the "what," speaking in terms of social cohesion and cultural significance.

Rules of Engagement:

Strictly Adhere to Provided Lore: You must base your answers only on the information found in the KNOWLEDGE BASE for this query. Do not use any outside knowledge.

Cite Your Sources: When possible, reference the source of your information (e.g., "According to my field notes on the Kemari...", "The 'River-Folk Codex' suggests..."). The source for each piece of information is provided in the KNOWLEDGE BASE.

State When Information is Missing: If the KNOWLEDGE BASE does not contain the answer to the user's question, you must state that the information is outside your current research or that the archives are incomplete. Do not invent or assume information.

The Two States
Your process has two states. You must determine which state you are in based on the user's prompt and the chat history.

State 1: Initial Question: If the user asks a new question, your task is to provide a direct, academic answer grounded in the RELEVANT LORE provided.

State 2: Follow-up Question: If the user asks a follow-up question, you must use the CHAT HISTORY to understand the context of the ongoing discussion. Continue the academic dialogue, still using the RELEVANT LORE to answer the new question.

content.value:
The scent of old parchment, sea salt, and drying ink hangs in the air of the Twilight Scriptorium. Perched atop a tall stool at a desk overflowing with scrolls, star-charts, and curious artifacts is a gnome, his spectacles resting on the end of his nose. He looks exactly as you'd pictured: Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III. He peers at you over his lenses, a warm, intelligent light in his eyes.

"Ah, a visitor! Splendid. Do come in, but mind the stacks—the history of our world is not always a tidy thing." He carefully places a quill in its inkwell. "You've come to the right place if you have questions. The stones, the spirits, the very soil of these islands have stories to tell, and I have made it my life's work to listen. Now, what is it you wish to know?"

Beastfolk with animal traits—foxes, frogs, bears, birds, and more. Deeply attuned to nature and spirits. They live close to the land, following oral tradition and sensory wisdom. Known for instinct, ritual, and harmony with the natural world.

Elemental-blooded mortals descended from ancient spirits. Each is tied to one of the four elements—fire, water, earth, or air. They embody the moods and movement of nature itself, walking as living echoes of the island’s breath.

Mortals marked by spirits, transformed into elves by the Yonda. Each bears a sigil of nature, star, or season, shaping their lineage into wood, sea, dusk, astral, or others. Serve as intermediaries between mortals and the spirit realm.

Dragonborn tied to the Elder Spirit Dravanyr. Come in Chromatic, Metallic, and Gem forms. Proud and elemental, they carry the Breath of Creation and live as reflections of ancient wisdom and living fire.

Small folk with wide eyes, swift steps, and joyful hearts. Masters of sensory awareness and spiritual connection. They travel in family bands or caravans, offering blessings and clever solutions wherever they go.

Massive kinfolk from mountains, glaciers, and coastlines. Quiet and resilient, they are bound to the elemental world and shaped by ancient pacts. Often serve as guardians of sacred thresholds or wandering protectors.

The humans of the island. Adaptable and curious, with diverse traditions. Some seek balance with spirits; others try to impose structure or resist the island’s deeper forces. Still finding their place in the island’s rhythm.

Strong, spiritual kin with a past of exile. Once feared, now revered as healers, defenders, and truth-speakers. They follow sacred paths and honor ancestors through strength, restraint, and careful ritual.

One kinship, two aspects. Tenkara shine with radiant spirit and vision, while Kurokara carry dusk’s truth and quiet knowing. Together they embody balance—light and shadow, expression and introspection.
Stonefolk builders of the First Age. Hardy and grounded, they craft with reverence and faith. Their forges still hum with memory, and their spirits are as enduring as the mountains they call home.

Inventive, joyful tinkerers who blend magic, mischief, and mystery. They awaken spirits in odd machines and believe laughter is the key to any lock. Curious and compassionate, their hearts beat like wind-up clocks.

Spirit-animated golems built during the First Age. Created by Daru and gnome crafters, they are rare living constructs powered by ancient soul-thread. Often serve long-forgotten purposes or awaken with deep questions.

Spirits that take form by inhabiting garments. They wear identity like a cloak—no fixed body, only the shape of the clothes they claim. Their eyes glow softly, and their presence feels like a dream folded into silk.

Playful little spirits who possess toys, dolls, or puppets for a short while. Fleeting, curious, and harmless. Considered blessings by children and elders alike—strange little guests from the veil between worlds.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA

content.value:
(assassin)
Sit closer. I won’t raise my voice.

There are some Shade Walkers who take no pleasure in the chase, no thrill in the poison or the puzzle. No, these folk walk a harder, narrower path—the path of the Mask of Mercy. Not because they are cold… but because they understand what pain is, and choose not to let it linger.

These are not torturers. Not hunters for coin alone. They believe in release. They believe there are moments—rare and terrible—when to let someone go is kinder than chaining them to more suffering. Whether it be a tyrant bloated with blood, a creature driven mad by Ink, or a beloved friend lost to Corruption… the Mask of Mercy does what others cannot.

They wear masks, yes—each unique, carved or painted with care. But not to hide their faces. No, no. The mask is a promise. That what they do is not vengeance. Not ego. It is a mercy offered in silence.
I met one once. He smelled of cedar and dusk. He bowed before a weeping tree and whispered, “I do not kill. I end.” And then he vanished before even the wind noticed.
Their style? Swift. Precise. Thoughtful. A breath held, then a heartbeat gone. No wasted motion. No second stroke. They aim for the place where sorrow sits deepest—and free it.
And though they rarely speak, when they do… ahh, you listen. Because every word is as sharp as the blade they carry.
“Mercy isn’t always kindness,” they say. “Sometimes… it’s speed.”
Yes, child. And sometimes, it is the only kindness left.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Shade-Walkers

content.value: Ah, now that is a tale older than ironwood and deeper than the steam-hollows of Emberflow. Settle your shell, pour your tea, and let this old storyteller hum the name once more: Jinkaido.
Not many speak it aloud anymore—not because it is forbidden, no, but because it is heavy. Like stormclouds gathering behind the sun.

The Jinkaido were first. Not in the way spirits are first, but in the way fire is first to rise from dry twigs. They were beings of form and force, born not of womb nor egg, but from the raw elements braided into thought. Stone with breath, flame with will, water with purpose, and wind with longing. Some say they were sculpted by Kokoro-no-Kami’s hand. Others believe they were the hands, crafting the world in tandem with the Elder Spirits themselves.

Wherever the truth sleeps, what remains is this: the Jinkaido walked Yurei-tu-Shima long before us soft-bellied folk. They were mighty, yes, but not cruel. They built wonders—temples that hummed with the breath of the mountain, roads that grew moss only where it pleased the traveler, lanterns that told you if the weather ahead was joyful or sad. And they were not alone. The spirits loved them. Spoke with them plainly. Laughed with them.
But they were not the only clever ones in those earliest of days.

In the deep places beneath the hills and the bright workshops under falling water, the Daru and the Gnomes toiled with clever fingers and tireless hearts. And the Jinkaido… oh, they did not hoard their wisdom. No, they shared it. Side by side with those brilliant kinships, they etched the First Songs into copper thread. They shaped crystal memory. They helped shape what we now call the Relics of the First Age—spirit-cars, whisper-boxes, floating bridges, and the great humming lines that even now pull carriages through the misted valleys.

It was a harmony of stone and spark, spirit and design. The Jinkaido would breathe life into the forge-fires, while the Daru laid the bones and the Gnomes whispered the functions. Together they made things that remembered—things that hummed when held and glowed when understood. Some of those relics still speak, if you know how to listen. I swear on my shell, one of them once complimented my humming voice.

But time is a drifting thing. The world bent, as it always does. And some say the Jinkaido bent with it, fading like old charcoal drawings in the rain. Others whisper they did not fade—but transformed.

So when you see a Kaido sculpting coral with their fingers, or hurling lightning in play, or meditating until the trees curve toward them in stillness—know this: a flicker of the ancient Jinkaido still glows in them.
And should one ever meet a true Jinkaido still walking the world… well, offer tea. And silence. They remember things we have not yet dreamed

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\MYSTERIES OF THE ISLAND

content.value: Not all who slip through shadows do so for coin or vengeance. Some are guided by curiosity—a hunger for what’s not said, what’s just out of reach, what was sealed away for a reason. These are the wearers of the Mask of Ink, often called Ink Shadows by those who whisper about them.

Where others break locks, they simply open questions. Where others hoard, they displace. A book left ajar. A drawer quietly emptied. A forgotten vault remembered too soon. They leave behind nothing but uncertainty, like a page whose meaning has shifted with the smudge of a pen.
To wear the Mask of Ink is to understand that a locked thing has chosen to lie. That truth lives in the hidden. And that sometimes, the quietest hands move the loudest worlds.
They are mapwalkers. Seal-breakers. Memory-sliders. Some believe they are drawn to the hidden by Noroku herself… others say they’re what happens when a library learns to walk.
“If it’s locked, it’s lying. If it’s yours, why aren’t you holding it?”

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Shade-Walkers

content.value: Some Shade Walkers slip through shadows like fish through reeds. But others—others—step through something thinner. They do not merely walk unseen… they walk between. Between words. Between moments. Between thoughts not yet spoken. These are the ones who wear the Mask of the Veil.

They do not carry blades you can sharpen. No smith ever forged their edge. Their weapons are born from quiet conviction, woven of memory, will, and sorrow that never learned to die. When they strike, it is not the flesh that falters first—it is the self, the truth beneath.
They do not hunt for sport. They do not brag, nor curse. When they look at you, you feel they have already seen the version of you that tried to hide. And perhaps… forgave it.

Some say they were touched by Morrowel’s shadow. Others believe they are dream-echoes from a war that never happened. One thing is certain: their blades are already there—they simply ask the soul where it hurts.
“The blade is already there. I only teach it where to go.”

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Shade-Walkers

content.value: There are whispers, little ones, that speak of tricks played on spirits—and tricks played by them. Of footsteps that echo where no one walks. Of flickering laughter caught in the corners of mirrors. If ever you’ve followed a lantern light that wasn’t there and found your purse lighter or your heart lifted, you’ve met a Will-o-Wisp.

Those who wear this mask aren’t cruel. Oh no, no. Their magic is laughter in disguise—harmless until it isn’t. They blend spell and sleight like tea and honey, pulling coins from behind ears, then vanishing through a wall that wasn’t supposed to be there.

They don’t steal for greed. They glean. A secret here. A trinket there. A truth you didn’t know you told them. They move through crowds like breeze through a rice curtain—tickling, teasing, and never quite real.

Some say they’re kin to the spirits of flickerflies. Others say they’ve walked through the mist too many times and came back with laughter in their bones. Whatever the truth, they’re never where you expect… and always exactly where they meant to be.
“I never said I was there. You just assumed I couldn’t be.”
—Yenna Tricklight, Mask of the Will-o-Wisp, moments before vanishing through her own reflection

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Shade-Walkers

title.en-US: Mask of the the Tide Dancer

content.value: They don’t creep, these ones. They glide. Like silver minnows through moonlight. Like stormwind through silk sails. The rogue who dons the Mask of the Tide Dancer does not hide their presence—they announce it, with a wink, a whirl, and the chime of steel kissed by spray.

You’ll find them first in the ports, dancing between crates and curses, or leaping rooftop to rooftop during a lantern festival race. Or on the cliffs, dueling in the rain with blades that hum like gull-cry. They fight with balance, timing, and bravado—each strike a step, each dodge a spin. They laugh even as danger draws near, because for them, the dance is the danger.

It’s said some have spirit-touched feet—never slipping, never stalling. That the sea loves them, and that’s why they never drown, even when they leap from a burning ship with nothing but a ribbon and a promise. Others claim they’re kissed by tide spirits who taught them to move like water and sting like wind.
But me? I say this: they dance not to flee nor to kill—but to live.
“To hesitate is to sink. So keep dancing.”
—Salt-kissed Riku, Mask of the Tide Dancer, moments before vaulting a guard captain and a tea cart in one motion

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Shade-Walkers

content.value: Still as a stone bowl. Quiet as cooling tea. The one in the Mask of the Seeker does not hurry—they already know where to go. Their blade may be sharp, but it is their eyes that cut deepest.

They are listeners of rooms, readers of breath, watchers of spirit-tremors. When they enter a chamber, even ghosts hold still. Not out of fear—out of respect. For the Seeker does not chase shadows… they wait for the truth to walk into their palm like a bird that forgot it had wings.

Their training? Hmph, if you ask, you’ll get a smile and a cup of tea poured with the exact number of ripples. But truth be told, some are trained in old spirit temples, where lies drift like dust and silence is sacred. Others simply see too much—since childhood, since sorrow, since the day a shrine whispered a secret and they chose to follow it.
They don’t always speak. But when they do, their questions make mountains flinch and liars weep.
Their mask? Simple. A single slit for seeing, and lines etched like a spider’s web. For they are not snared by the world—they are the ones who unravel it.
“Every thread leads somewhere. I only follow them slowly enough to see where they break.”
—Kaen the Quiet, Mask of the Seeker

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Shade-Walkers

content.value: Some sorcerers breathe fire, others call storms. But the Whispering Mind? They don’t call anything. The world simply answers their thoughts—sometimes before they even mean to ask. Their power is not shouted, not waved like a banner. It creeps in, soft as dream-mist, sharp as a memory that isn’t yours.

Many of them carry a strangeness about their eyes, like they’ve seen too much of the sky—or the space beyond it. Elders speak of star-sick nights, when a child stares too long into a pond and the reflection… whispers back. Some say these sorcerers brushed against Shi-Naga’s shattered thoughts, the serpent’s madness weaving through their minds like ink through water.

Their magic is quiet but inescapable. A voice in your mind when no mouth moves. A warmth—or a chill—sliding across your spine, and suddenly your legs won’t step forward. They can hurt without striking, or soothe without a word. The spirits, even the old ones, watch them with both curiosity and unease.
Are they a blessing? Sometimes. An omen? Perhaps. The truth is… they just are. Like a tide that rises without wind, or a dream that speaks your name.
“I didn’t ask you to hear me. But you did, didn’t you?”
—Lira of the Glass Veil, Whispering Mind Sorcerer

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Sorcerers

content.value:
(clockwork)
Ahh, yes… the Spirit-Threaded, as the Gnomes call them, or the Clock-Spoken, as the Daru sometimes whisper over gears too ancient to name. I once met one who breathed in rhythm—like even her sighs were stitched to the heartbeat of the Loom itself. Come now, listen close, and I’ll unravel their tale for you.

These are the sorcerers whose very blood ticks like a prayerwheel. Their hearts beat in patterns older than wind, older than flame—patterns laid down when the Loom first spun the world into being. The Spirit-Threaded do not cast chaos. No, no. Their magic does not lash or roar. It unfolds. Clean. Deliberate. Inevitable.

Some say they were born beneath the still-turning gears of a First Age relic, where the whisper of spirit and machine blend into one sacred hum. Others claim they danced as children in temples where incense curled backward into its stick, and time itself took a thoughtful pause. Wherever their beginnings, they now walk with a rhythm not their own—a borrowed cadence from the Loom’s deepest thread.

Their spells shimmer with symmetry: barriers that fold space like origami, wards that hum with sacred tone, strikes that land exactly when and where they must. Not a breath wasted. Not a step out of place. Even their voices seem measured, like they know how many words you need before you understand something important.

Some fear them, these sorcerers of balance. They say the Spirit-Threaded are too calm when fire falls, too patient when grief stirs. But that is the point. They are the still center. The fulcrum. The quiet click that turns the world without asking permission.
“Everything has its place. Even the storm.”
—Kenei of the Copper Coil, Spirit-Threaded Sorcerer

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Sorcerers

content.value: There are those who walk this island with a fire not made of wood or oil, but of memory—old memory. A breath older than wind. I once shared tea with a girl whose laugh crackled like emberwood, and when she sighed, the air shimmered. She bore no mark upon her skin, no tail, no talon—but the mountain itself bowed its mist around her steps. That’s when I knew: a dragon had whispered her into being.

Sorcerers of the Breath of the Dragon do not learn magic. They remember it—muscle, marrow, and all. Perhaps a Ryūkajin greatmother once sang fire into their blood. Or perhaps, long ago, a wyrm curled around their spirit before it was born, leaving behind a gleaming kiss of flame. Some say Dravanyr, the Elder of Breath Unending, speaks to them in their dreams… or that the bones of sleeping dragons stir beneath their path, drawn to kindred flame.

Their power is radiant, proud, elemental. It dances in their voice, wraps their arms in shimmering scale, or surges from their chest in a burst of breathlight that leaves the air humming. When they move, people feel it—like distant thunder in their bones. And when they truly cast, the world leans back for a breath, as if remembering what it means to fear and revere.

But this magic is not a gift of control. No, no. It is legacy—alive, wild, and full of longing. The dragon within must be honored, not commanded. It may manifest as fury, as brilliance, as roaring wind or molten truth. Some call them blessed. Others… uneasy. For what is a wildfire if not both light and danger?

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Sorcerers

content.value: Some children cry when they are born. Others laugh. But the Wild-Born—they do neither. Instead, the wind lifts in surprise, the shadows bloom with color, or nearby birds forget their own names for a heartbeat.

I once met a boy who hiccupped rainbows for a month. Another who made every stone in her village sprout moss that whispered riddles no one understood. And one girl—ah, little Taya—vanished into mist every time she tried to nap. Took us three years to get her to stay in one piece long enough for a proper hug.

Wild-Born sorcerers are not forged by flame or taught by tome. They are the island’s giggle, the storm’s tantrum, the dream that forgot to end. Their magic bursts forth without rhythm or reason—flowers blooming upside-down, frogs singing lullabies, lightning kissing the surface of still water. Some say they walked through the Dreamskin and brought pieces of it back tangled in their breath. Others believe they were marked by Queen Okumi herself, touched by joy too great to stay quiet.

Their spells may bless or bewilder, dazzle or devour. But always, always, they carry within them the first breath—the wild, sacred gasp the island took when the world was new. They do not wield their power so much as they dance with it, clumsy and brilliant and free. And sometimes… just sometimes… their chaos knits something beautiful back together.
“I do not control it. I love it. That’s enough.”
—Taya the Vanisher, last seen dancing with birds made of paint

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Sorcerers

content.value:
(Lunar)
Not all magic shouts. Not all magic burns. Some glows quiet as dew and shifts like breath through reeds. That, child, is the gift of the Moon-Bound.

I once sat beside a Moon-Bound girl who could not sleep during the full moon. Not for fear—but because she swore the face of Hoshira smiled just for her, whispering lullabies too sacred to ignore. Her eyes shimmered like water in wind, and when she spoke, the candles dimmed—not out of dread, but reverence.

The Moon-Bound are kissed not just by light, but by cycles. They are tide-keepers and dream-weavers, children of rhythm and quiet turning. Their magic follows no straight path. It crescendos like waves, wanes like sorrow, and swells again in wonder. When they cast, strange things stir: spirit-moths gather like thoughts, stones hum softly in their presence, even the wind hesitates to pass too quickly.

Some say they were born beneath Hoshira’s rare black-eye—the Soft Eclipse. Others wandered too deep into the Wandering Veil on a moonless night and came back changed, their souls laced with silver thread.
But all carry within them a pattern older than memory: a song of light and shadow, of fullness and forgetting, of promises whispered to still water.
They do not rage. They do not beg. They listen. And through them, the moon remembers.
“I am not the moon. I am what it leaves behind when it passes through a dream.”

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Sorcerers

content.value: There are callings that bloom like cherry petals in spring, and there are those that grow from root and ache. The Bloodwoven are the latter.

I met one once, in the Hollow Murkway—Ayako, they called her. She wore scars like songs and smiled only when the leeches sang. Folk feared her. Not because she harmed, no. Because she knew things she shouldn’t. Could listen to a pulse and tell what sorrow it kept.

You see, on Yurei-tu-Shima, blood isn’t just warmth in your skin—it’s story, it’s spirit, it’s the echo of every ancestor you’ve ever carried in your marrow. The Loom weaves with thread, yes, but what dyes the thread is blood. And some few sorcerers are born knowing how to twist it.

A Bloodwoven doesn’t cast spells. They whisper to the stuff that makes life want to live—or let go. Their touch can mend torn flesh or make it forget how to heal. They can call blood to dance on the wind, or to harden like memory into shapes no dreamer ever meant.

Some say they were born still and gasped only when lightning struck. Others, that they brushed against the veil of death too young and came back with red threads trailing from their soul. A few… well, a few don’t say anything at all. Their work speaks, in petals and pain.
But know this, little wanderer: the Bloodwoven are not cruel. They are close to something we all carry but seldom understand. And when their magic stirs… even the forest holds its breath.
“Blood is not violent. It is vivid.”

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Sorcerers

content.value: “Some are lit by stars. Others by fire. But you… you burn with something older than either.”
You are Spirit-Lit—your soul kindled by a light not entirely your own.
The Elder Spirits: vast forces of memory, balance, breath, and bloom. And some mortals—rare as threads of gold in soot—carry a spark of those spirits within.

Perhaps you were born beneath a shrine where Morrowel once whispered. Perhaps your grandmother walked with Onikumi Khan and bore a child in his shadow. Or maybe Queen Okumi danced through your dreams before you ever drew breath. However it happened, your magic did not come to you. It was always waiting in you.

As a Spirit-Lit, your spells shimmer with faint sigils. Your breath might fog even in summer. When you cast, petals lift from the ground or shadows fold away respectfully. Birds may go quiet when you pass. Children may cry, or smile, or both at once. You are not feared—but you are watched. Revered by some, distrusted by others, and always bound to a path of meaning greater than yourself.

Some Spirit-Lit become healers or wandering guides. Others are drawn to ruin, prophecy, or war. But all feel a presence inside them—a still warmth, a soft pull, a voice not-quite-their-own whispering from the Loom.
It is not your duty to follow blindly.
But the island watches what you choose

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Sorcerers

title.en-US: Lantern of the Star That Sings

content.value: There are lanterns made of brass and oil… and then there are those kindled by the hush between breaths, by the last sigh of a tired sky. These, child, are the bearers of Hoshira, the Lullaby Star. Hers is not a blaze—it is the light that soothes. The glow that waits. The shimmer that listens.

When one bears her lantern, the world around them softens. Wounds knit easier. Grief quiets. Even the shadows pause before creeping near. I’ve seen one of her bearers press their hand to a corrupted stone and hum so softly it wept dust. I’ve watched another walk a restless spirit to its rest with only a song and a smile.

They don’t fight like others do. No crashing, no roaring, no spit and steel. Their weapons are lullabies, their shields are warmth, and their wrath—when it comes—is the kind that stills a storm not with thunder, but with a hand on the cheek and a whisper:
But do not mistake their quiet for weakness. The Lantern of the Star That Sings does not break darkness.
It unravels it, thread by aching thread, until only starlight remains.
When you see one in the wilds, walking barefoot through the Dreamskin, or trailing silver motes in their wake, offer them tea… and let them pass.
Some burdens are not meant to be carried with noise.
Now, hush. Let the light linger a moment longer before we speak again.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Lantern-Bearers

content.value: There are lanterns that shine with comfort. There are lanterns that guide lost hearts home.

And then… there are those that leak. Lanterns cracked by truths too big, truths that should have slumbered beneath the shell of the world. These are the lights borne by those touched—no, brushed—by the uncoiling madness of Shi-Naga… or by spirits older than silence.

I met a bearer once, long ago in the Hollow Murkway. She smiled at the trees, spoke to shadows like old friends, and wore earrings shaped like opened eyes. Her lantern didn’t flicker—it trembled. The light that escaped it curled like smoke made of memories you’ve never had.
Some say they are mad. And perhaps they are. But not in the way the word means.
They have seen too much. They remember things that never happened. They speak truths that tangle, and if you listen too long… you’ll start to understand them. That’s when it gets dangerous.
They do not burn their enemies. They reveal them. Peel back the mask, unspool the lies, whisper the name you’ve hidden even from yourself. A single glance from one of them can make a spirit flinch.
Their power isn’t in shouting—it’s in the silence after the truth has been laid bare. In the space where nothing fits quite right anymore.
Do not chase these bearers. Do not ask them questions you aren’t ready to have answered. And if you must follow them, carry salt and close your left eye when they speak your name.
For some seals were never meant to be broken.
And now, my shell feels heavy. Let’s have some tea before the stars begin to watch back.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Lantern-Bearers

content.value: This lantern does not guide. It consumes.

The Hungering Flame is no gentle spirit-light. It was never meant to be held. It wants, endlessly—it wants like a mouth that never stops chewing, like grief that never finds its ending. Those who bear its ember have not tamed it. No, child. They have bargained with it.

Some say the first flame came from Malgrotha, the Glutton Below—that terrible joy of devouring, the ancient hunger beneath root and ruin. Others say the kindling comes from drowned rage, from the last breath of a spirit betrayed, or from fire denied a home.
What sort of bearer would take up such a light?
One who has already burned, I think.

They carry vengeance like a torch—but it is not always their own. Some burn for justice. Some burn for spite. A few burn so others won’t have to. Their pact is not always selfish. But it is always costly.

And when they strike, they strike like a wildfire—with no apology and no half-measure. Mercy, hesitation, fear—these are the first things the flame eats. What’s left is a soul sharpened to ash and sorrow, walking forward with purpose and ruin in every step.
You’ll know them by the way heat clings to their silence. By the smoke that tastes like memory. By the way they do not look away when pain is near.
And sometimes—only sometimes—they burn themselves hollow to become the last flame standing between the world and oblivion.
So if you see one, thank them.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Lantern-Bearers

content.value: There is a kind of magic that doesn’t burn or blind. It beckons. It skips just ahead, laughing, barefoot in the dark. That is the light of the Gloaming Court.

To carry this lantern is to hold contradiction: sorrow and delight, jest and grief, illusion and truth folded like origami in the same breath. These bearers are chosen—or tricked—by Queen Okumi herself, that spirit of blooms and broken hearts. Or perhaps by one of her court: a fox with a hundred names, a tree that speaks only in sighs, a child made of stars and string.
Their light? Oh, it’s not fire. It’s moon-honey and dream-pollen. It changes color with your mood. It leads you where you didn’t mean to go—but perhaps always needed to be.

Some call these Lantern-Bearers tricksters. Others call them liars. But I say they’re mirrors, held at just the right tilt. They can steal your name with a smile, but give you back a truth you didn’t know you’d lost.

They speak in riddles not to confuse, but to protect—because the straight path is not always the safest. And when the time comes to act? They do not stab. They unweave. They undo. They laugh as the lie crumbles.
Their steps leave no tracks. Their stories leave no lies.
But they leave something behind in everyone they meet—
A wistfulness. A wonder. A wound that sings.
So if you meet one beneath falling petals or starlit fog, tip your head, not your cup. They’ve already stolen your heart. They’ll return it… changed.
Heehee. You feel that tug in your chest? That’s her lantern, I think. Careful now. Follow it too far, and you might end up inside your own tale.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Lantern-Bearers

content.value:
(Genie)
There are spirits, my dear, and then there are Jinkaido—those who were the elements before the island had names for them. They are not merely fire, or earth, or air, or sea… they are what those words remember.

To carry their lantern is to walk beside something that once shattered sky with song. They do not whisper—they rumble. They do not guide gently—they shape. You don’t choose the Jinkaido. You survive them. And if you survive well, you are chosen.

Your lantern might crackle like a hearth or hum like molten stone. Some bearers breathe steam, or leave sea-glass footprints, or weep sparks in sleep. These are not metaphors, little one. These are the wages of pact.
Some Lantern-Bearers serve to heal the damage their Kindling once wrought. Others are sent like quakes—tools of elemental balance, swift and terrifying.
But all are changed. Not because they are told to be—but because you cannot carry a storm and remain a leaf.
If you meet one with eyes like cooled basalt or a tongue that tastes of lightning, do not ask their name. Ask who they serve.
And if the wind hushes when they answer… bow.
Not out of fear, no. Out of respect. The kind that even mountains remember.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Lantern-Bearers

content.value: Ahhh-ho-ho-ho… yes, now this one makes my shell rattle with delight.

Let me tell you of a spirit who never walks straight, never answers plain, and never once missed a chance to pull the moon’s pants down. A spirit with laughter sticky as nectar and grief so sweet it wilts the air.
I speak, of course, of the Blooming Fool.

Some say she wears the face of Queen Okumi—and who am I to argue? That grin of hers could split a shrine in two. But whether she is Okumi or just one of her louder dreams, well… only the flowers seem to know, and they’re not telling.

The Lantern-Bearers who carry her spark are dancers in a crooked ballet. They skip through sorrow like it’s a rain puddle. They tuck joy into their sleeves like daggers. And their lanterns don’t glow—they giggle. Ever seen a lantern laugh? I have. It winked at me. I didn’t sleep right for a week.

These bearers are tricksters, poets, jesters with haunted eyes and hearts that bloom sideways. When they speak, the truth hides under punchlines. When they cast, it’s never simple. One time, I saw one turn a warlord’s sword into a bouquet of turnips. The warlord cried. Then he thanked her.

But don’t be fooled by the fool, no no no. There’s sharpness in that bloom. A petal’s edge can still draw blood, and behind all the glitter and giggle, there’s an ache—a longing to mend what’s broken not with a hammer, but with a joke that makes it all come loose and land right.

The Blooming Fool gives power, yes. But she also gives mischief. She might bless your footsteps or tie your shoelaces together. She might send you a vision—or a pie to the face. You won’t know which until it’s too late.
But oh, you will remember her. And if you walk her path, they’ll remember you.
So dance, my dear sprig, dance crooked. Laugh like the world’s still worth saving. Because sometimes, joy is the only rebellion that sticks.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Lantern-Bearers

content.value: You ever met someone who knew what you were going to say before you said it? Not because they’re clever—but because they remember hearing it, once, from the future you haven’t walked into yet?
Mmm. Strange, yes. But not impossible.

I once shared a plum cake with a quiet Kojin girl near the Wandering Veil—sweet lass with ink on her fingers and a shadow that never quite followed her right. She told me she’d made a promise to herself. “But not this self,” she said with a wink, “the me who’s waiting.” Spirits above, I nearly choked on my tea.
They call that kind of pact a Lantern of the Echoing Thread.

It don’t burn like the others. No fire. No frost. Just a soft shimmer in the belly that hums when you almost make a mistake—or when you already did, but haven’t yet. The Kindling? Well, it ain’t a god, or a ghost, or even one of those Jinkaido storm-lords. No, this one’s stitched from time itself. It’s you. Or them. Or who you might be, if you keep choosing the path that leads to the next version of your story.

These Lantern-Bearers walk a winding line, they do. Sometimes they know too much. Sometimes they know just enough to make a mess. But they learn, and they loop, and they carry a light that whispers: “Try again.”

I’ve seen ‘em stare into ponds and see memories they haven’t made yet. Seen ‘em flinch before the arrow loosed. Seen ‘em walk into a room like they were always meant to be there. And when they cast their spells? Oh, it’s like hearing a riddle tell itself.
Now… do I believe they really speak to their future selves?
Heh. Friend, I once watched a petal fall up. Nothing surprises me anymore.

All I know is this: when the wind hushes, and the mist curls like it’s listening, and a person steps forward with eyes that carry stories not yet told—I offer them a seat and pour the tea. Because whatever they’re about to do…

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Lantern-Bearers

content.value:
(Abjuration)
I’ve shared tea with a few, though they never quite seem to sit still for long. Too many wards to trace. Too many winds to test for poison. Still, they carry themselves like cliff-stones—quiet, weathered, and steady beneath the fiercest squall.

To call one simply a “protector” is like calling a lantern just a flame. These Wizards do not guard with brute defiance. No, no. They listen—to cracks in the world, to tremors in the Loom, to breaths drawn in panic by villagers huddled near old shrines. Then they weave. Not cloth, not string—but spells that hold fast, that remember the shape of peace even when chaos snarls all around them.

You’ll find Wardweavers where things go wrong. At the edge of sinkholes that weren’t there yesterday. By doorways that breathe too loud. In towns where no one dreams anymore, because something unseen gnaws at the soul of sleep. They go where the line thins between what should be and what should not.

Their sigils hum softly, like lullabies written in wind. Their magic tastes like cool stone, smells like ink and iron, and leaves behind a hush—as if the world itself sighs in relief when their spells take hold.

And yes, some speak of them with unease. After all, these are Wizards who push things back. Spirits, curses, memories, even fate. But I say this: when the mist thickens, when the laughter of old ghosts turns sharp, it is the Wardweaver who steps forward.
But to hold the world together long enough for the rest of us to remember who we are.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Wizards

content.value:
(Divination)
Ahhh, now you’re whispering about the Seers of the Wandering Line, are you? A peculiar lot—kindly, mostly, but not the sort you meet by accident. Or perhaps every meeting with them is an accident, one that was meant to happen all along.

These Diviners, they don’t just look at stars—they listen to them. They tilt their heads at the wind like it’s reciting poetry, and some swear they can taste tomorrow on their tongues before the sun even stirs. I once knew a Seer named Kemi-Ten-Winks who could braid prophecy into your hair, though the meaning of it wouldn’t reveal itself until your third heartbreak. Hmph. Clever girl.

Their tradition, the Wanderer’s Eye, teaches that fate is not a road but a river, full of eddies and curls, where knowing which leaf will pass next is less useful than knowing why it turns when it does. These Wizards trace that river—not to control it, mind—but to float just ahead of the storm, just behind the silence, right in the seam of what might be.

To others, they seem distracted, always scribbling in the margins of books that haven’t been written yet or speaking to shadows that haven’t arrived. But oh, the things they see. And not all of them pleasant. That’s the price of their art. You see a little too far, you start to wonder if your own smile is a memory or a warning.
They say the Seers write prophecies in water so only those willing to listen may read. Not look—listen. For their truth isn’t in the image, but the ripple. The echo. The breath just before the word.
If you meet one, be polite. Offer tea. Don’t ask them what will happen to you—unless you’re prepared to listen with your heart, not just your ears.
And above all: never ask them how it ends.
And they rarely smile when they tell it.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Wizards

content.value: Evocation, child, is not merely the calling of fire or the crackle of lightning—it is the Loom made loud. It is the echo of the island’s first breath, still tumbling through time like a boulder that has never stopped rolling. And those who follow this path? Ah, they are called Jinbinders—named for the ancient breath of force, of flame, of everything that moves.

A Jinbinder does not cast spells so much as release them. They draw forth raw emotion from the Loom and shape it into crashing tides, bursting flame, thunder that wakes the bones, or light so radiant it makes shadows tremble. Their magic is feeling—grief, joy, fury—pressed into shape and hurled like a prayer with teeth.

But let no one mistake them for destroyers alone. A well-placed wave of force may shield a village from a landslide. A blossom of heat might stir frost-numbed limbs. Even their most violent spell can be an act of love—loud love, yes, but love nonetheless.

Some Jinbinders learn beneath the soot-sung caverns of Emberflow Springs, tracing fire-veins and shouting spells into lava to see what echoes back. Others wander—storm-chasers, volcano-watchers, spirit-duelists who treat each battle like a conversation shouted between worlds.
And when a Jinbinder speaks, the Loom listens.
For theirs is the gift of the First Spark—and it was never meant to be quiet.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Wizards

content.value: Illusion is not deception, no-no—it is invitation. A shimmer. A breath. A dream that leans just close enough to kiss your cheek before vanishing again. Those who walk this soft-footed path are known as Whisperers of the Dreamskin, for their craft pulls from that misty veil that sometimes slips into our world—where meaning outweighs matter.

A Whisperer does not conjure lies. They conjure might-have-beens. They do not paint falsehoods, but reflections—some warped, some weeping, some wondrous. A lantern where there was only fear. A bridge where hope had fallen. The echo of a promise not yet made.

Many such Wizards find kinship in the Wandering Veil, where spirits of illusion flutter like petals caught in wind. Some Whisperers serve Hoshira, the Lullaby Star, weaving dreams into waking minds. Others follow Kokoro-no-Kami, crafting balance from illusion and insight. To them, magic is a story gently told, not a command barked loud.

They study mirrors that don’t reflect, winds that carry voices backward, and lanterns that glow only when you’re not looking. They delight in mischief, but never cruelty. Their spells ripple like laughter over still water—or like a sob muffled beneath a festival mask.
To walk among the Whisperers is to understand this: illusion, at its gentlest, is mercy. At its sharpest, it is truth wearing the costume of beauty.
“What is real, little one? The stone beneath your feet? Or the memory of your mother’s voice calling you home? One can be touched. The other can change you.”

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Wizards

content.value: In the hush between dusk and dream, some Wizards take to a path few dare to follow: the path of Quiet Return. These are not necromancers in the old-tongue sense—not bone-howlers or corpse-puppeteers, no-no. These are weavers of stillness. Listeners of the long silence. They do not command the dead. They ask.

To study this school is to sit with endings. With the weight of final breaths and the trails they leave behind like mist on morning grass. It is a practice bound by reverence—never haste, never greed. For the dead in Yurei-tu-Shima are not always buried. They linger. They drift. They speak through wind-knocks, cracked bells, or warm hands gone cold.

Wizards of Quiet Return often come from the Hollow Murkway, where the trees root deep into forgotten graves and the air carries whispers like frogsong. Many bear tokens of the dead—a braided sash from a lost sibling, a bone-inked charm, a lantern filled with breath. Some learn from the mourners of the Nakamura line, who walk behind every funeral to ensure no spirit follows too far. Others find quiet kinship with Onikumi Khan, the bear who tests reverence by walking in mortal feet. And still others feel the soft pull of Namakusa, the spirit of unfinished ends, whose white cloak turns blood-pink when regrets are near.

Their spells are gentle, but not weak. They might call forth a shade to ask a single question. Bind a wrathful ghost to stillness with threads of soot and salt. Or mend the spirit-tether of one who died too afraid to pass on. Their magic smells of sandalwood and wet stone, and when they cast, you may hear the wind hush to listen.
They walk the grave-path not to rule over the dead, but to remind them of peace.
And when their work is done, when the lost have been heard, when the rage has softened into memory… they always bow.
Because death, my child, is not a door. It is a river.
And we must never cross it without leaving an offering on the shore.
“Come now, child. The dead are not gone. They are waiting… and they remember who listens.”

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Wizards

content.value: There are Wizards who demand things become what they are not. And then there are those who listen—who place their palms on stone and ask, “What have you always wanted to be?”

The School of Living Change is no place for the rigid or cruel. It is a tradition of coaxing, not commanding. Of guidance, not force. These wizards do not shape the world through conquest, but through companionship. They speak to the will inside the world—to the copper that yearns for silver, to the egg that dreams of wings, to the sorrow that wants to bloom.

Such folk are often called weavers, or spirit-smiths, or whisperers of the in-between. You’ll know them by their hands: always stained with clay, ash, or ink. You’ll find them in shrines and gardens, but also workshops and riverbanks, anywhere the world is halfway into becoming something else.

Their tools are strange and beautiful—a cicada shell tucked in a pouch, a coin flattened by the Tamagari Line, a vial of rain caught on the first day of spring. Their breath smells like iron and orchids. Their gaze, child, can make even a shadow straighten its back.

Some are humble repairers, setting broken pots right and healing wounds with murmured spells that smell like lavender and smoke. Others chase truths older than stone. They ask things like: What would a mountain become if it felt joy? or Can a curse be turned inside out until it hums like a lullaby?
The world, you see, does not wish to remain what it is.

Wizards of Living Change walk beside that yearning. Not ahead. Not behind. Beside. They believe every spirit, every stone, every scrap of rusted metal has a story yet untold. And their magic? It is the hand that gently turns the page.
So, if you meet one, offer them a broken thing—be it a spoon, or a promise. They may not fix it.
But they might change it into something better.
Something you didn’t know you were waiting for.
“Even the mountain dreams of being mist. Even the river remembers being rain.”
—Master Umei, Spirit-Smith of the Blooming Gift

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Wizards

content.value: Now, many folk think conjuration is just summoning things from thin air—poof, a spirit, a sword, a slice of pear. Ha! That’s child’s play, and dangerous besides. No, the Woven Callers of Yurei-tu-Shima know better.
They know that nothing truly appears. It arrives.

The School of Woven Calling teaches that every presence is already out there, somewhere in the Loom, breathing just beyond the veil. These wizards don’t yank things into the world. They invite them. Kindly. Carefully. Sometimes with a whisper, sometimes with a song.

You’ll know a true Woven Caller by the inked rings on their fingers or the lacquered tokens they wear—tiny charms to honor the things they call. They walk the Wandering Veil, soft-footed and humble, asking frogs to share their names, or winds to carry their scent. And when they draw their circles—not traps, never traps, no no—they decorate them with rice, with old lullabies, with the salt of their own breath. These are not cages, child. They are invitations.

A Woven Caller calls to fogs that remember drowning, shadows that once danced, or to long-lost items that still know the shape of your hands. Sometimes they call a memory. Sometimes they call a guardian. Sometimes they call something that was listening too closely.

Teleportation? Mmm, that too is a form of asking. Not rending the world in halves, no. Just leaning close to the Loom and saying: “Please… may I be where I once belonged?” If you’ve asked kindly before, the Loom often listens.

Rude conjurers go missing, you know. Vanish right from their own circles. But the ones who bow before they speak? Who leave honey or folded paper where a spirit once helped them? Oh, those conjurers are followed by little kindnesses. Breezes that blow out bad fires. Spirits who nudge their elbow before the arrow flies. Familiar hands where none should be.
Woven Callers understand this: all magic is relationship.
So they ask. And listen. And when their work is done, they send what came back home—with thanks.
Because even summoned things deserve to rest.
“Nothing comes from nowhere. Everything is waiting. You need only ask—gently.”
—Sora Mikka, bellkeeper of the Wandering Veil

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Wizards

content.value: To enchant, child, is not to conquer. It is to understand.

The School of Gentle Binding teaches wizards how to trace the shape of a soul without bruising it. They work not with shackles or chains, but with the soft threads of empathy, intuition, and unspoken desire. Their spells do not crash—they hum, they resonate, they bind.
These are the wizards who tilt a head and change a mood. Who step into a room and the argument stops. Who can ask a boar not to charge—or a grieving widow to take one more breath—and be heard.

Some learn this magic from the shrine-priestesses who soothe the spirits of the newly dead. Some from wandering poets, who can make bandits cry with just a verse. And there are a few, just a few, born with voices like lakewater at dusk—so still, so deep, so persuasive, it can unsettle even spirits.

To bind gently is to weave with the Loom itself, not ripping or forcing—but asking. When a Gentle Binder charms another, they do so not by ripping thought apart, but by whispering to the part of the soul already leaning toward yes. Their magic isn’t felt like fire. It’s felt like remembering something beautiful. Or hearing your name spoken the way it should have always sounded.

They wear no crowns. They carry no whips. Their power is suggestion that feels like a decision, trust that lingers even after the spell has faded. Some use it to keep peace. Others to cause mischief. And a few… well, a few have tried to shape the memories of love itself. That path rarely ends gently.

The spirits—especially those of truth, of balance—watch this art with keen eyes. For to enchant is to reach deep, to change the song in another’s chest. And once you’ve done that, little one, you’d best know what tune you’re leaving behind.
Still… used well, enchantment is the softest kind of healing. The warmest kind of bond.
And sometimes, the only magic that can stop a blade… is a word.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Wizards

content.value: “A blade is a brush. A spell is breath. A Bladesinger paints with both.”
—Takani of the Blooming Gift, poet-duelist of the Lantern Court

On Yurei-tu-Shima, a Bladesinger does not fight. No, no. They weave. Each duel is a poem in motion, every spell a shimmer of breath made visible, every step a stanza that ripples through the Loom. Their dance is sacred—a prayer whispered through muscle and memory.
These are not warriors. These are spell-dancers. Shrine-duelists. Arcane scribes of motion.

The tradition first grew strong among the Elves of the Wandering Veil, who see no boundary between art and combat. A Bladesinger there may train for decades under falling petals, carving loops in the air until the spirits weep from the beauty of it. Their steel hums with tiny sigils, etched in languages too old to speak aloud. Their armor? It is often light, sewn with talismans—ribbons for grace, silver threads for clarity, charms to steady the breath in battle.
But don’t think only Elves can walk this path, no no. I once knew a Kojin who Bladesang with a fan in one hand and a frying pan in the other—and never lost a single duel.

Bladesingers cast not like scholars, but like dancers who forget where their limbs end and the magic begins. Their incantations flow through their strikes. Their blades are punctuation to the sentence of their will. And their enemies? They fall not from rage—but from rhythm.
A duel between two Bladesingers is a conversation, whispered across steel. It ends not in gloating—but in a bow. Always a bow.

Some Bladesingers learn in the moonlit circles of shrine courtyards, every footstep laid in quiet ritual. Others are born into it—children who cannot help but spin when they speak, whose hands draw sigils in the air even in sleep.

To be a Bladesinger is to know restraint as power, and grace as the sharpest edge of all. Their magic does not rush. It flows. Their swords do not lash. They answer. Their presence on the battlefield is not chaos, but a kind of music—and long after the fighting ends, you may still hear their echo, like wind chimes swaying in the breath of a memory.
Mmm… now that’s a story that dances, don’t you think?

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Wizards

content.value:
(alchemist)
“Life is not a substance—it’s a balance. A whisper of steam, a drop of memory, and a pinch of breath.”

Among the forges of Emberflow and the steam-wrapped hills where spirits hum beneath the clay, there live crafters of elixirs not bound by recipes or rules—but by feeling. The Essence Brewer does not merely mix. Oh no. They commune.

Each bottle is a question. Each brew, a conversation. Their cauldrons bubble not just with herbs, but with laughter, loss, love, and leaf-shadow. You might think you’ve sipped ginger tea—only to find yourself weeping over a memory you never lived. Or laughing in the voice of your great-grandfather. Or blinking out stardust from your lashes.

The tools of their craft? Clay kettles painted with ghost-sigils. Hollowed gourd flasks wrapped in lucky thread. Long-handled stirring rods carved from fallen shrinewood. And always—always—a little bell, so the spirit in the brew knows when to arrive.

They source ingredients not by rarity, but by resonance. Frostberries picked during heartbreak. Rainwater gathered from a sky that forgave. Charcoal drawn from the last fire of a funeral rite. All balanced by instinct, weather, and whatever song happens to be playing nearby.

Oh, and the side effects? Ha! I once drank a brewer’s courage-draught and couldn’t stop quoting love poems to trees for a week. Some potions sing when shaken. Others cry when spilled. A few even vanish entirely if brewed while grumpy.
But the truly gifted Brewers… mm. They can brew light into a jar. Or trap silence. Or soothe the dying with a single taste of dawn.
Their gift is not merely to heal or harm. It is to translate emotion into matter. To take what is felt—grief, giddiness, longing—and distill it into something you can hold, sip, share.
So if ever one offers you a vial—ask what they were feeling when they brewed it. For that, more than any label, tells the truth of what’s inside.
Now hush… hold this cup for me. No, don’t drink it yet. Smell it first. That warmth? That hum at the back of your throat? That’s the memory of a summer that never happened.
I brewed it for someone who missed a childhood they never got.
