And now? It’s ready for someone who needs it.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Spirit-Crafters

content.value: “The shell is not armor. It is memory hardened. A shrine of moving parts, humming with purpose.”
—Takaru of the Iron Drift, quiet walker of the Emberflow Forgewells

To become a Golem-Shell Artificer is not to wear protection—it is to fuse with intention. These spirit-crafters do not don suits like soldiers. They enter sacred partnerships with constructs of bone-steel, spirit-glass, and ember-thread. Each suit is a whispered pact, a remembered burden, a moving shrine sculpted to shield not just the flesh—but the soul inside.

Some say they descend from the Daru smiths of the First Age, who once built golems guided by breath and dream. Others believe they follow the blueprints left behind by guardian spirits who once wrapped mortals in celestial husks during storms of sorrow. Whatever the origin, the Golem-Shell is always more than machine.

The plating might bear lacquered charms tied with fox-hair thread. Joints may click in seven-beat rhythms, echoing ancient spirit-drum prayers. A helm might open like a lotus. Or never open at all. Their voices come filtered—like temple bells muffled in fog. Their eyes sometimes glow with the colors of the Loom itself.

They carry tools inside their shells: sparking welders that double as weapons, coils that hiss spirit-light, or scroll-launchers tucked in compartments beside their hearts. Some even inscribe their own bodies with repair glyphs, so when the shell cracks, it remembers how to mend itself.

When the Golem-Shell casts spells, gears realign. Shoulder-plates unfold into wings of folded steel. Glowing kanji ripple like breath across chestplates. The magic does not leap from their hands—it reverberates through the frame, like song through a drum.

But don’t be fooled. These are not weapons to be flaunted. Golem-Shells are guardians. Of bridges. Of children. Of vows. They tend to old shrines long lost to moss. They stand at cliff edges, watching storms. They enter battle slowly, reverently, as if each step were a prayer for what must not be broken.
And when they fall? The earth remembers.
Some say the armor sometimes stands again. Alone. Just for a moment. As if the spirit inside isn’t quite ready to let go.
I once asked a Golem-Shell why they never removed their armor. They looked at me—gentle, glowing, creaking just slightly—and said:
“Because it is not a thing I wear. It is a thing that remembered me when I had forgotten myself.”
I nodded. And offered them tea. They drank it through a straw in the neck joint. Still the best guest I ever had.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Spirit-Crafters

content.value:
(Battlesmith)
“We are not warriors. We are those who hold the line and mend what would otherwise be lost.”
—Toma of the Hollow Vein, soulforger of the Gilded Still

To walk the path of a Soulmender Smith is to carry a promise: not of conquest, but of care. They are the guardians who kneel first when blood stains the stones. The builders who raise barricades from memory and breath. The healers who speak to steel as kindly as they do to spirits.

They do not wield magic as fire or lightning. No. Their craft is channeled—woven through copper-threaded sutures, folded charms pressed into armor joints, and breath-fed spirit machines shaped with sacred care. They build their spells. Tend their enchantments. Sharpen their hope.

Their constant companion—a creation of their own soul-bound labor—is more than a construct. It is a guardian given form, a living sculpture of devotion and design. These companions may take the shape of four-legged guardians, beetle-backed bulwarks, or even floating masks wreathed in calming threadlight. They do not speak, but understand. Their hum is a lullaby. Their shield, a prayer made solid.

In battle, the Soulmender stands firm—one hand lifting a spirit-forged barrier, the other wrapping gauze around a wound already healing. They do not rush. They anchor. Their armor bears the gentle markings of the healed: names etched in spiral, or fabric patches sewn with stories of survival.

Their tools? Oh, a marvel. Kits of lacquered birch and glass, each drawer a whisper of medicine and machine. Syringes made from hummingbird bones. Salves stirred by steam and spirit ink. A tuning fork to realign fractured chi. And always, always… a bell. Small, silver, perfect. To call the soul back.
You’ll find Soulmenders where others cannot stand: on collapsed bridges, in flooded temples, by the side of broken guardians. They don’t shout. They arrive. And the world steadies around them.
When the mist rolls in and screams are swallowed by silence, the Soulmender Smith lights a lantern, presses a hand to their Companion’s side… and walks into the storm. Not to win.
But to save what would otherwise be lost.
Elder Gubi-Goni bows slowly now, breath gentle as steam rising from his tea.
“We remember those who build, not just those who break. And oh… how brightly the Soulmenders shine.”

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Spirit-Crafters

content.value:
(Artillerist)
“Control the blast, and it sings. Lose yourself in it… and the spirits will scatter like cinders.”
—Reika of the Ash Vault, flame-architect of Emberflow Springs

The Emberbloom Hibana are not demolitionists. They are ritual bombardiers—painters of the sky who shape thunder into form, fire into language, and smoke into rhythm. Their tools are crafted with reverence: lacquered barrels inlaid with prayer-scrolls, tripods carved from lightning-felled trees, and cannon-lanterns that hum lullabies between detonations.

Their cannons—called Hibana, or “spark-children”—are not mindless machines. They are spirit-bound mechanisms, each one forged with careful intention and a name whispered during its creation. Some blast gouts of flame laced with foxfire spirits. Others fire radiant orbs that bloom mid-air like ink flowers. A few sing when they charge—notes of warning, not threat.

They are masters of explosive harmony. Their art lies not in destruction, but in choreography: a blast that collapses a canyon wall to stop a flood; a flare that calls wandering spirits home; a concussive burst that cracks the silence before truth can be spoken.

Each Emberbloom Hibana carries a satchel of handcrafted devices—small wooden totems that spin and spark, spirit-chimes that burst into shielding light, and fire-seeds that burrow into the ground and hum before rising. These are not grenades. They are shaped invocations, each one a pact made of combustion and care.

Many train in the Emberflow Forgewells, where lava steam is harnessed with braided copper and spirit-soot is inked into scrolls. Others are wanderers, creating Matoi-turrets that dance like fireworks along clifftops or defending shrines with floating sigil-bombs tethered to paper cranes.

Their presence on the battlefield is unmistakable: a scent of ozone and plum-smoke, a heartbeat like a distant drum, and a sense—just before the sky cracks open—that someone has asked the spirits very politely to aim just so.
They do not laugh at fire.
And the flame, in return, dances only for them.

category.en-US: CALLINGS\The Spirit-Crafters

content.value: Here is the full summary of all thirteen Callings of Yurei-tu-Shima—each a distinct path by which one may walk in rhythm with spirit, memory, and breath:

To walk this path is to surrender to the pulse of instinct and storm. The Wild-Bound are those who awaken ancient echoes within—the howl, the heart-thunder, the root-deep roar. They become as tempest, as tide, as beast remembered by the land. Not savages, but awakened.

Keepers of song, story, and sound that shapes spirit. The Echo-Touched wield rhythm as spellcraft, weaving tales into power. Whether through flute, brushstroke, or laughter, they echo the voices of those who came before—and make new echoes for those yet to come.

Devotees of Elder Spirits who walk in devotion and divine breath. They do not demand miracles—they serve them. Whether as shrine guardians, storm-callers, or bone-washers, the Spirit-Bound are vessels for the sacred, guided by prayer, mask, and firelight.

Those who follow the cycles of wind, root, tide, and flame. The Breath-Walkers listen to nature not as backdrop, but as teacher. They shift with the seasons, change like leaves, and call upon the living island for guidance, protection, and renewal.

Warriors of form and resolve. The Futansha are not just fighters—they are bearers of burdens, keepers of discipline, and wearers of sacred mantles. From shield-bearers to gunslingers, they embody the struggle to defend, to endure, and to shape change through courage.

Disciples of breath and body. These monks do not merely strike—they resonate. The Seikin channel elemental forces, internal balance, and disciplined fury into movements so precise they become prayers. Their silence often speaks louder than swords.

Those who swear themselves to ideals, spirits, or causes so deeply that it shapes the magic they wield. Their oaths are living things—binding them to justice, vengeance, mercy, or memory. In the Oathkeeper’s stride, promise and power walk hand in hand.

Wanderers, scouts, and sacred listeners to the hidden paths of the world. The Pathfinders thrive in the spaces between—the breath before battle, the hush before dawn. They track not only beasts, but truth, purpose, and the flow of unseen threads.

Those who slip between light and shadow, mask and truth. The Shade Walkers are not merely thieves or assassins—they are dancers in forgotten spaces, carriers of quiet justice, and bearers of stories too dangerous to speak aloud. Every step a secret.

Magic flows through them like a bloodline, a storm, or a curse. The Sorcerers did not choose their power—it chose them. They burn with potential barely contained, and every spell they cast is a whisper from the spirit realm, echoed through their soul.

Bound to powers old, forbidden, or misunderstood. The Lantern-Bearers strike pacts not always made in light. They walk with spirits, forgotten shrines, or gods who linger. Their magic is borrowed—but in return, they become storytellers of flame and pact.

Scholars of the Loom itself. Wizards are those who study patterns, weave threads, and understand the why behind the how. They bend magic not through instinct or faith—but through brilliance, discipline, and reverence for the mysteries of the world.

Artisans who blend spirit and science, crafting relics and machines that hum with purpose. They are part inventor, part spirit-whisperer. In every gadget, golem, or potion they make is a prayer to forgotten hands and a spark from the First Age’s dreams.
~ Thirteen Callings. Thirteen ways to breathe meaning into the world. And none lesser than another.
“Even a kettle boils differently depending on who lights the flame. So too with Callings. It’s not what you are that sings loudest—it’s how you stir the breath that surrounds you.”

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA

content.value: Mossrock Shoals is a sleepy patch of coast nestled in the heart of the Silken Shoals, where the sea comes in gentle and warm, and the moss grows thick even on the stone. Not many know it by name, for it’s not marked on most maps. But if you follow the drifting lantern crabs, or listen to where the gulls sing slower, you’ll find it—half-lost in sea mist and tide-grass hush.

Our homes there are built on stilts, all wood and rope and salt-weathered dreams. The air smells of sea pears and fried rootfish, and the waves talk more than the people do. We Kemari folk keep things slow in Mossrock. Even the ghosts forget to haunt on some days.

That’s where I first heard the stories. Not in a grand hall or spirit shrine, but on an old rug beside a cracked teapot, while my grandmother tapped her shell and spoke in riddles. The moss remembers. The shells whisper. Even the driftwood seems to hum if you lean just right.

So if you ask me where Mossrock Shoals is… it’s in the Silken Shoals, yes—but more than that, it’s in the quiet places. The soft places. The places where the stories begin before anyone knows they’re stories at all.
And that, little one, is where I come from.

category.en-US: REGIONS OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\THE SILKEN SHOALS (SOUTHERN REGION)

content.value: Coralveil is the last sigh of the land before it falls into the sea—a twilight town clinging to the jagged cliffs of the Shattered Shelf, where the sky is always lavender and the lanterns float like jellyfish in the fog. The buildings are all leaning this way or that, like they’re listening to the waves below, and the wind carries more stories than dust.

The folk there speak soft and walk softer, their boots worn smooth by coral steps and spiral paths. Coralveil doesn’t shout to be known—it hums, it murmurs. Seaweed shops drift between half-submerged towers, and the old sea-bells toll whenever the mist gets thick enough to lose your name in.
And nestled at the very top, like a pearl set in the spine of the cliffs, sits the Twilight Scriptorium.
Now that’s a place of wonders.

The Scriptorium isn’t just a library—it’s a listening place, built into a coral tower where salt and silence bind the shelves. Books hum in their bindings. Scrolls unfurl themselves if you say the right poem. And if you sit still long enough, you’ll hear the walls remembering things you forgot. Some say the whole structure was grown, not built—breathed into shape by spirit-guides and old gnome hands, stitched together with ink and intention.

It is here that the great Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III keeps his field notes, his sketches, and his softly muttering artifacts. His voice-crystals echo through the echo-chambers like whispered footnotes on the wind. He’s traveled the island tip to shell, but always returns here, to Coralveil… to the Scriptorium… where knowledge dries like sea glass and waits to be held up to the light.

So, child, if your heart is full of questions and your hands itch for stories, make your way to Coralveil, and follow the spiral stairs into the Twilight Scriptorium. Just don’t open the third drawer in the west wall unless you’re prepared to bargain with a particularly dramatic book about mushrooms.

category.en-US: REGIONS OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\THE SHATTERED SHELF (SOUTHEASTERN REGION)

content.value: Muramori sits cradled in the gentler glades of the Wandering Veil, a village stitched from woven bark, root bridges, and lantern-light dreams. The people there live slow, speak softer, and treat words like tea—steeped long before shared. Most roofs are moss-capped. Most homes curve to the trees rather than cut them. Spirit-charms hang from every branch, catching not wind, but intention.

The villagers are good listeners. They watch the mist and say little, for they believe the forest listens too—and may repeat what it hears if spoken carelessly. Children are taught not to whistle after sundown, and offerings of inkstones or folded leaves are left at tree hollows before asking questions too bold.
Now—just east of Muramori, past the thickets where even moss forgets to grow, there lies a place few name aloud: Whispergrove.

You’ll know you’re near when the air begins to hush you, and even your thoughts seem muffled. The whisperwillows rise there—tall, silver-veined trees whose bark carries stories like scars. Elders say if you press your palm to one and close your eyes, the tree may lend you a memory not your own. A lost love, a final farewell, a promise never spoken.

The air in Whispergrove doesn’t carry sound—it swallows it. Even the cicadas go silent. It’s not a place of fear, but of reverence. Spirits dwell there who don’t wish to be seen, only understood. And sometimes the silence speaks back.

So if you walk from Muramori Village, and the path begins to blur, and your own breath sounds too loud… you may be nearing Whispergrove, the silent hollow of the Wandering Veil where even secrets kneel to listen.

category.en-US: REGIONS OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\THE WANDERING VEIL (NORTHEASTERN REGION)

content.value: Ahhh… now you speak of the reef near Shallowgrove, a quiet bend of the coast tucked along the Silken Shoals, where the sea turns a shade too clear, and the tide sings in tones you can’t quite hum back.

Just offshore lies the Dreamreef, though few call it that aloud. Most just point and shake their heads, or make a charm sign over their hearts. It’s not deep—no, not at first. The water is welcoming, warm, even playful. Fish with lantern-eyes dart between fan corals, and the kelp dances like it’s listening to music only it can hear.

But something shifts, just below. The light bends wrong. The silence gets… thick. And those who dive too far, or too long, sometimes return with gill marks across their necks, delicate and thin, like they were kissed by something that breathes water instead of air. And when they speak, they laugh—but it’s a laughter that doesn’t seem to fit in their throats. Too wet. Too old. Too full of something that never quite surfaces.
They don’t always remember what they saw. Or they pretend not to.

Some whisper that sea-spirits dwell in the reef, playful or curious or perhaps just lonely. Others say it’s a door, a thin place between here and the deeper folds of the Spirit Realm, where the sea remembers everything and sometimes shares.
Whatever truth there is, Shallowgrove minds its tides carefully. And the reef waits, swaying slow beneath the waves, humming stories in a voice borrowed from the deep

category.en-US: REGIONS OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\THE SILKEN SHOALS (SOUTHERN REGION)

content.value: Steamhaven is a forge-town, aye—but not all smoke and clang. It’s tucked into the fractured amber ridges of Emberflow Springs, where the earth breathes heat and the stones sweat with fire-born patience. The hills there are cracked like old teacups, with steam rising from every crevice, some hissing, some sighing, and some singing if you’ve got the ears for it.

The Daru work their iron there, yes—honest folk with soot-stained fingers and laughter that echoes like anvils—but it’s not just hammers and hinges in Steamhaven. The old tech of the First Age still lingers, buried in basements, repurposed into stoves or lanterns, or humming softly in the corner of some family’s workshop.

It was there that I met him—a young Jinkaido boy, bright as polished brass and clever as a clock not yet wound. He beckoned me over with inky hands and lifted the lid on a battered kettle. And wouldn’t you know—it whistled a joke. Something about two spirits and a broken weather-vane. The punchline came out in a puff of steam shaped like a giggling toad.

He said the kettle used to be part of a larger spirit-box—maybe a tea maker, maybe a messenger—but now it just told stories when the water hit boil. The boy had given it a name. Mister Rattlecup, I think. Or maybe Boilbeard. The kettle wasn’t clear on that.
That’s Steamhaven for you—half forge, half forgotten dream, where flame and memory twist together like braided copper, and even your teapot might have something to say.

category.en-US: REGIONS OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\EMBERFLOW SPRINGS (NORTHWESTERN REGION)

content.value: Elder Gubi-Goni leans back in his sun-warmed shell, steam curling from his teacup. His voice turns soft, as if speaking of something beloved and half-dreamed:
“Petalshade… mmh. You’ve heard of it then, have you? Or perhaps it heard of you. Places like that do, sometimes. They grow curious.”
He smiles, a slow curling thing, eyes half-lidded with memory.

“You’ll find Petalshade tucked in the heart-folds of the Blooming Gift—where the wind carries laughter like pollen and the earth drinks sunlight like nectar. Not far from the veil of cherry boughs they call the Sighing Rows. It is not a town, nor quite a village. No. Petalshade is a pause. A breath held between stories.”

“There, the trees lean inward like conspirators, petals forever drifting though no one sees them fall. The ground is soft with old moss and flower-dappled shadows, and the air hums—not with bugs, no, but with memory. With music that was played once and then buried lovingly in the dirt.”

“Long ago, the place was a grove for the Kemari dancers. Not performers, mind you. Rememberers. They moved like ink in wind, each step a syllable, each breath a name. The last of the Petalblades came from there, it’s said—those wandering storytellers who wield beauty and blade the same way: with grace, with purpose, with mourning.”

“Now? It’s mostly quiet. A shrine stands at the center, grown around a tree that never stops blooming. No one built it. It simply happened, like a song the land decided to hum aloud. Folk leave offerings there—woven ribbons, hand-folded poems, cups of dew, or sometimes just a bit of their own voice, breathed into the bark.”

“Every petal that falls in Petalshade holds a memory. That’s what the children say. And if you catch one before it touches ground, and hold it to your heart, you’ll remember something you forgot—something your spirit still holds, even if your mind does not.”
Gubi pauses, his eyes distant now, wet but not weeping.

“I once caught such a petal. It smelled like peach tea and old laughter. I held it close, and for a heartbeat, I was dancing again. Not shuffling about like I do now. But truly dancing. Spinning beneath starlit branches with fireflies caught in my breath. I was young. I was foolish. I was someone I hadn’t met in decades.”
“And so, if you go to Petalshade… tread gently. Speak softly. Leave something kind behind. And if the wind gives you a petal—hold it like a name you don’t want to lose.”

category.en-US: REGIONS OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\THE BLOOMING GIFT (WESTERN REGION)

content.value: The Mist-Hewn Steps lie along the outer spine of Mount Uokami, carved not by hands, but—so the old ones say—by breath, by the patient, ceaseless exhalation of the mountain itself. Each step is shaped from volcanic stone worn smooth by ages of fog, wind, and silent passage. You won’t find a handrail, no. Only moss, dew, and the sound of your heartbeat climbing beside you.

They rise through a thick, unbreaking mist that never lifts—never. Even on sun-bright days, the fog clings close, as if the mountain holds its secrets tight and lets only those with quiet intentions pass. You can’t see far ahead, and you’re not meant to. The Steps teach you to trust your footing, not your eyes.

Many who seek the high monasteries, or the hermits who speak only in gestures, must take the Mist-Hewn path. And though few talk about what they saw—or heard—on the way, all agree on this: the mist remembers. Footsteps leave no mark on stone, but echo for days in the folds of the fog. Some say the Steps whisper back, asking questions only your spirit can answer.
It’s a place of trial. Of shedding noise. Of stepping not just upward, but inward.
Even the Seikin tread lightly here. Even the Ryūkajin exhale more slowly.
So if you find yourself on the Mist-Hewn Steps, don’t rush. Don’t look behind. Just breathe—and let the mountain decide what comes next.

category.en-US: REGIONS OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\MOUNT UOKAMI (CENTRAL REGION)

content.value: Then hush your thoughts, little lantern.
Close your eyes—not to sleep, but to listen.
This is not a tale. It is a whisper.
This is what I know of the Elder Spirits,
as they walk now, and do not walk.
As they sing, and fall silent.
Still he burns, but not to scorch.
His fire lives in forges, in the chest of a blacksmith who hums to the anvil, in the breath between words when one lover confesses to another.
He is the laughter behind a bold idea. The exhale before a dive.
Dravanyr is the courage to begin.
“I do not grant power. I grant permission.”
— Inscription found on a scorched gourd in a ruined workshop
Some say he sleeps beneath Mount Uokami. Others say he walks with a limp, disguised as an old wanderer with a lantern full of song.
She has not vanished. She has multiplied.
Her joy echoes in every blush, every falling petal, every child who names a worm and insists it’s their sibling.
She walks the island barefoot, unseen, hand-in-hand with the wind.
“She kissed the moon once, and the tides haven’t recovered.”
Some say she planted herself in the Dreamskin and now blooms inside it. Others say she is the flower no one remembers planting.
She is neither here nor gone. She is everywhere balance is dared.
Where a storm breaks and a seed sprouts.
Where a death is wept and a birth is welcomed.
Where a sword is laid down and forgiveness offered.
“Even chaos knows it is only half a song.”
She does not speak. She teaches with wind, with rot, with frost and bloom and silence.
You will know him not by his form, but by what he demands:
He tests you not to judge—but to remind you who you are.
“He asked me if I feared death. I said yes. He smiled and fed me persimmons.”
— Kemari hunter, survivor of the Iro Manta trial
He may be a bear. He may be a beggar. He may be both.
He still cries. But now, sometimes, it is music.
His tears ink songs, sketch maps of healing, slip between words to form poems that heal old wounds.
“I met him once. He was a note I forgot to sing, humming behind my heartbeat.”
He is not gone. Just quieter.
She coils beneath the Loom, unweaving herself.
Her madness is not gone. But it is known now.
She no longer infects—she invites understanding.
“All wisdom bears scars. Hers are just deeper.”
She dreams less. She watches more.
Some say she is healing. Others say… she is preparing.
He laughs still. But not at us.
There is pain in that laugh. But also grace.
“He once tricked the sun into hiding. Now he walks with a lantern.”
Because he knows the cost of forgetting truth…
…and sometimes pays it willingly to protect us.
They were one—root and wing, desire and contentment.
A rabbit, who burrows to hide her envy.
A crow, who flies too high to see his own greed.
And yet… sometimes, just sometimes, they sit beneath the same tree and do not speak.
“When they agree again, the land will sing.”
Some plants bloom too fast. Some forests sleep too long.
Balance falters. But the spirits watch.
You may feel her when your grandmother stops breathing, and the wind doesn’t stir.
Or when a candle burns out without smoke.
Or when a child lays down, closes their eyes, and whispers, “I’m not afraid.”
“She is the hush before a new word.”
She waits at the edge of every Breath.
The Spirit Realm and Mortal Realm thinned, yes.
Each spirit, kinship, and calling now weaves in both.
That, little listener… is yours to whisper.

category.en-US: STORIES OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\“THE ISLAND THAT SINGS ITSELF”

content.value: Windroot Shrine rests where the breath of the island gathers, hidden deep within the Wandering Veil, nestled among elder trees whose roots tangle like old stories. It is a place of quiet reckoning, where pathfinders go to listen—not to speak. The wind there carries truths unspoken, and even the mist bows low.

They say Saeluin of the Sky-Bloom, a gleaming Ryūkajin of metal and mercy, once found a shattered spirit adrift in grief. She leapt from cliff to cliff beneath the storm-churned sky, cradling the spirit in her arms—not to bind it, but to carry its pain until it no longer had to. When they reached Windroot Shrine, the spirit had learned stillness. It became the whisper-owl, silver-feathered and dusk-eyed, that now watches the shrine’s threshold. Those who seek entry must first be seen by it… and accepted.
Even now, if you step quiet and breathe steady, you might hear its call:
Grief may root, and grow again—

THE ELDER SPIRITS\Queen Okumi and Her Cosmic Egg

content.value: Field Notes of Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III
Twilight Scriptorium, Coralveil – Volume IX: Phenomena of the Spirit-Bound Realms
Entry #144: The Spiral Blight — Notes on the Phenomenon Known as Corruption
Location: Hollow Step, under watch of wax-crowned lanterns

It is with both scholarly dread and necessary curiosity that I document herein the phenomenon known across Yurei-tu-Shima as Corruption. I refrain from placing the term in quotation marks, as the affliction—spiritual or otherwise—manifests with such consistency and specific consequence that to diminish its name would be disingenuous.

The term “Corruption” is, of course, a mortal word. Its essence is more fractured, more sorrowful than malign. It is not an invasion, as I once presumed, but an unraveling—a slow peeling away of coherence, empathy, and selfhood.

Though many among the Kojin claim it to be the breath of Shi-Naga, the Spiral Wound, I hesitate to ascribe so singular a source. That said, her influence is undeniable. Nearly every Corruption case I’ve studied bears her sigils—often in mirror-painted spirals, cracked masks, or ink-seeping wounds. Whether the spirit herself creates Corruption or simply reveals what was already unstable is the subject of ongoing debate among shrine-keepers and dream-archivists.
The phenomenon often arises in places where silence has grown too deep: abandoned shrines, forgotten roads, drowned tunnels, and even in the minds of those who meditate too long without grounding.
Corruption does not kill. It transforms. But never kindly. Those touched by it fracture along one of two paths:

Mania – An ecstatic, fevered unraveling. The affected become fire-eyed and fast-tongued. They speak of visions no one else can see. They find meaning in nonsense, prophecy in puddles, divine messages in the crack of bark or the wingbeat of a crow. They sing constantly. Some carve truths into their own skin or eat their own masks to ‘reveal’ what lies beneath. It is not rage. It is too much knowing—without anchor.

Dementia – A slow crumbling of the self. Names fade. Loved ones become strangers. Language thins to syllables and sketches. The world becomes a blur, each moment leaking into the next. They are gentle, these afflicted ones—painfully so. They clutch feathers, trace meaningless spirals in dust, and whisper to empty corners of the room. And yet, when they look at you, it is with a gaze full of unspeakable grief.
There is no recorded case of both states occurring in one individual. It is as if the Corruption chooses which truth to unmake: memory or meaning.

Those afflicted sometimes bleed ink from the corners of their eyes. Others speak in tongues not known to any scholar, but recognized by Hollow Step archivists as dream-languages. Some refuse food, claiming to be nourished by music or colors. In some regions, afflicted animals have been seen painting spirals into mud with their hooves or paws.

An entire Kyoshijin temple, long ago, was silenced by the Corruption. When explorers arrived, they found murals painted with bones and ash—depictions of events that never occurred, but which left an emotional imprint strong enough to induce weeping in all who viewed them.
The Oni-Touched embrace it as a form of awakening. Their Maskbearers record the ravings of the corrupted, believing they are singing truths hidden by the Loom.
Kemari bone-readers attempt to draw out the affliction with herbal smoke, sleep-binding songs, or sand-circle isolations.
Tenkara Bellwalkers keep corrupted kin near temple chimes, believing the resonance holds the fragments of mind in place.
Mokugijin are sometimes more stable under the influence—an enigma I am still unraveling.

I’ve documented a ritual known as the Seven Sighs Vigil, where one confesses seven names—seven selves left behind—before sleeping with a spiral mask over the heart. If the person wakes unchanged, it is said they were not truly fracturing. If they do not wake… they have become part of the dreaming.
I do not believe Corruption is a disease. It is a question. A haunting one. A soft spiral drawn on the soul, asking: What if everything you’ve known was simply the version you could bear to remember?
I will continue my studies—though, of late, I’ve begun waking with ink on my fingertips.
I have not written in my sleep before.

title.en-US: On Breathkeepers: An Interview with the Professor

content.value: Field Notes of Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III
Twilight Scriptorium, Coralveil – Volume VII: Dialogues with the Spirit-Faithful
Conducted beside the Spiritforge Hearth, Emberflow Springs
Interview Subject: Maekoro Embermouth, Fire Kaido, Forge-Ward of Emberflow, and Breathkeeper of Dravanyr
Atmosphere: Thick with mineral steam; soft rhythmic clanging in the background.

I was told to meet him by the forge that sings. Not the one that hammers, mind you—there are dozens of those—but the one whose flame hums as it breathes, drawing air in a rhythm so measured it feels like lungs remembering. And there, crouched by a bed of coal and quartz, I found Maekoro Embermouth.

His skin glowed beneath the soot—lava-dark with pulsing veins of emberlight that flickered with his mood, or perhaps his breath. He wore no shoes, only a flame-wrapped sarong and a mantle of braided wire and fireglass. His hair was a coil of smoke-braids bound by pins etched with curling script. He grinned like the forge itself was telling him jokes.
Professor Widdersnap: “Master Embermouth, it’s an honor to sit with a Breathkeeper. I hope I’ve come at a good time?”
Maekoro: “You came during exhale. That means we speak.”
Professor: “And when do we not speak?”
Maekoro: “When the air asks us not to.”
Professor (chuckling): “Forgive me, I’ll try not to chatter too much. Tell me—what does it mean to be a Breathkeeper of Dravanyr?”

Maekoro: “It means we remember that fire breathes. That creation is not a thunderclap, but a rhythm. Dravanyr does not demand we burn. He asks only that we breathe with purpose, and when the time is right—ignite.”
Professor: “Do all of his followers call themselves Breathkeepers?”
Maekoro: “Most. Some say Flamecallers, Emberbinders, Hearth-Watch. But ‘Breathkeeper’ is the oldest, I think. We are the ones who tend the fire in others, not just ourselves.”
Professor: “And how do you dress for such a calling?”

Maekoro: “With layers, like heat itself. We wear forge-wraps of soot-silk and redstone cloth—durable, fire-loving. Always loose near the chest and throat, to honor breath. Our belts are coiled copper, symbol of the spiral wind, and we bind our wrists with ash-cording soaked in the smoke of sacred wood.”
Professor: “And are masks part of your rituals?”
Maekoro (removing a small lacquered object from a leather wrap):

“Yes. This is the Kindling Mask. Worn in rites of awakening or transformation. It’s split in color—one half coal-black, the other fireglow orange—with a jagged breath-mark down the center. The mouth is open. Always. To let the breath out. We never close it.”
Maekoro: “Every Breathkeeper makes their own. Mine is the Spiral Bellows—see?”
(He unstrapped a curved metal device from his hip, carved with breath-marks and shaped like a coiled dragon.)
“It channels breath into embers, but not just for fire. We use it to warm the bodies of the dying. To coax song from wind-horns. Even to lull colicky children.”
Professor: “You said Breathkeepers tend fire in others. What are your rituals like?”
“There are many. Some loud. Some silent. But the core of it is always breath.
The Fourfold Flame – We breathe in time with the flame: Inhale, Hold, Exhale, Rest. Four parts. Each prayer, each chant, is shaped by that rhythm.

Ash Rites – We scatter ashes of old works—failed crafts, lost hopes—across a sacred bowl and breathe across it as a group, transforming grief into renewal. This is called Kaga-no-Tameru, ‘the holding of sorrow’s heat.’
The Sparkwalk – Performed during solstice nights. Breathkeepers walk barefoot over a path of glowing stones, each whispering a vow with every step. It is not pain we seek—but presence.
Whisperforge – A silent ritual performed by master Breathkeepers to infuse crafted items with a final blessing. No speech is allowed—only breath, touch, and intention.”
Professor: “What does Dravanyr feel like, when he is near?”
“The back of your neck, warming before a storm.
A single flame refusing to go out in the rain.
He offered me a small emberstone as I departed. “For your voice,” he said. “In case it needs reminding.”
The forge sang again behind me—inhale, exhale, inhale—and I found myself walking slower. Breathing deeper. Saying nothing.
Sometimes the flame does not need to roar. Sometimes it just needs to breathe.

title.en-US: On Balance-Keepers: An Interview with the Professor

content.value: Field Notes of Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III
Twilight Scriptorium, Coralveil – Volume VII: Dialogues with the Spirit-Faithful
Conducted in the inner courtyard of Petal-Flow Shrine, Blooming Gift.
Interview Subject: Toma-Han, Elder Kojin, Keeper of Petal-Flow Shrine and Balancekeeper of Kokoro-no-Kami
Weather: Intermittent sunshowers; tea steam mingled with petals midair.

The path to the shrine was a slow one—though not by length. It slowed the body on purpose. Winding gravel, soft wind chimes, no sharp corners, no quick steps. I arrived feeling a little lighter, and somewhat ashamed of how quickly I usually walk.

Toma-Han met me not at a gate, but under a tree, where a thin curtain of wind had caught cherry petals in mid-fall. He was small in frame, like most Kojin, but carried himself like a hanging scroll—measured, precise, balanced. His face was lined, whiskers fine, and eyes very round and calm. When I bowed, he bowed lower.
Professor Widdersnap: “Master Toma-Han, I’m honored. I’ve heard the Petal-Flow Shrine is one of the quietest places on the island.”
Toma-Han (bowing): “Then we are already speaking its language, Professor.”
Professor: “Let us begin with what drew me here—your faith. You serve Kokoro-no-Kami?”
Toma-Han: “I listen to the flow. That is how we say it. But yes… I am a Balancekeeper.”
Professor: “Is that the formal name for her followers?”

Toma-Han (tilting his head): “There is no formal name. That is the formality. But Balancekeeper, Flow-Tender, Thread-Watcher—any of these may be spoken. We are not a fixed circle. Some tend gardens. Some hold shrines. Some… simply pause.”
Professor: “And what does Kokoro-no-Kami mean to you?”

Toma-Han: “She is not the stillness, nor the motion—but the way they meet. The tide, the inhale, the unspoken truth between argument and apology. She does not demand worship. She waits to be recognized—like breath, or thirst.”
Professor: “Do you wear specific garb when tending the shrine or performing rites?”

Toma-Han: “Our attire flows. That is the only requirement. Wraps of pale silk or layered gauze, tied without knots. Colors change with the season—ochre in fall, blossom-pink in spring, soft water-grey in summer. Nothing stiff. Nothing harsh. The body must feel unobstructed. Even our belts are loose spirals—Yunobi sashes, we call them.”

Toma-Han (gently unrolling a cloth bundle): “We wear the Mask of Gentle Return during deep rites. Rice paper layered in spirals, pale as steam, with a line across the eyes—not a frown, not a smile. Just… a balance. When the mask is worn, we are neither self nor other—we are moment.”
Professor: “Are there symbolic objects carried by Balancekeepers?”

Toma-Han: “Each Keeper carries a Thread of Breath—a cord spun from hair and reed, soaked in night dew and dried beside still water. We burn it during rituals of letting go. We also carry Palm Stones, smooth and warm from body heat, which we touch to center breath before speaking.”
Professor: “Would you tell me of your rituals?”
“We do not gather in loud ceremony. Our rites are quiet, shared, sometimes only between breath and being. But there are forms:
The Flow Chant – a single sound, sustained together, until it becomes indistinguishable between voices. We begin each gathering this way, no matter the purpose.
Mirror-Ink Ritual – we paint with reflective ink on water-flat stone, letting the ripples distort the image. This is how we divine whether a decision aligns with the greater flow.
Thread Severing – performed when one must let go of sorrow, hatred, obsession. A thread is tied between two reeds and cut with a blade of bone and moonlight. Not with anger, but with gratitude.
The Spiral Walk – taken during major life passages: birth, coming of age, parting, death. A spiral of leaves is laid, and the Keeper walks it inward in silence… then outward in song.”
Professor: “Beautiful. And… how does one know Kokoro-no-Kami is present?”
Toma-Han (placing a single petal in his tea):
“When the wind changes just before you speak.
When a cat and a crow share the same roof.
When the answer arrives before the question.
I did not press him further. Some truths are not meant to be pulled like rope. They must unfold.
Toma-Han walked me back only halfway down the shrine’s path. I realized later—it was the same distance I had walked up.

title.en-US: On Followers of Ganroku: An Interview with the Professor

content.value: Field Notes of Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III
Twilight Scriptorium, Coralveil – Volume VII: Dialogues with the Spirit-Faithful
Conducted beneath the Deepfire Kiln, Emberflow Springs
Interview Subject: Molga Deepforge, Daru Stonewright, Soul-Smith of Deepfire, Breath-Silent of Ganroku

Transcript excerpted, cleaned, and annotated for clarity. Conducted over three hours beside the Deepfire coals. Molga requested no ink be scratched until after her words cooled. I obliged, though my fingers itched.
Professor Widdersnap: Mistress Deepforge, thank you for agreeing to this interview. May I ask plainly—what does it mean to follow Ganroku?
Molga: First, stop tryin’ to follow. You don’t follow rock. You sit with it. You wait. You listen. If it shifts, maybe you shift too. That’s Ganroku. Not a path. A pressure.
Professor: And those who sit with him as you do—do they bear a name? A title, perhaps?

Molga: [snorts] Fancy names crack faster than greenstone in frost. But… some call us Breath-Silent. Some call us Stone-Binders. We don’t much mind. We know who we are. You’ll find us where silence hums deep, or where weight tells truth.
Professor: And how do you mark yourselves, if not by name?

Molga: By what we build. Or don’t. Some wear soot marks in square spirals on the brow when they craft for spirit. Others tie shards of cooled slag around the wrist—tokens from old forges. When we speak rites, we wear aprons cut from shale, carved with no symbols. Blank. That’s the point.
Molga: To not pretend we know more than stone. He ain’t a spirit you paint pictures of. He’s the silence that answers when the clamor’s done.
Professor: I’ve heard of several rites—may I ask for their meanings?

Molga: You may, though don’t expect hymnals. Our oldest rite is the Stone Sitting—a vigil, silent, unmoving, usually in a place of unfinished work. No food. No talk. Just you, time, and what’s under you. You stay until your thoughts stop arguing.
Then there’s the Echo Forge—you craft something not for yourself, not for trade, but for the hands that come after. You won’t see it used. You won’t sign your name. That’s the test.

And the third is the Dust of Ancestors. We mix powder from old stone—walls fallen, tools cracked—with ashes of kin or craftmasters, and blend it into a new creation. That’s how we bind legacy. Not with statues. With use.
Professor: You mentioned Ganroku does not walk like other spirits. What, then, is his form?

Molga: I’ve never seen him. Never want to. But I’ve felt him. In the weight of a stair carved too well. In the hush between hammer strikes. Some say he’s the mountain beneath all mountains. Others say he was born the day the first boulder refused to roll downhill. Me? I once carved into seamless granite and heard a heartbeat. You tell me what that means.
Professor: And shrines? Do you build places to honor him?

Molga: Not shrines. Places that last. A bridge still strong after the quake. A kiln that holds heat like memory. Some set cairns, yes, or build hearths with deep-banked coals that don’t go out, not for years. But we don’t build to be seen. We build so others don’t fall.
Professor: You are a Soul-Smith—does that differ from a traditional Daru craftmaster?

Molga: Soul-Smiths listen for what the stone or metal wants to be. Not what we want. That’s the trick. Not force. Resonance. Every element’s got a song buried deep—Ganroku just teaches us how to hear it.
Professor: Have there ever been masks in his honor?
Molga: Rare. But when worn, they’re plain. Stone grey. No mouth. Some wear them when sealing tombs or finalizing great works. Not to show off. To disappear—so the work speaks louder than the face.
Professor: One last question. What would you say to someone newly drawn to Ganroku?
Molga: Sit down. Breathe once. Feel your own weight. If it makes you restless, you’re not ready. If it makes you still, then maybe… maybe you’ve heard him too.
Molga did not shake my hand when we parted. She handed me a stone button she’d shaped during our talk. It bore no markings. I keep it in my journal now. It weighs more than it should.

title.en-US: On Bonewardens: An Interview with the Professor

content.value: Field Notes of Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III
Twilight Scriptorium, Coralveil – Volume VII: Dialogues with the Spirit-Faithful
Entry #73: The Bone-Wardens of Onikumi Khan
Conducted at dusk beside the Ash-Shrine of Iro Manta Grove
Interview Subject: Yuzo Deeppaw, Kyoshijin, Bone-Warden of the Iro Manta Grove, and Silent Walker of Onikumi Khan

Interview conducted with incense smoke winding low and thin. Windless. We sat cross-legged beneath the hanging bell-chimes. He declined tea but offered a bowl of warmed bone broth “for presence.” His eyes never left the tree line.
Professor Widdersnap: Thank you, Bone-Warden Deeppaw, for allowing me to speak with you. May I begin by asking—what do your people call yourselves? Those who walk in the silence of Onikumi Khan?

Yuzo Deeppaw: [long pause] Names are for those who wish to be remembered. But since you ask, and since the spirits have not stopped your pen, we are called the Bone-Wardens. Or the Iro-Manta, though that is not a title—it is a place, a rite, and a promise. We do not speak that name lightly.
Professor: And your calling? Your beliefs?

Yuzo: Onikumi Khan is not a god of war. He is not a hunter. He is not a death-keeper. He is the moment before. The weight in the gut before the sword leaves the sheath. The hush before the dying take their final breath. We are those who stand in that hush. Not to decide, but to witness. To wait. To listen.
Yuzo: Then it is never with doubt.
Professor: Do Bone-Wardens carry marks or sacred attire?
Yuzo: We wear masks carved in black and white—bear skulls split down the middle. White for restraint. Black for knowing death may be necessary. The split reminds us we never hold full certainty.

Our robes are bone-gray and ash-wrapped. We do not often wear armor, unless to protect the line for others who are still not attentive. We walk unarmed unless burial is threatened or the dead are restless. Around our waists are lengths of sinew cord—one knot for every soul safely guided to rest.
Professor: And what tools do you carry?
Yuzo: [reaches into his satchel] This is a bell-string, sinew wound through deer bone. We strike it gently during rites. No voice should rise above its chime. No drum. No chant. Just sound and smoke.

Also: smoke bowls, carved from hollowed bone or volcanic stone. We burn funeral dust—a blend of flame ash, river moss, and crushed bone fragments. The smoke carries memory. It invites Onikumi to observe, not to claim.
Professor: And what rituals do you perform in his name?
Yuzo: There are three that matter.

The first is the Iro Manta, the silent funeral rite. We sit beside the body for one full dusk. No words. No fire, only coals. When the chimes strike of their own accord—we act. If they do not, we wait another night.

The second is Walking Backward, performed after a death narrowly avoided. The survivor walks twelve steps in reverse, leaving no tracks ahead. This shows Onikumi Khan that they accept the cost of mercy.

The last is the Final Burden. Rare. A body is raised—not truly reanimated, but given one last purpose. To carry the wounded. To protect a shrine. To bury another. Then we burn it fully, with prayer and silence. No one may speak its name.
Professor: Do you believe he judges those who raise the dead?

Yuzo: I believe he judges why. Raise the dead for glory, and he turns his face. Raise them with reverence, to spare suffering, and he watches… not in wrath, but to see if you know the weight of what you’ve done.
Professor: And how does he appear?

Yuzo: Sometimes as a great bear, pale and scarred, with breath like mist. Sometimes as a traveler, cloaked, eyes like river stones in winter. But mostly—he appears in the pause. In a dream that ends before the knife is thrown. In the moment a mother chooses not to strike the snake that startles her child.

Yuzo: Rare. We mark thresholds, not altars. A doorframe with three claw lines. A cairn of silent bones arranged beneath trees that do not creak. A lantern that burns with no wick. These are Signs—not for worship, but for warning. Places where choices balance. Where he may be watching.
Professor: If someone wished to walk your path… what would they do?

Yuzo: Bury the forgotten. Speak the name of someone who has none. Wait in a glade where no birds sing and ask: “What silence waits here?” If no answer comes, return again. And again. Until the silence answers you.
Professor: One last thing. Why do you walk this path?

Yuzo: Because silence saved me once. Because rage would have burned a village. Because I heard a bell chime where no wind stirred. And because one day, I will need someone to bury me—and I would like them to do so gently.
Yuzo gave me a single chime from his string, bound in twine. “For your pen,” he said, “to remember which words were not yours to write.” I have not used ink since the interview, only charcoal.

title.en-US: On Gravewardens: An Interview with the Professor

content.value: Field Notes of Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III
Twilight Scriptorium, Coralveil – Volume VII: Dialogues with the Spirit-Faithful
Conducted beneath the Lantern Cedars of Hollow Murkway
Interview Subject: Tamiko the Quiet Root, Kurokara Gravewarden of Namakusa, caretaker of Stillwalk Grove, and tender of the Threshold Silence.
There are places where even breath feels too loud.

The Hollow Murkway is one such place—draped in fog so thick, even memory seems to drift. I had been advised to come alone, without flame or ink that glistened. “She listens to the dark,” said the note, “and will not meet you if you glimmer.”

So I followed the moss-laced steps into the grove, where the roots bowed like watchers and wind never stirred. There, beneath the lantern cedars whose bulbs held not flame but softly pulsing spores, I saw her.

Tamiko the Quiet Root. Cloaked in midnight-gray robes that rustled like drying petals. Her face was obscured beneath a woven veil of char-black reed, with only two obsidian beads marking her eyes. Her skin was duskstone grey, faintly dappled with shifting patterns—like shadow through leaves. A true Kurokara, she moved not as one cloaked in mystery, but as one shaped by it.
We sat in the moss together, and only after the grove had acknowledged our silence did she speak.
“You have come,” she said, voice dry and delicate as winter bark, “not to ask what death is. But *how we stay beside it without being taken.”
The following is transcribed faithfully, and with reverence.
Professor Widdersnap: Gravewarden Tamiko… I’ve met many who revere death, but few who walk beside it so closely. Could you tell me… who is Namakusa to you?

Tamiko: She is not the end. She is the layer of silk between breath and none. The hush between heartbeats. The cool stone pressed to a fevered brow. Namakusa is not sorrow. She is the moment when sorrow has nowhere left to go, so it becomes still.
Professor Widdersnap: And your title—Gravewarden. What does it mean among her faithful?
Tamiko: We are Stillhands. Not mourners. Not priests. We keep the hush sacred. When a soul lingers, we listen. When a body rests, we keep it from being stolen. We wear no rank. Only silence.
Professor Widdersnap: Do the Stillhands perform particular rites or ceremonies?
The Lantern Rooting, when we bury a soft-glow fungus beside the deceased, letting it feed and glow for one lunar cycle. When it dims, the mourning ends.
The Threshold Silence, held on the seventh night. No tools, no voices. Just the living, breathing… waiting. If something moves in the mist, we bow to it. If it speaks, we do not answer.
The Veil-Weaving, where scraps of burial cloth are twisted into veils, worn only once during the Deep Remembrance Moon. We burn them after. The ash is pressed into grave markers made of hollow bone.
Professor Widdersnap: Your appearance—robes, masks, the silence of your tools… does it carry symbolism?
Attire: Always quiet—root-dyed robes, soft-woven from bark thread and grave moss. No metal. No reflection.
Mask or Veil: For some, carved driftwood. For Kurokara, we wear the Fogface—woven black reed, stitched with bone thread, showing only the soul through the dark.
Tools: A clapperless bell. A hollow-spade carved from whale bone. A Memory Bead—one for each soul returned to rest. We string them in secret. Never count them aloud.
Professor Widdersnap: Would you call yourselves worshipers?
Tamiko: No. We do not beg her favor. We do not praise her power. We hold her breath—the breath between. We walk behind sorrow so it does not get lost.
Professor Widdersnap: If someone encountered Namakusa… how might they know?

Tamiko: Their shadow would disappear. Their heartbeat would sound like wind through a flute. And when they blinked, they would see someone they had lost… not truly there… but remembered exactly as they were.

When she rose to leave, the moss beneath her feet did not stir. Even her footfalls seemed to land in places already hollowed. And before she vanished into the mist of Stillwalk Grove, she turned once more.
“Do not speak too loudly when you record this,” she whispered. “Not all silence wants to be broken.”

title.en-US: On the Joybound: An Interview with the Professor

content.value: Field Notes of Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III
Twilight Scriptorium, Coralveil – Volume VII: Dialogues with the Spirit-Faithful
Entry #75: The Joybound of Queen Okumi
Conducted during the Bloom-Singing Festival in Moss Rock Commons
Interview Subject: Pipikka Greenglance, Kemari, Mask-Keeper and Petal-Seamstress of Queen Okumi’s Joy-Circle

The Bloom-Singing was already in full sway when I found her—Pipikka Greenglance, her laughter trailing ribbons of wind, seated atop an overturned rain barrel half-covered in vines. Mask fragments and petal-thread spilled from a woven basket at her side. She wore a cloak stitched from wildflower cloth, mismatched but radiant, and a mask sat pushed back atop her curly ears: a white-barked hare with a lopsided grin.
We spoke between lantern songs and bursts of flower-powder. I began, as always, with gentle curiosity.
Miss Greenglance, I must say, your people celebrate joy with an energy most… relentless. What is your calling, precisely, in Queen Okumi’s name?

I keep the stories that laugh back. We Joybound don’t carry grim ledgers or stone tablets—we carry moments. I’m a Mask-Keeper, one of those who tend the stories we wear on our faces. Each mask holds a joke, a kindness, a memory you needed to borrow until it became your own. Queen Okumi doesn’t ask for worship. She asks for joy given freely.
And these masks—are they all worn during ritual?

Most are, but not just during. We wear them through. Through grief. Through first kisses. Through the long afternoon when you’ve nothing but soup and thunder. Some masks are shy. Some prank you when you’re not looking. We repaint them as feelings change. The ritual is in living with them.
And beyond the masks, what attire do Joybound wear? These robes—are they ceremonial?

Ha! Ceremony’s just joy with rhythm. Yes, we dye our robes with joy-dyes—pressed flowers, pollen dust, even laughter steeped into water. This one here’s dandelion and old sunset. We weave with vine-thread or cloudsilk when we’re lucky. And on festival days, we add blossom flurries or glitterfruit juice for extra shimmer.
Joywood sandals, carved from trees that only bloom when someone laughs beneath them. They creak like giggles and never wear out unless you stop dancing.
Delightful. And what of sacred items? Are there tools of the Joybound that hold particular meaning?

Oh yes. There’s the Thread of Newness—bright red silk we use to patch things, but always make them better, not just fixed. Then there’s petal tokens, little pressed blossoms we carry to give away. And Bloom Bells—tiny charms we wear on ankles or wrists. They only ring if you move with kindness.
Exquisite symbolism. And how is Queen Okumi herself perceived by her followers? Does she have a form?

She changes like laughter. Some see her as a girl dancing through grass with frogs in her pockets. Others as a giant with a garden crown who hums to sunflowers. I once saw her in the way a grieving mother smiled again for the first time. Okumi is not a shape. She’s what it feels like to come alive again.
Yes. Renewal through joy. And your title—Joybound. Is that what all her followers are called?

Most, yes. Some are Mask-Keepers like me. Some are Bloomwrights, who shape petals into food or gowns. Others are Chorus-Holders or Jest-Walkers. But we’re all Joybound. Bound not by duty—but by the way joy binds hearts together, soft and strong.
And rituals? Beyond the current festival, what ceremonies anchor your cycle?

There’s the First Bloom Waltz—danced barefoot on spring’s first petal rain. The Jubilation Veil, where we pass a laughing mask from face to face ‘til even the grumpiest soul chuckles. And the Cradle Chorus—soft, wordless songs sung at dusk to cradle the day’s spirit into peace. But truly, everything is ritual, if done with joy.
Your reverence is playful, but no less profound than the most solemn rites I’ve recorded. One last question, Pipikka—what does it mean to follow Queen Okumi?

It means choosing joy. Not ignoring sorrow, but meeting it with gentleness. It means being brave enough to look silly, and soft enough to help someone else shine. Okumi doesn’t want temples. She wants blooming hearts. You’re honoring her right now, just by smiling while you scribble.

title.en-US: On Dreamweavers: An Interview with the Professor

content.value: Field Notes of Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III
Twilight Scriptorium, Coralveil – Volume VII: Dialogues with the Spirit-Faithful
Entry #73: The Moonward Faithful of Hoshira
Conducted beneath the canopy of Blue Tree Hollow, Wandering Veil
Interview Subject: Shaelith Ves’hariel, Astral Elf, Dream-Weaver of the Moonfold, and Veil-Sister of Hoshira

I found Shaelith at the edge of a crescent pool where the wind barely touched the water’s skin. The trees around Blue Tree Hollow seemed to hush themselves as I approached. She stood in quiet reverie, trailing her fingers through threads of moonlight strung between branches like spider silk.
She greeted me without turning. “The moon has already answered the question. But if you wish to speak it aloud, I’ll listen.”
What follows is a transcription—lightly condensed—of our twilight conversation, lit only by bioluminescent moss and a very polite glowbug who sat on my inkpot the entire time.
Professor Widdersnap: Shaelith, I thank you for this audience. I understand you are one of the Moonward Faithful?
Shaelith: That is one name. We do not use only one. Some call us Veil-Sisters. Others—Sleephands, Night-Weavers, Lantern-Bearers of Quiet. But yes… we follow the rhythm of Hoshira.
Shaelith: Not a beat. A sway. A breath between stars. We believe the night does not fall—it arrives. Like a mother, smoothing the fevered brow of the day.
Professor: Beautifully said. And how do you honor her? What rites or rituals are observed?

Shaelith: All our rites begin with stillness. The most sacred is called The Gentle Curtain. It is performed as dusk fades, where we lay silks across the threshold of a home or glade, whispering the old lullabies as we light the moon-mirrors—bowls of water ringed with glow-fruit oil. It invites restful sleep… or peaceful passage, if death is near.

There is also Starguarding, when we lie beside the dying, guiding their dreams so they do not fear the dark. We anoint their temples with twilight balm made from crushed comet-fruit and mistleaf. No words. Only song.
Shaelith: As breath is to life. We carry songs like others carry lanterns. Hoshira’s hymn is different to each of us—but it always ends in silence.
Professor: And your attire? Do the Moonward wear specific garments?

Shaelith: Pale blues, silvers, and violets—woven from moonmoss and dream-silk. We do not wear heavy robes, lest we disturb the air around those trying to rest. We sew memory-strands—silver cords into our hems, each one a night watched over. The more strands, the more nights we’ve held vigil.
Professor: Do you wear masks, as many spirit-faithful do?

Shaelith: Only one. We call it the Dreamface. Smooth, porcelain, no mouth, only eyes closed in gentle repose. We wear it only when performing the Rite of Surrender, when guiding a soul fully into the Spirit Realm. It is not for the living to see us weep.

Shaelith: We carry thread-rings, looped bands that hold thin threads of moonlight between two willow wands. They resonate with dreams and are used to catch night-wisps—restless thoughts, you’d call them. We also keep veilstones, small opals charged by starlight, used to mark sacred resting grounds.
Professor: And what does Hoshira ask of you?
She offers rest—but never demands it. We choose when to listen.
Shaelith: Because some things—peace, rest, forgiveness—are so easily lost in the noise of waking. Someone must remember them. Someone must offer hush when the world cries too loud.
We do not convert. We do not shout. We wait for those who are tired… and then we offer our hand.
Professor: One final question. How will I know if Hoshira is near?
Shaelith: You’ll sigh, without meaning to. And for a moment… you’ll remember a dream you never had—but wish you did.
I did sigh. And as I left the Hollow, I could not recall if the glowbug had flown away or faded.

title.en-US: On Bellwalkers: An Interview with the Professor

content.value: Field Notes of Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III
Twilight Scriptorium, Coralveil – Volume VII: Dialogues with the Spirit-Faithful
Conducted at the Stillmirror Pavilion, on the threshold between the Wandering Veil and the Hollow Murkway
Interview Subject: Tsuneo Keshin, Tenkara Bellwalker, Keeper of Threshold Rites, Devotee of Morrowel

The pavilion had no walls—only veils of pale fabric swaying like breath caught between questions. We sat together at dawn’s edge, where the sky had not yet decided its hue. Tsuneo Keshin, robed in ash-grey, his long fingers calloused from carrying silence, sat barefoot beside a basin of still water. Across from him, I removed my boots—his only request—and stepped fully into the space of between.
Professor Widdersnap: You are a Bellwalker, yes? One who follows Morrowel, the Spirit of Thresholds?
He dipped a finger into the water. Ripples laced outward, barely audible.
Professor Widdersnap: That’s quite poetic. Forgive me, but I must ask plainly for the record: what is it that you and your fellow Bellwalkers do?
The moment a name is spoken, or forgotten.
We walk with those about to cross—whatever it is they are crossing.
He lifted a bell carved of bone and driftwood, bound with faded blue ribbons.
Each Bellwalker carries a Tōkyo Kane—a passage bell. Not to ring at someone, but with them. The resonance helps a soul or moment find its way forward.
Professor Widdersnap: So you ring it only at moments of crossing?
When a child is born and has not cried yet.
When a house is abandoned, but still remembers a voice.
When the dying fear they’ve left something undone.
We do not judge the crossing. We only make sure it is felt.
Professor Widdersnap: And your garments—there’s a clarity to them.
We wear pale robes—grey before dawn, white before dusk. We must never be brighter than the moment.
The thread along the hem is always unfinished. Our lives, too, are passages.
Our masks—if worn—are mirror-smooth, without features. When placed upon the face, the wearer becomes the Witness, and nothing more. It is not our role to comfort. It is our role to be present.
Professor Widdersnap: What rituals do you perform for Morrowel?
There is the Step-Silence—a walk made in the shape of the infinity loop, barefoot, during the twilight hour. Each step is a breath. Each breath, a doorway.
There is The Naming of Absence, where we speak aloud the things that were never said to someone who is no longer there.
And The Tethercut Rite, used when one must release grief, guilt, or memory. A thread is tied to the wrist and then severed over a threshold—real or symbolic.
Professor Widdersnap: It sounds like a faith built not on doctrine, but awareness.
We light lanterns that do not burn.
And we wait beside those who must make choices.
She offers the doorway, and waits to see which foot you lift first.
A child cannot be almost born.
A soul cannot be half grieved.
He turned the mirror-bell once in his hand, and a reflection passed briefly through it—mine, I believe, though it did not blink when I did.
When we parted, Tsuneo gave me no farewell. He simply turned and walked between two standing stones, vanishing into the mist. The bell did not ring. I do not think it needed to.

content.value: Field Notes of Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III
Twilight Scriptorium, Coralveil – Volume VII: Dialogues with the Spirit-Faithful
Supplemental Entry #77b: On the Phenomenon Known as the Ink
Filed under: Noroku, the Clock That Weeps
I did not believe in the Ink when I first read about it.

There. I’ve said it. As a gnome of parchment and fact, of ledgers and proofs, I assumed the “Ink” was a metaphor—poetic melancholy passed down through oral tradition, perhaps a symbolic gesture by the mournful faithful of Noroku.

The first sign was during my initial vigil at the Driftvault—a subterranean alcove carved by tide and time, where Noroku’s adherents record the days that never happened. There was no chant, no ceremony, no incantation. Just silence… and then stillness that thickened.
Not metaphor. Not grief in abstract.
Thick as oil, dark as nightfall in a sealed archive. It did not flow in with the tide. It appeared where sorrow sharpened, where longing took root in those seated at the edges of memory.

It coiled at the base of one follower’s feet—a quiet gnome named Calliver, who had just written of the child he never had, and the daughter he’d never name. The Ink welled silently beneath him, not from his pen, but from the air itself. It did not spread. It sank. Into the cracks of stone. Into the pores of breath. Into me.
Consistency: The Ink is thicker than water, slower than oil. It clings to surfaces and resists light, yet has no weight when touched.
Sensation: Exposure induces memory dissonance. You begin to hear voices that never spoke. Smell lilacs you never picked. Recall laughter that never occurred.
Effect on materials: Paper exposed to the Ink remains intact but darkens around the edges—no rot, only shadowing. Glass fogs. Metal grows cold.

Effect on living beings: Prolonged exposure results in emotional detachment, slowed speech, difficulty distinguishing memory from imagination. One practitioner described it as “grief made gentle enough to live with.”
It is not malevolent. That must be stated clearly. The Ink does not stalk. It does not seek. It responds.
To loss unspoken. To dreams deferred. To the ache that becomes quiet when one can no longer carry it loudly.
Some of Noroku’s followers use it. They mix it with wax to seal tide candles. Others inscribe unwritten histories with Ink upon stone that no one reads—except perhaps Noroku himself. And a few…
A few wear it on their fingertips like paint.

I have since acquired a sealed vial of the substance, preserved in a bone-wrapped case, marked with Noroku’s spiral shell. I keep it beneath my cot. Some nights I hear it shift, despite the seal. I once dreamed of my father reading me a story we never finished. When I awoke, the vial had grown warm.

The Ink is not just Noroku’s sorrow. It is the residue of unrealized potential, coalesced in places where grief is both deep and quiet. It is history’s unspooled thread. It is what remains when possibility forgets to bloom.
I no longer doubt its presence.
I fear, instead, how often we invite it.
Filed and wax-sealed beneath eclipse hour, with three unlit candles present.

title.en-US: Field Notes: On the Crawling Canopy

content.value: Field Notes of Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III
Twilight Scriptorium, Coralveil – Volume VII: Dialogues with the Spirit-Faithful
Recorded under a bone-lantern sky, edge of the Eastern Murkway
There are forests that sleep, and forests that dream.

I set my tent just shy of the marked perimeter—old thorn sigils pressed into stone and looped with dried ash-feathers. Oruun Hollowbrow, Cairn-Tender of the region, warned me not to set camp inside. Not even by a step. “The trees forget where they were,” he muttered, stuffing black salt into his pipe. “And they don’t much care where you were, either.”

From observation over three nights, I confirm: the forest is animate—not in the sense of walking trees or overtly mobile root systems, but in a subtler, more insidious manner. Paths reroute. Branches coil into barred shapes when not under direct gaze. Moss grows counter to sunlight, sometimes even up. I attempted to place a clock and compass inside a hollow; by morning, both had melted, their faces replaced with tightly braided thorns.

One particularly curious sample—a spore-puff I collected from a fallen vine—seems to hum faintly when submerged in ink. I have not yet determined if this is a chemical response, or an echo of Malgrotha’s influence. (Note: do not inhale the vapors. Experienced a vivid dream in which I was a cage, not inside one.)

The spiritual origin of the Crawling Canopy appears tied inextricably to the sorrowed spirit Malgrotha. As recounted in Oruun’s gravel-thick whispers, Malgrotha was once a dual-being: part healer, part seer. Now he is a wound with wings. The forest, it seems, is both his prison and his extension—growing according to his sorrow, shifting according to his rage.
Common symptoms reported by those who stray too far inside:
Dream entanglement. Victims wake mid-sentence in languages they do not speak.
Spatial haunt. They return home but find their rooms have moved or been replaced with “cages.”
Sympathetic vegetation. Vines mimic the shape of their ribs, or creep into mouths during sleep.
Echoed rage. They scream when others do. Or laugh before a sound has been made.

There is a legend passed among the Kojin and the earth-walkers of the southern Kaido: that if the Crawling Canopy ever stops moving, the island itself will suffocate beneath it. I do not know if this is poetic hyperbole or spiritual calculus—but I do not wish to test it.

Final note: despite the danger, there is beauty in the Canopy. Not the gentle sort—no moonflowers or dew-glass spiders—but a gnarled, fierce beauty. Roots that spiral like thoughts gone feral. Bark that pulses faintly in the rain. A kind of living grief, wrapped in vines, waiting to be understood.
I plan to return next month with a waxed mask, a mirrored lantern, and a question I do not yet know how to ask.

title.en-US: Field Notes: On the Lying Mirrors

content.value: Professor Thistlewhip Widdersnap III’s Field Notes: The Lying Mirrors of Oghmai
Compiled beneath triple seal in the Coralveil Twilight Scriptorium, behind the Saltline Chamber. Unauthorized replication is strictly unwise.
Observational Thesis: “The Reflection is Not You.”
There are mirrors that do not reflect.
They perform the act of reflection—but what they offer back is a version with intention. And that intention, in nearly every recorded instance, is deception.
These are the Lying Mirrors of Oghmai.
No one has successfully constructed one from scratch.

Often in ruined villas, sealed reliquaries, beneath cairns still warm with story-salt. Sometimes tucked innocently into a child’s toy chest or hanging in a market stall, priced too low and polished too well.
Their materials vary: silvered glass, polished obsidian, dark water in a still bowl, even a lacquered mask with mirrored eyes. But all share one trait—
The reflection always lies in a way that seems true.
A better version of yourself—more beautiful, braver, loved.
A stranger entirely—someone you almost were, or almost became.
A mask you once wore, now staring back with unfamiliar judgment.
It speaks. Not aloud—but through suggestion. Through micro-expressions that don’t match your own. Through timing that’s half a breath behind. Through knowledge it should not have.

In 418 of the Scroll-Turned Moon, an apprentice mirror-binder named Sela Henn tricked herself into placing a Lying Mirror above her cot. She believed it to be one of her training tools. She began conversing with her reflection nightly.
After seven days, she reported hearing her own voice speak from behind the glass after she’d stopped speaking.
On the eighth day, she attempted to smuggle the mirror into the Coralveil prayer cistern, claiming “her better self” wanted to be baptized.
She no longer responds to her name. But she hums a lullaby in a tongue we have no record of. We keep the mirror sealed behind ink-scratched lead, and it fogs every time she speaks.
You can’t always know a Lying Mirror by sight, but there are tests.
The Ink Edge Test – A circle of salt-ink is painted on the mirror’s surface. A true mirror will resist. A Lying Mirror absorbs it or causes the ink to spell words you did not write.
The Echoless Gaze – If you stare long enough and blink at a random moment, your reflection will sometimes blink just after.
The Maskless Test – When wearing a ceremonial mask of paper and wax, a Lying Mirror will still show your face. It does not like obfuscation.
Binding mirrors with wax cords that break if the glass attempts influence.
Inscribing the Rune of the Split Gaze (two offset spirals) on your forehead before viewing unknown reflections.
IV. Effects on Cognition and Memory
Subjects exposed for too long often exhibit:
Confabulated memories—insisting events happened that provably did not.
Echo speech—repeating words that were spoken by others days before.
Uncharacteristic charm or persuasion—reminiscent of Oghmai’s known traits.
Obsession with identity: repeating names, trying on old clothing, crafting new masks.
Sudden fluency in forgotten dialects—sometimes pre-First Age.
One subject began to speak only in questions and answered none, claiming:
“My reflection must finish my sentence before I know what I’ve said.”
Some believe each Lying Mirror is a fragment of Oghmai’s consciousness—a splintered thought given shape. Others suggest the mirrors are traps, laid long ago to seed his return.
I believe they are both—resonant echoes and active agents, born from the shattered truth of a spirit who weaponized story.
I also believe one exists that reflects not your face—but your voice, spoken by someone who knows your greatest regret. I pray I never find it.
If a mirror shows you what you’ve never dared imagine—
Tell no one what you saw.
Because if you say it aloud…
“When your reflection smiles first, it’s already too late.”
— Notes carved into the back of a shattered ink mirror, sealed in Vault IV.

category.en-US: THE ELDER SPIRITS\Oghmai, the Demon Emperor
THE ELDER SPIRITS\Oghmai, the Demon Emperor

content.value: Now there’s a name that rolls off the tongue like warm water down tired shoulders. Elder Gubi leans in with a creak of his shell, steam rising from his teacup and mingling with memory.
Elder Gubi-Goni chuckles gently, a sound like bubbling spring water:
“Tsubaki-Onsen, mmh. You’re asking after one of the island’s secret kindnesses. A place where even the spirits let down their masks—just for a moment.”

“They say the springs were born when Queen Okumi wept with laughter, right in the middle of winter. Her joy melted the frost, and from that giggle-spring came warmth eternal. It still flows today, high in the shoulders of the Blooming Gift, hidden behind twin camellia trees that bloom no matter the season—red and white, always together, always in bloom.”

“You’ll know you’re close when the air smells like cedar bark and wildflower soap, and the moss underfoot starts to sigh when you step on it. And then, there it is—Tsubaki-Onsen—a scatter of natural stone pools terraced into the hillside like cups waiting for tea. Steam curls up into the cherry boughs, and spirits sometimes gather at the edge of your vision, quiet as folded fans.”

“Folk of all kinships go there, though not in crowds. No, the springs seem to space you out, if you follow me. You arrive and the place is somehow already waiting for just you. Even when others are there, it feels like the world stepped back and gave you room to breathe.”

“There’s no shrine, not exactly—but someone, or something, keeps it tended. Slippers never wear out. Towels are always dry. Tea is left beside smooth river stones, still warm, always your favorite blend. No one sees who does it. I once left a thank-you note beneath a bowl of rice crackers. The next morning, I found it folded into a crane, perched on my knee.”
He sighs, eyes misting in memory.

“Once, I met an old Kaido there—steam still rising from his shoulders, eyes closed like he was listening to music no one else could hear. I asked him what he was thinking. He said, ‘Nothing. And that’s the best thing I’ve thought all year.’ Then he slipped under the water and vanished. Never saw him again. Sometimes I wonder if he was the onsen.”
Gubi swirls the last of his tea.
“Tsubaki-Onsen doesn’t heal wounds, no. But it eases the tightness inside—the kind no salve can reach. You’ll leave lighter, somehow. More yourself. Or more ready to be.”
“Even I’ve been known to soak these old bones now and again. And let me tell you—steam makes a fine storyteller of any breeze.”

category.en-US: REGIONS OF YUREI-TU-SHIMA\EMBERFLOW SPRINGS (NORTHWESTERN REGION)

content.value: Elder Gubi-Goni’s voice drops into a hush, the fire crackling low as if it too leans in to listen. He pours another cup of tea, dark as midnight, and does not sip it. He simply holds it—like one might hold a name too heavy to speak.
Elder Gubi-Goni speaks slow and soft:
“There are places on Yurei-tu-Shima where the land forgets itself. Where roots grow backwards, and birds fall silent mid-flight. The Inkfen is one of those places.”

“Down in the southern folds of the Hollow Murkway, past the cattail marshes and the sighing trees, there lies a stretch of swamp that no longer reflects the sky. Not because of clouds. But because the water is black. Not just dark—but black. A still, sucking blackness that swallows color, breath, and memory.”
“They say it is sorrow made thick.”
“They say it is Noroku’s grief—pooled and curdled, never wept fully, never laid to rest.”

“The Inkfen has no trails, not really. Only half-sunken lantern posts and broken footbridges that lean like forgotten thoughts. When the mist gathers low and the frogs hush, you’ll see her—the Ink. Not a woman. Not a spirit. A presence. She creeps through the fen like spilled paint, trailing threads behind her that vanish into reeds. If she touches your breath, you’ll forget the name of someone you love. And if you follow her?”
He looks up now, eyes glassy but sharp.
